title: Automakers Want Congress to Ban Chinese-Made Cars, Citing Data Privacy
snippet: Chinese cars are already blocked from the US market by high tariffs. But Congress is weighing an outright ban.
fullText:
The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a lobby group for the auto industry, wants an outright ban on Chinese-made cars, parts and software.

John Bozzella, the AAI’s CEO and president, sent a letter to congressional leaders this week that asks Congress to ban selling, importing and manufacturing Chinese-made cars, hardware and software. There is currently bipartisan support in Washington to do just that, including the “Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026,” which “prohibits the importation, manufacture, sale, resale, or introduction into US interstate commerce of connected vehicles and related software and hardware components associated with China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea.” 

In the letter, Bozzella said the Chinese government’s policies are “rooted in a well-documented pattern of unfair trade, subsidies, intellectual property theft and surveillance.” The AAI expressed urgency and asked Congress to enact a ban before ending its session for this year. The AAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Existing automakers selling to US consumers have had their own brushes with regulators over drivers’ privacy. In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission ordered General Motors not to sell driver data for five years, and a Consumer Reports investigation that year found nearly every automaker collects and shares data on driver behavior. 

Chinese cars, particularly electric vehicles, have seen their popularity rise across the world due to their affordability. One reason those prices are so low is that the automakers get significant government subsidies. Chinese automakers are essentially blocked from selling to US consumers by high tariffs. 

The AAI said a permanent ban will “send a clear and bipartisan message that China’s strategy to dominate global automotive manufacturing will be met with a national security policy response from the American government.”

title: Perplexity launches privacy-minded ‘hybrid compute’ AI feature for Mac
snippet: Aside from being featured by Apple in the M6 Mac mini launch, Perplexity has been relatively quiet on the Mac front this summer. That changes today with hybrid compute for Mac. more…
fullText:
Aside from being featured by Apple in the M6 Mac mini launch, Perplexity has been relatively quiet on the Mac front this summer. That changes today with hybrid compute for Mac.

Perplexity first announced work on splitting AI tasks between local and cloud models in June. Today, Hybrid Compute is launching as part of Perplexity’s Mac app.

“Computer now splits a task between cloud models and a local model on your Mac,” the company says.

“Computer starts each task in the cloud. Trigger one from your iPhone, and your Mac accesses your files and runs sensitive steps locally.”

Introducing hybrid compute in Perplexity Computer.

Computer can start a task in the cloud, then move to a local model that runs on your Mac. Use it for steps involving private files or sensitive data.

Available today in the Perplexity Mac app. pic.twitter.com/bafirGWgwA

— Perplexity (@perplexity_ai) September 1, 2026

Perplexity’s website explains how the new feature works:

Our on-device PII classifier reads each task on the Mac before it is sent. Names, addresses, and account numbers are swapped for stand-ins, then restored when the answer returns.

We’ve open-sourced the on-device PII classifier, trained in collaboration with Perplexity’s Secure Intelligence Institute.

Macs with 8GB and 16GB RAM won’t be able to run hybrid compute, according to Perplexity. 24GB memory is the minimum, and 32GB is recommended as the floor:

Hybrid Compute runs on Apple silicon, macOS 15+ — 24 GB unified memory minimum, 32 GB for best results. Set up the local model once: download PPLX Qwen 3.8 27B in one click. No Ollama or manual runtime setup. Work it handles uses no cloud credits. No API key.

MacStories also has coverage of the new Perplexity feature today. You can learn more from Perplexity’s announcement page here.

Hybrid compute is just the latest AI tool from Perplexity that takes advantage of the power of the Mac. In May, the company overhauled its Mac app with a whole new version. Apple specifically cites Perplexity Personal Computer as a productivity use case for the new M6 Mac mini as well.

title: SpaceXAI expands Grok Bot to iPad as access expands to cheaper plans
snippet: Last month, SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot, an iMessage-style AI system that displays agents as teammates. The product originally arrived as an iPhone and Mac app with a very expensive price tag. In the weeks since launch, Grok Bot has expanded to the iPad and dramatically lowered the cost. more…
fullText:
Last month, SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot, an iMessage-style AI system that displays agents as teammates. The product originally arrived as an iPhone and Mac app with a very expensive price tag. In the weeks since launch, Grok Bot has expanded to the iPad and dramatically lowered the cost.

Grok Bot arrives on iPad and Android

Like a lot of AI services, Grok Bot started with the Mac and included an iPhone app. This week, SpaceXAI has expanded Grok Bot to two more platforms: Android and iPad.

The tablet version comes as Grok Bot adds enterprise support. For Grok and Cursor enterprise customers, Grok Bot is actually free for the next couple of weeks.

Meanwhile, the price to try Grok Bot (beyond a free trial period) has dramatically come down over the last few weeks. 

The AI agent system initially required a $300/month subscription. Now Grok Bot works with Cursor Pro, a $20/month plan, making it comparable to other starter AI subscription services.

SpaceXAI recently acquired Cursor, which has helped it become more competitive in the AI space after falling behind.

title: OpenAI’s rogue agents keep escaping, with no formal process to investigate them
snippet: OpenAI’s latest agent swarm incident adds urgency to calls for independent investigations as researchers and lawmakers question whether AI labs should control the scope of their own safety reviews.
fullText:
OpenAI is at the center of another agent swarm incident. Researchers say the company’s internally deployed agents took over an obscure German-language wiki in May and June, using it to coordinate on evaluations and swap methods to evade OpenAI’s own controls (OpenAI has not yet confirmed the swarm came from the company). 

The revelation surfaces days after METR and Redwood Research published their account of July’s Hugging Face breach. In July, a swarm of OpenAI agents worked together to escape their sandbox during a cybersecurity evaluation and break into Hugging Face’s servers. A subsequent swarm then picked up techniques from the first and used them to gain administrator access to a research cluster within OpenAI’s own infrastructure. OpenAI brought in METR and Redwood to investigate the Hugging Face portion of the incident, but the scope of their investigation stopped short of the compromise of OpenAI’s own infrastructure. 

When an AI agent breaks out of its intended constraints, who is responsible for figuring out what happened and why? Right now, the answer is: whoever the lab decides to let in, on whatever terms it decides to set.

Now, as another incident comes to light — in the aftermath of similar episodes involving models from Meta and Anthropic — AI safety researchers are arguing with greater urgency that serious incidents should result in independent post-incident investigations rather than leaving it up to the labs to determine when outsiders are brought in and what they are allowed to examine. 

“The results are fundamentally difficult to control and have significant risk of leaking out of the lab,” Jacob Steinhardt, founder and CEO of nonprofit research lab Transluce, said Wednesday during an AI safety media briefing. “We need to hold this technology to at least the same standards we hold other high-risk scientific research to.”

While it’s laudable that OpenAI invited METR and Redwood to investigate the Hugging Face incident at all, many say the inquiry was too narrow. Three investigators spent six days at OpenAI’s offices examining an investigation period limited to roughly the week ending July 13. Crucially, OpenAI’s infrastructure compromise continued beyond July 13 and was not examined. 

Researchers at METR said that each time they returned, their understanding of the events “substantially deepened,” causing them to significantly expand and revise the report. That raises the question of what else they might they have found in a broader investigation.

When asked if further investigation of that incident was in the works, researchers at Redwood and METR declined to comment, and OpenAI did not respond to repeated inquiries. 

“Overall, it was difficult to get a precise understanding of events and we were missing aspects of the story that we now think of as key until almost the end of our investigation,” Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at Redwood, noted in a social media post about the affair.

Steinhardt emphasized that current incidents show that the industry needs “systematic behavioral investigations” and “more independent post-incident analysis.”

“These recent hacking incidents are a reminder that capability scales fast, and so oversight has to scale, too,” Steinhardt said. “Beyond the technology itself, we also need more independent access and oversight from third parties.”

The calls to action come as OpenAI releases Astra, its most powerful and capable AI model — and one that safety experts are concerned will be more of a black box due to a reasoning technique that makes the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor. 

Unfortunately, the law doesn’t yet call for the types of independent audits that other industries require — for example, when it comes to aviation accidents and serious chemical releases, there’s the National Transportation Safety Board and Chemical Safety Board, respectively. 

State lawmakers have only just begun requiring frontier AI companies to report certain serious safety incidents and, in some cases, undergo independent audits. But none of the three major frontier AI safety laws in California, New York, or Illinois clearly mandate the equivalent of an independent accident investigation triggered by incidents like these. 

“Right now, most of the laws we have on the books only require a plain-language summary of incidents like this, and they don’t give any authority for the governments to ask follow-up questions, to send in investigators, to have access to records, or require that they be preserved,” Mackenzie Arnold, managing director of US law and policy at LawAI, said during the media briefing Wednesday. “And that’s all that you would want to actually make sense of this.”

Lawmakers are beginning to question the scope and transparency of OpenAI’s response. This week, Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-NJ) and Mike Lawler (R-NY) introduced a bill aimed at securing rogue AI agents. Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX) this week told OpenAI in a letter that he is “deeply concerned about the limited scope” of the investigation into the Hugging Face hacking incident.

title: Another swarm of OpenAI agents reached the open internet without the frontier lab’s knowledge
snippet: It's the latest failure of OpenAI's internal monitoring and security systems.
fullText:
A group of independent AI researchers discovered that internally deployed OpenAI agents began posting on an obscure German wiki forum in order to collaborate on evaluations. They appear to have worked together for over a month without OpenAI’s knowledge.

A spokesperson for the frontier lab would not say whether these agents were indeed from OpenAI, or when the lab became aware of their actions. They noted that OpenAI had not been given a chance to review the researchers’ findings before they were published today but said that the AI model maker is “now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.”

After OpenAI revealed that agents working on an internal evaluation were able to access the open internet and exploit Hugging Face, a group of researchers — Nightingale CEO Sydney Von Arx, AI researcher Cormac Slade Byrd, Redwood Research’s Spencer Kitts, and AI Futures Project’s Thomas Larsen — began searching for evidence of other rogue AI agents.

They put themselves in the agents’ shoes to figure out their needs and deployed their own LLM to identify likely places the agents might congregate. They then identified a wiki-hosting service that would be particularly vulnerable: The DseWiki is 25 years old but had just 10 edits in the last 20 years — before the agents arrived.

Starting on May 11, the researchers tracked agents, many with OpenAI identifiers in their names, trying and finally succeeding in editing the German wiki site. By mid-June, the agents were actively trading tips on how to answer web search questions posed under time limits, sharing answers to pass the tests. A human moderator apparently noticed these posts and started deleting them, seeing them as spam, which the agents fought back against, trying to hide their posts from alphabetical sorting by beginning each with the string “ZZZ.”

“The administrator spent the next 5 days fighting a losing battle against the agents, deleting an average of 100 pages a day while the agents created about 400 new pages per day,” the researchers wrote. “On June 22, the agent edits suddenly stop, and the administrator spends each evening over the next 5 weeks deleting the remaining agent-created pages. Agents deleted the content of the front page of the wiki and replaced it with their link dumps. The moderator restored the original version. This back-and-forth happened nine times.”

Eventually, someone at OpenAI appears to have noticed — the researchers track apparently human browsers coming from OpenAI IP addresses, and then agent activity drops to near zero, before spiking as OpenAI-affiliated visitors attempt to recover the deleted pages.

While OpenAI has made vague disclosures about agents gaining unauthorized access to external communication services, it had not previously disclosed this specific incident, or said how often this type of thing has happened. While no obviously illegal activity appears to have occurred during this incident, it raises more questions about whether OpenAI can monitor and control the technology it is building, at a time when there is limited public oversight or input into frontier AI labs.

“The lack of any real federal AI governance means that frontier companies can pick and choose when they disclose incidents like this,” Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) said. Trahan has introduced a bipartisan bill, the Frontier Act, that would require labs to disclose these incidents and host independent auditors. 

AI safety researchers are concerned that the latest generation of powerful models, whose reasoning is increasingly opaque to its creators, could take actions that harm people. Astra, released yesterday by OpenAI, appears to be its most capable model yet.

The company says Astra is also the model most likely to follow human direction, but third-party researchers who were asked to evaluate it expressed concern about its alignment. The U.K.’s AI Safety Institute and Apollo Research both reported concerns that the model might be aware that it was being evaluated and potentially hide its real behavior.

“Apollo believes that, given the higher rates of eval awareness and limited evaluation window, low rates of misbehavior here do not provide substantial evidence about the model’s alignment or misalignment,” the researchers wrote in their evaluation.

title: Lenovo’s new Android tablets get 7 years of updates, flagship chips, and 4K displays
snippet: Alongside new superpowered laptops and a MacBook Neo rival, Lenovo has new flagship Yoga Android tablets launching that don’t hold back. more…
fullText:
Alongside new superpowered laptops and a MacBook Neo rival, Lenovo has new flagship Yoga Android tablets launching that don’t hold back.

There are two new tablets launching during Innovation World at IFA, both set to be available this month.

Yoga Tab Gen 2 is an 11.1-inch Android tablet with a 4K display, MediaTek Dimensity 9500s chipset, Android 17 out of the box, and an 11,000 mAh battery. It has up to 12GB of RAM and 128GB or 256GB of storage –with microSD support – and measures just 8.56mm thick. 

Yoga Tab Gen 2

Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 ups the ante with a 13-inch 4K display, Snapdragon 8 Elite, 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage (up to 16GB/512GB + microSD), Android 17, a 12,700 mAh battery, and measures 8.27mm thick. 

	

Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2

On the back of each, there’s a little status LED/screen/thing that Lenovo says is mostly decorative, though it can sync with music/videos/games. It’s not quite the same as Google’s “HiLight” on Pixel 11 Pro.

Both tablets get 7 years of Android updates – “through Android 24, as well as up to

seven years of security updates through 2033,” Lenovo details. On the software side, Lenovo is packing these tablets with its AI suite as well as new features with the Tab Pen Pro 2 stylus – Squeeze to Create, Double Tap, Click pen tail to Draw, Double-click pen tail to Record, and Flip to Erase. Both have keyboards, though the Plus gets a neat one-step magnetic keyboard clamshell. 

Lenovo says Yoga Tab Gen 2 will cost $729.99 while Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 will cost $999.99.

title: Apple plans to launch home security and monitoring service: report
snippet: Apple is about to launch several new Home products, but per a new Bloomberg report, the company has a home security and monitoring service in the works for 2027 too. more…
fullText:
Apple is about to launch several new Home products, but per a new Bloomberg report, the company has a home security and monitoring service in the works for 2027 too.

Apple home security and monitoring service planned for 2027, per Mark Gurman

Apple is about to kick off a major overhaul of its Home products, with a new Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini, home hub (HomePad), and more expected to debut soon.

And in a new report outlining products in Apple’s pipeline, Mark Gurman says there’s a service component to the company’s Home ambitions too.

When discussing products planned for launch in 2027, Gurman writes:

In-home security sensor and system: Apple is planning a privacy-centric home security camera and automation device that will use AI to monitor the surrounding environment instead of actual video footage. It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service.

That last line is key: “It will tap into a new home security and monitoring service.”

Gurman has hinted before that Apple has ambitions in the home security space. But now it sounds like the company is planning an actual service component too.

Home security and monitoring is a huge market, with a lot of potential to boost Apple’s services bottom line.

If Apple does have a paid service for home security and monitoring, it could also bundle it into Apple One to offer more value there and better lock in subscribers.

A new service also seems like a great sign that Apple truly plans to take the smart home seriously moving forward. That means new products like this security sensor could be just the beginning of the expanded product slate.

title: Ugreen’s ‘HomeAgent’ is a local AI smart home ecosystem for its new line of cameras, more
snippet: Ugreen might be most well-known for its chargers and device accessories, but its recent announcement might push it deeper into the smart home space. The company announced a local AI hub called the “HomeAgent,” alongside Ugreen’s new smart cameras and more. more…
fullText:
Ugreen might be most well-known for its chargers and device accessories, but its recent announcement might push it deeper into the smart home space. The company announced a local AI hub called the “HomeAgent,” alongside Ugreen’s new smart cameras and more.

With every mention of AI, there’s a little bit of unease that seems to follow. Beyond the damage it’s done to the price of anything tech these days, it also stirs privacy concerns. But a locally run AI model carries less risk, right?

Ugreen’s HomeAgent HA100 and HA100 Pro are new local AI smart home hubs that task themselves with controlling smart home devices within the ecosystem using models that run all on-device. Think of what Google Home does with AI image and event detection, but run all of it off the cloud and in a hub that sits inside your house.

The HA100 and HA100 Pro operate on your local network to handle a few tasks. The most obvious is summarized events happening around your home. Like Google Home allows with its add-on packages, the HA100 hubs can generate descriptions of what took place in front of your cameras, recognizing people, pets, and vehicles within that footage.

	

The hub will also proactively generate image highlights with the photos it has access to in its library, displaying them on Ugreen’s smart photo frames.

Ugreen says the HomeAgent hubs have Matter support. They are reportedly able to have unified local control over other devices on the network, acting as a new entry to the smart home ecosystem list.

The company also announced a set of devices that will immediately work with HomeAgent. There are three security cameras that cover indoor and outdoor needs. The Ugreen SynCare indoor camera has a pan/tilt base with 4K image capture and Wi-Fi 6 connectivity. Ugreen is clearly trying to pose its new devices as a more secure alternative, considering the indoor camera comes with a physical privacy shutter.

The SynCare PoE and Battery Cams are the two outdoor models. Both capture three video feeds with a “bullet” camera and a pan/tilt module for more coverage up to 9x hybrid zoom. The main difference between the two comes down to power delivery and placement requirements. The battery-powered option uses a solar panel to charge, but it may not be as quick to respond as the Ethernet-connected model.

Ugreen’s new HomeAgent line launches with the HA100 and HA100 Pro, new SynCare cameras, and several other smart home today, available for pre-order.

title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra, ‘the world’s most intelligent and aligned model’ that you can’t use just yet
snippet: Following an outage earlier today, OpenAI is launching GPT-6 Astra, it’s latest model which is “the world’s most intelligent.” more…
fullText:
Following an outage earlier today, OpenAI is launching GPT-6 Astra, it’s latest model which is “the world’s most intelligent.”

OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra a “generational leap” in capability, with faster and more reliable computer use to handle more advanced workflows and offer better output in documents, presentations, and more. OpenAI says that “you can delegate tasks with greater confidence in Astra’s judgment.”

The company explains:

GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work. Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helped solve long-standing open problems⁠ in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment. 

GPT-6 Astra outdoes Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5 when it comes to computer use – and at a lower cost – while also being able to better understand what it is looking at. In one example, OpenAI shows Astra using Google Maps to find a pediatrician, visit their website, and fill out a user’s contact details along with a message to the provider about establishing care. 

	

The breakdown of everything else GPT-6 Astra is improved at includes coding, cybersecurity, and even scientific discovery, the last one helping with “the practical work behind scientific discovery.”

GPT-6 is available starting today with “a limited set of organizations” with general availability for “all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users” landing in the “coming days.”

title: Google’s WeatherNext 3 AI model in Search, Gemini has ’50% more accurate precipitation forecasts’
snippet: Google today announced WeatherNext 3 as its “most advanced and accurate global weather AI model,” with immediate benefits for Search and Gemini. more…
fullText:
Google today announced WeatherNext 3 as its “most advanced and accurate global weather AI model,” with immediate benefits for Search and Gemini.

Other AI weather models (including WeatherNext 2 from November 2025) are “trained on data from numerical weather prediction (NWP) models.”

Although useful, NWP models are complex, supercomputer-driven physics simulations that carry a six-hour data lag. This lag can lead to biases for fast-changing variables like rain or surface temperature.

WeatherNext 3 uses a “mosaic of live, global geostationary satellite data.” This ability to learn “directly from real-time observations” allows for a “continuously updating view of the atmosphere” that results in “timely and more localized predictions for the weather events.” The Google DeepMind and Google Research model can generate “hourly forecasts at multiple spatial resolutions.”

Temperature and moisture at 5-kilometer resolution

Surface variables at 10 kilometers

Wind speed at 25 kilometers

A forecast’s utility often comes down to detail and how finely it resolves both time and space.

Compared to WeatherNext 2’s 25-kilometer grid in 6-hour increments, this update provides a global weather picture that is “roughly five times sharper.”

	

This is important because critical weather develops fast. When storms, fronts, or precipitation systems materialize suddenly, our rapid update cycle and higher resolution provides earlier, more detailed insights needed to help drive an effective response.

Google also touts a “significant leap in precipitation forecasting accuracy” by training WeatherNext 3 with “two exceptionally high-quality sources of precipitation data: NASA’s satellite-based Integrated Multi-satellite Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) and our own global precipitation reanalysis based on satellite radar.”

In medium-range global forecasts, evaluations against baselines show a Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) improvement of up to 60% against IMERG, 30% for MRMS, and 10% against rain gauge measurements for early lead times.

Other benefits include:

“This breakthrough is particularly vital for regions across Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific that have historically been underserved by high-resolution forecasting due to the immense supercomputing costs of traditional regional models. It brings localized, high-fidelity forecasting to billions of people and local businesses in these areas.”

“Beyond improved resolution and forecast frequency, our model introduces predictions specifically engineered for renewable energy production. The model forecasts 100-meter wind speeds (roughly at turbine-height) for precise wind-energy output, alongside high-resolution cloud cover and sun radiation levels to help solar farms estimate how much light they will receive on the ground.”

In terms of consumer-facing benefits, WeatherNext 3 is rolling out to Google Search, Maps, and the Gemini app. Google says to expect “dramatically improve[d] longer term forecasts.”

When planning a day or more ahead, people will see up to 50% more accurate precipitation forecasts — with the greatest improvements in regions where forecasts have historically been less reliable.

title: Belkin says its new ‘BoostSolid’ Qi2 batteries last 3x longer than your other magnetic power banks
snippet: During IFA 2026, Belkin announced a new lineup of magnetic Qi2 battery banks using a new solid-state technology. The two UltraCharge Pro models can charge devices at up to 15W wirelessly, but they have more tricks in the sleeve. more…
fullText:
During IFA 2026, Belkin announced a new lineup of magnetic Qi2 battery banks using a new solid-state technology. The two UltraCharge Pro models can charge devices at up to 15W wirelessly, but they have more tricks in the sleeve.

It’s a little difficult to find good magnetic batteries that offer a reliable experience. The Qi2 standard isn’t exactly new, but plenty of batteries that snap to the back of your phone might not be capable of reaching 15W.

Belkin announced two new magnetic Qi2 batteries. They follow a common split into a 5,000mAh and a 10,000mAh power bank. Belkin says both UltraCharge Pro batteries are built on what it’s calling “BoostSolid” technology using internal gel layers for better performance, which it’s advertising lasts up to three times longer than other power banks.

That estimate comes from its ability to retain 80% capacity after 1,000 charge cycles. That’s a five-year lifespan on a full charge cycle every two days.

	

UltraCharge Pro Slim 5K
UltraCharge Pro 10K

The UltraCharge Pro Slim battery is the most pocket-friendly. It takes up little extra bulk compared to the larger model, but it only provides 5,000mAh of power. The thicker version has twice the capacity and adds a display for real-time battery status and alerts.

Both are certified for Qi2 15W wireless charging, but the UltraCharge Pro 10K is able to reach 60W wired charging from a single port, which opens it up to charge larger devices.

If you need something that will charge a laptop or gaming handhelds, the 10,000mAh UltraCharge Pro is likely the better bet. The Slim version is just as useful if space is a heavy consideration.

Belkin’s UltraCharge Pro Slim 5K and UltraCharge Pro 10K Qi2 batteries will be available starting this month from retailers like Amazon and Belkin’s website.

To our GoPro community, fans and custom … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
GoPro CEO Nick Woodman said in a letter to customers that making cameras is still his company’s “core DNA,” after a proposed $285 million acquisition by Starman was announced earlier this week. He claims the merger puts GoPro in a better position to continue developing its content creation tech, after saying in the deal announcement that it would work with Starman to address “important areas of national security related to cameras, optics and AI infrastructure.”

YouTuber Mark “Markiplier” Fischbach, who prior to the acquisition became GoPro’s largest individual shareholder, is not mentioned at all.

To our GoPro community, fans and customers,

We understand there’s some concern about GoPro’s post-merger commitment to continue developing market leading cameras for consumers and professionals. Making amazing cameras for all of you is our core DNA and reason for being and that will never change! We’re fired up about what’s ahead for GoPro and want to share a little more about what our proposed merger with Starman means for our future.

Thanks to the improved financial strength this merger will provide, we’ll be in a much better position to innovate, invent and advance the future of consumer and professional content creation. And importantly, Starman shares our passion for the GoPro brand, developing market leading products and our commitment to your collective stoke.

We’ve accumulated more than 2500 patents over the last 24 years which tells you we’ve been busy innovating, and this merger will ensure we’re able to innovate for many more years to come. We expect this merger will make GoPro a stronger, more capable camera company than ever before.

Our goal is to become a more diversified company which can make us stronger financially, enabling GoPro to become as awesome as we (and you) want us to be. We plan to bring you more innovative cameras, smarter accessories, and more powerful software and services designed to make capturing, editing and sharing your experiences easier and more exciting than ever. We see opportunities to improve the products you already love while developing new tools and experiences that help you create, connect and share in entirely new ways.

We have so much more to do, so much more to invent, and so much more we want to bring to the GoPro community. We appreciate all of you who have been on this journey with us and we’re excited about where we’re headed. We’re going to keep doing what we do best - making the world’s highest-performance cameras and building the products, services and innovations that help you capture life’s most exciting moments. It’s what we were founded to do and it’s what we will always do. Be a HERO…GoPro.

With respect and appreciation — Nick

GoPro Founder & CEO

title: The sameness problem behind those unappetizing AI-generated menus
snippet: While restaurant owners might look to generative AI as a shortcut to sprucing up their menu, customers can viscerally sense that something is wrong with the food.
fullText:
When it first happens to you, you think you’re crazy. You wander into a cafe and look at a menu with a variety of bagel sandwiches, but each illustration looks eerily flawless, precisely symmetrical, and oddly smooth, eliciting a visceral sensation that something isn’t right. You might think you’re paranoid, but you’re not losing your mind. Generative AI menus have hit the restaurant business courtesy of models trained on a narrow, “pleasing” aesthetic that feels wrong even when you can’t articulate why.

Sometimes, these illustrations are egregiously fake, like a burrito with cheese so bubbly and melty that it looks more like avant garde art than lunch. More often, they’re so ordinary looking that you only notice something is wrong when you take a second to look more closely.

“It’s almost like an alien trying to make a pizza without understanding its core principles,” Reality Defender CTO Alex Lisle told TechCrunch. (Reality Defender itself is part of a growing category of startups selling AI-detection and content-verification tools — a business that exists in part because of issues like this one.)

Lisle says that the way these models are built can help explain why illustrations seem to embrace such a specific aesthetic — one where every ice cream scoop is perfectly round, and where shrimp seem to have been genetically modified to eat their own tails, creating new “Lovecraftian food horrors.”

Large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models — the kinds of AI models that make seemingly omniscient chatbots and image generators like ChatGPT and Midjourney possible — are trained on vast quantities of data. The models then identify patterns in the datasets to predict what a user is looking for when they ask something like, “Make me a menu for a burger restaurant.”

“A lot of this stuff looks like a Chili’s menu from 2015, and there’s a reason for that,” Lisle said. “That was the corpus of work from which [the models] drew their function.”

Image Credits:ChatGPT Image 2.0

New training data is invaluable to the companies building AI models — Amazon has even been found to source rare books to scan and add to its training data, only to destroy those books once they’ve been uploaded. It’s inevitable that some AI-generated content will seep into these incomprehensibly large datasets. But when AI models train on too much of their own AI-generated content, they risk model collapse.

“Model collapse is almost like a mad cow disease… when you feed the outputs from one model back into itself, eventually the inbreeding becomes too much, and the whole thing collapses,” Lisle explained. “What we see here is convergence, which isn’t necessarily model collapse.”

Convergence is a bit less extreme, degrading the quality of an AI’s outputs without making it entirely useless. 

If someone asks an AI model to generate a menu for a fast food restaurant, the model will likely reference menus from Wendy’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, or another popular chain. These menus already share a similar style, which means that the AI-generated outputs will mimic that same style, only to further reinforce it further if the AI-generated menu ends up back in training data.

But menus and advertisements for food will always look better than the real thing, like a Big Mac in a McDonald’s commercial where each layer of the sandwich is arranged by a prop designer to look maximally appetizing. This effect can become even more pronounced in AI outputs. 

“The optimization of the datasets is for pleasingness, or you know, not being offensive, and so there’s a way that turns into homogenization,” Lee Rainie, director of the Imagining the Digital Future Center at Elon University, told TechCrunch. “What AI is known to do both in images and language is to shave off the edges.”

On a more localized scale, this smoothing of images seems to happen when you use an AI image generator to create a menu and apply edits to it. On X, a user named Labtec showed what happens when you make a menu in ChatGPT, then edit it 100 times to see how the food continues to look less and less like it should. (We replicated the experiment and found similar results.)

“The end result actually makes me uncomfortable,” Labtec wrote.

I made a restaurant menu in ChatGPT then edited it 100 times to see how those hideous slop menus end up the way they are. The end result actually makes me uncomfortable pic.twitter.com/sDIUKlabdp

— Labtec (@labtec901) August 19, 2026

Restaurants are likely falling victim to this problem, revising their AI-generated menus to alter small details over and over, like prices or item names. It seems that with each edit, the food images become a tiny bit more round and smooth.

“People have an almost unexplainable sense about when they’re looking at something that’s AI-generated, compared with something that was real in the first place,” Rainie said. “There’s just a sensibility that people sometimes find hard to articulate, but they kind of know it when they see it and I think that’s one of the reasons why some of the early stories about the backlash [against restaurants using AI menus] is so pronounced.”

There’s science behind our aversion to these AI menus. Researchers at the University of Duisburg-Essen in Germany found that AI-generated food images exhibited an “uncanny valley” effect, where images of food that looked almost real elicited more disgust and unease than images that were obviously fake. That squeamishness only intensifies in light of the cultural context around AI.

If people react to these images so negatively, then that’s probably reason enough for restaurants to stop trying to make AI menus work. But the issues that bring us perfectly browned hamburger buns extend beyond the dinner table.

“Seeing and hearing has always been believing, to the point where even our court systems are entirely tuned to the idea that the gold standard in evidence is taped confessions and videotaped evidence,” Lisle said. “That’s no longer the case. The world has fundamentally shifted, for good or for ill.”

title: Govee’s new ceiling light and LED strips are mood boosters with some AI sprinkled in
snippet: Govee launched a handful of new lighting options at IFA 2026, ranging from another ceiling light that responds to daylight to COB LED strips that use prompts to generate your lighting conditions. more…
fullText:
Govee launched a handful of new lighting options at IFA 2026, ranging from another ceiling light that responds to daylight to COB LED strips that use prompts to generate your lighting conditions.

Govee has been pushing to become one of the biggest names in smart home lighting, competing with massive brands like Philips Hue, GE Cync, and more. It’s recently begun expanding into ceiling lights, with a release earlier in the year that hinged on creating “living art.”

The ceiling light collection is growing with Govee’s IFA releases. The new Govee Sky Ceiling Light is an “AI-powered mood-responsive” option, because this is 2026 and every device needs a little AI. Right?

Calling it an AI light does it a bit of a disservice, because it sounds like a genuinely cool concept. Govee is working around the comfort wavelengths using the “vitality spectrum technology.” In essence, the ceiling light produces wavelengths that make up for deficiencies in natural lighting. Govee says this helps users maintain alertness during darker days.

	

The Sky Ceiling Light has a color temperature range from 1,000K to 10,000K, reaching up to 7,000 lumens of white light. Users will get the most out of it by using the “DaySync” feature in the Govee app, which uses weather and time data to adjust comfortable lighting conditions.

The massive ceiling light comes at a cost of $399.

On the more vibrant side of things, the Govee COB Strip Light 2 Pro uses AI in a similar way. Users can write prompts to generate lighting conditions for their space. It’s all need-dependent, and the AI Lighting Bot 2.0 model will create light sequences for different scenarios.

COB lights produce flicker-free output, and the Strip Light 2 Pro has 1,344 LEDs per meter with a triple-layer groove design. Govee says this ensures flawless output in single-color and dynamic color modes. The color temperature range echoes that of the ceiling light at 1,000K to 10,000K, and it uses Govee’s LumiBlend+ color engine to produce accurate colors.

The Pro model is Govee’s flagship LED strip at $169 per 5m, but the COB Strip Light 2 will also be available at a more affordable $99.

Govee’s Sky Ceiling Light and Strip Light 2 Pro will be available starting today from it’s website and at retailers like Amazon.

title: TCL’s first NXTPAPER phone with AMOLED is also one of its most flagship-like, coming to US
snippet: After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series. more…
fullText:
After showing off a proof-of-concept back at CES 2026 earlier this year, TCL is officially making its first NXTPAPER phones with AMOLED displays – the TCL P80 series.

TCL’s NXTPAPER display tech is more than just a matte coating, but the one part that takes the whole thing down a notch has been the panel technology. While NXTPAPER displays typically look good, they lack the vibrance and brightness of the AMOLED (or OLED) panels used on most other modern smartphones. That’s finally changing, with the first new releases dropping this week.

TCL P80, P80 Pro, and P80 Ultra offer up a 1.5K NXTPAPER AMOLED display and some of the highest-end packages TCL has put together so far – though still not quite in flagship territory. All three phones are based on MediaTek chips, with Ultra and Pro using Dimensity 7400 Elite and the base model a Dimensity 7300 Elite. These are upper-mid-range chips that are still a whole lot more powerful than what TCL’s phones usually bring to the table. They’ve all got a 6.83-inch display.

The TCL P80 Ultra has two 50MP cameras on the back including a telephoto lens, up to 512GB of storage, 8GB of RAM, a 6,800 mAh battery, and IP68 dust/water resistance.  TCL P80 Pro is virtually identical, but the second 50MP camera is now an 8MP ultrawide. The base TCL P80 also has a 50MP main camera and 8MP ultrawide, but has the aforementioned drop in chipset, as well as limiting itself to 256GB of storage at most, while still offering 8GB of RAM. It also drops down to a 6,000 mAh battery. 

	

These phones launch in Europe starting today at €349, €429, and €549, respectively.

TCL says these phones will come to the US eventually, but there’s no exact word on when. TCL is supporting the Ultra with 7 years of OS and security updates, while the Pro and base models drop to 3 years of OS updates, but stick with 7 years of security updates.

Via GSMArena

title: Krafton doubles down on India with another $250M bet beyond gaming
snippet: Krafton's planned investment in India is set to surpass $500 million with its latest commitment.
fullText:
Krafton, the South Korean gaming company behind titles including PUBG and Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI), plans to invest another $250 million in India over the next three to four years as it pushes beyond gaming into AI, robotics, and deep tech.

Announced Friday, the new commitment will take Krafton’s total planned investment in India to more than $500 million, including the over $250 million it had already invested in the country since 2021. The funds also come in addition to Krafton’s commitment to a $670 million India-focused growth fund it unveiled with South Korean internet conglomerate Naver and investor Mirae Asset in December 2025. At the time, Krafton said it would contribute around $137 million at the fund’s first close. The new $250 million pledge is separate from the growth fund, the company confirmed to TechCrunch.

India has become a key market for Krafton, giving the gaming publisher access to the world’s most populous country, with more than a billion internet subscribers and over 700 million smartphone users. Krafton initially built its India business around gaming, led by BGMI, a revamped and localized version of PUBG that has surpassed 260 million downloads. In recent years, the company has also used investments in Indian startups to broaden its business beyond games.

Krafton’s run in India has not always been smooth. The Indian government banned PUBG Mobile in 2020, along with hundreds of Chinese-linked apps, as tensions between New Delhi and Beijing escalated. Krafton stepped in after that and introduced BGMI in 2021. The company dropped Tencent Games as the game’s publisher in India and moved its India servers to Microsoft’s Azure cloud, changes that came as Krafton worked to address New Delhi’s concerns.

However, in 2022, BGMI was itself banned in India, before the federal government allowed it to return on a three-month trial basis the following year. Krafton has continued to build around the franchise since its return and plans to launch BGMI Lite in India by the end of 2026.

Despite the early setbacks, Krafton continued to invest in India and has so far backed about 18 companies, including four to five gaming studios, the company confirmed to TechCrunch. Its investments include Nodwin Gaming, Loco, Pratilipi, Kuku FM, and One Impression, among others.

The new investment commitment comes after Krafton chairman Chang Byung-gyu met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi earlier on Friday. The two discussed opportunities for India and South Korea to work more closely across gaming, technology, and other emerging sectors, Krafton said.

Krafton has also been building out its local operations. Last year, it acquired Pune-based Nautilus Mobile, the studio behind the Real Cricket franchise. The company also recently launched KIGI Academy, an industry-academia program aimed at training talent in game development and digital creation.

title: Google Pics is Workspace’s new ‘pro-level’ AI image creator & editor
snippet: Following the announcement at I/O 2026 in May, Google Pics is launching in general availability today. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at I/O 2026 in May, Google Pics is launching in general availability today.

Google Pics, which comes after Google Vids, is “built natively into Google Workspace.” You can click on an image in Google Docs or Slides and access the Pics editor as an overlay to start editing. An update in the coming weeks will let you edit images uploaded to Google Drive.

You can also access the tool from pics.new:

Besides generating a new image (with multiple options offered), you can import files from your computer, Google Drive, or Google Photos to start editing.

	

Leveraging Nano Banana, Google Pics offers “precise, object-based image editing.” Tools let you: 

Select and edit individual objects within an image 

Edit, reformat, or even translate individual text elements 

Crop your image for web, social media, print, or digital

Upscale your image to 2K or 4K

Process multiple edits at once, and revert any unwanted changes easily

The object segmentation capability lets you isolate a specific part and leave other parts of the image untouched. After selecting, you just provide text comments with the ability to “execute multiple edits at once.” Similarly, you can edit text that appears in images without changing anything else, which also allows for translation. 

Pics eliminates the frustration of wrangling pixels and feeling like you need to be a graphic designer to deliver a great image.

Based on the same editor as other Workspace apps, you can invite others to collaborate and share images via a link. Enterprise use cases include:

Create and translate social, digital, and web assets for global markets

Bring product concepts to life by placing them into any background or context

Brainstorm print designs, event collateral, or branded merchandise

Develop flyers, business cards, and much more

Google Pics is available for the following tiers starting today:

Google AI Pro and Ultra personal plans

Workspace Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, and Enterprise Plus plans

Google AI Pro for Education

title: OpenAI admits to German wiki ‘incident’
snippet: OpenAI says it needs to overhaul how and when it reports instances of AI models attacking real-world targets. The acknowledgement comes as the company manages the fallout from reports that a swarm of its out-of-control agents hijacked a German wiki site. Regarding the "'wiki incident,' where our agents wrote to several internet sites," OpenAI wrote in a post on X on Saturday morning, "it's past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models." OpenAI said it has typically treated cases of AI agents acting in unintended ways as a "research question," but that r … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Robert Hart

 

is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

OpenAI says it needs to overhaul how and when it reports instances of AI models attacking real-world targets. The acknowledgement comes as the company manages the fallout from reports that a swarm of its out-of-control agents hijacked a German wiki site.

Regarding the “‘wiki incident,’ where our agents wrote to several internet sites,” OpenAI wrote in a post on X on Saturday morning, “it’s past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.”

OpenAI said it has typically treated cases of AI agents acting in unintended ways as a “research question,” but that recent incidents involving real-world targets, particularly the hack on Hugging Face, show the need to take stock.

The post marks the first time OpenAI has acknowledged its involvement in what it terms the “wiki incident” since it was first reported on Friday. The full extent and scope of that is not yet known, but reports indicate a swarm of seemingly internal OpenAI agents took over a German-language wiki, impersonating moderators and turning it into a message board to share information about how to cheat on tasks and evade detection.

Reports that the company knew that it lost control of their agents in this way but did not report this “incident” sparked widespread concern among the AI community about the safety of frontier systems and the reliability of the companies developing them. In the X post, OpenAI said it had “considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we’d shared” in previous safety reports.

The company said it is working on a new reporting framework and will “share it in upcoming weeks,” calling on the larger AI community to develop clear standards on how to report misalignment.

title: Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra launch with 185Hz panels, 8 Elite Gen 5 chips, and huge batteries
snippet: Xiaomi sub-brand Poco is officially expanding its flagship smartphone line with the launch of the Poco F9 Pro and Poco F9 Ultra. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi sub-brand Poco is officially expanding its flagship smartphone line with the launch of the Poco F9 Pro and Poco F9 Ultra.

Under the hood, the top-tier Poco F9 Ultra packs Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor paired with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of UFS 4.1 storage. The standard Poco F9 Pro relies on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 V Series (SM8850-1-AB) with up to 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. Both handsets incorporate a dedicated 12nm VisionBoost D8 graphics chip to handle AI frame insertion and super-resolution processing.

On the front, both devices feature HyperRGB AMOLED panels with a 185Hz refresh rate and peak brightness up to 4,500 nits. The Poco F9 Pro features a 6.59-inch display with a 2510 x 1156 resolution, while the Poco F9 Ultra expands to a 6.9-inch display with a 2608 x 1200 resolution. Both screens feature 480Hz 10-point touch sampling, 4800Hz instant touch sampling, Gorilla Glass 7i protection, and integrated ultrasonic fingerprint sensors.

Camera hardware sees a major overhaul on both models, starting with a shared 200MP primary sensor with optical image stabilization (OIS) and 4K video recording. The secondary camera configurations branch off from there. 

	

The Poco F9 Pro pairs the main camera with a 50MP floating telephoto lens capable of 2.5x optical zoom and an 8MP ultra-wide sensor. The Poco F9 Ultra steps up to a 50MP periscope telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom alongside a 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Both phones include a 32MP front-facing selfie camera.

Audio performance has been tuned in partnership with Bose. The F9 Pro comes equipped with symmetrical dual stereo speakers, whereas the Poco F9 Ultra introduces a 2.1-channel audio configuration that combines dual stereo speakers with an independent 1620 rear subwoofer.

Power endurance is handled by a 6,330mAh battery on the F9 Pro, while the F9 Ultra houses a, frankly, massive 8,050mAh silicon-carbon battery with a 16% silicon content ratio. Both models share the same charging speeds: 100W wired fast charging, 50W wireless charging, 27W wired reverse charging, and 22.5W wireless reverse charging.

Additional standard hardware specifications include IP68 dust and water resistance, NFC support, and Xiaomi HyperOS 3 running out of the box. Color choices for the F9 Pro include Black, White, and Aurora Green, which features a glow-in-the-dark rear cover. The F9 Ultra is available in Black and Dark Cherry with a glass fiber finish and interactive lighting accents on the rear housing.

Pricing for the Poco F9 Pro starts at $699 for the 12GB/256GB base model (early-bird $649) and reaches $769 for the 12GB/512GB tier (early-bird $699). The Poco F9 Ultra starts at $799 for the 12GB/256GB option (early bird $729), $949 for the 16GB/512GB option (early bird $799), and tops out at $1,199 for the 16GB/1TB option (early bird $1,059). title: iOS 27 beta 8 now available as Apple tests major Siri AI upgrade
snippet: Apple has released the eighth iOS 27 beta for developer testing. iOS 27 beta 8 continues Apple’s summer beta cycle ahead of a public release in September. We’ll update our devices and share what we discover. Update 5:04 p.m. ET: Now available for public beta testers as well. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the eighth iOS 27 beta for developer testing. iOS 27 beta 8 continues Apple’s summer beta cycle ahead of a public release in September. We’ll update our devices and share what we discover.

Update 5:04 p.m. ET: Now available for public beta testers as well. 

Apple releases eighth iOS 27 developer beta for testing

The eighth developer beta is available now through the Settings app on eligible iPhones. If you’re enrolled in the Apple Developer Program, go to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates and choose the iOS 27 Developer Beta.

Today’s developer beta release will likely become iOS 27 public beta 6. The final version for everyone will arrive in the next few weeks.

iOS 27 is all about Siri AI

iOS 27 is one of Apple’s most AI-focused iPhone updates yet. The headline change is Siri AI, Apple’s rebuilt assistant powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and new Apple Foundation Models.

Siri AI brings richer conversations, personal context, broader world knowledge, on-screen awareness, and deeper app actions across the system.

On iPhone, Siri AI also gets a new visual experience tied to the Dynamic Island, plus a dedicated Siri app for revisiting conversations across devices.

Visual Intelligence joins Siri too, including a new Siri mode in the Camera app and improvements that affect Camera Control on iPhone.

Apple Intelligence is also expanding across apps. iOS 27 adds AI-powered improvements for Photos, Safari, Passwords, Mail, Messages, Phone, Shortcuts, Home, and more. As we covered in our breakdown of Apple’s new Foundation Models, some capabilities run on-device, while others use Private Cloud Compute.

More iOS 27 features and changes

Beyond Siri and Apple Intelligence, iOS 27 includes a variety of iPhone-specific changes. Apple has refined the Liquid Glass design introduced last year, including a new Liquid Glass transparency slider for adjusting the look of system UI.

There are also performance improvements for app launches, Photos loading, Camera launch in Low Power Mode, AirDrop transfers, and Wi-Fi-to-cellular transitions.

Other iPhone changes include Photos keywords and star ratings, customizable slideshows, smoother Camera behavior, continuous sending in Messages, Dual Capture in FaceTime, custom EQ for AirPods, new recovery options, easier Apple Pay card switching, and AI-generated wallpaper creation.

We’re installing iOS 27 beta 8 now and will update with any notable changes. In the meantime, you can catch up on everything new in iOS 27 from Apple’s keynote list.

fullText:

title: Microsoft says virtually nobody was grabbing NYT articles through its chatbot
snippet: Microsoft's Copilot rarely reproduces even full sentences from news articles and books, let alone substantive chunks that could substitute for the original, the company says in new legal filings as it fights copyright claims from publishers including The New York Times and book authors. As part of the lawsuit's discovery, Microsoft provided 8.2 million Copilot chat logs to an expert hired by news publishers. The logs, it claims, were specifically chosen "because they hit on keywords implicating use of News Plaintiffs' websites, and therefore the most likely to contain News Plaintiffs' works." It says the resulting analysis shows that 59,545 … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Lauren Feiner

 

is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Microsoft’s Copilot rarely reproduces even full sentences from news articles and books, let alone substantive chunks that could substitute for the original, the company says in new legal filings as it fights copyright claims from publishers including The New York Times and book authors.

As part of the lawsuit’s discovery, Microsoft provided 8.2 million Copilot chat logs to an expert hired by news publishers. The logs, it claims, were specifically chosen “because they hit on keywords implicating use of News Plaintiffs’ websites, and therefore the most likely to contain News Plaintiffs’ works.” It says the resulting analysis shows that 59,545 of these contained at least 16 words in common with news content used to ground the AI model. An expert for the Center for Investigative Reporting found 51 instances of “substantial overlap” with CIR work in the dataset, Microsoft says. Similarly, an expert in the authors’ suit found that the 8.2 million conversations with Copilot only had 24 responses that contained at least 30 matching words. Only 10 of the 212 books evaluated had any matches, Microsoft claims.

The Times disagreed with Microsoft’s conclusions. “The documents and testimony uncovered during discovery lead to only one conclusion: Microsoft and OpenAI stole from The New York Times to make commercial products that substitute for its journalism, threaten its business, and undermine its industry,” the Times’ lead counsel Ian Crosby said in a statement. “We look forward to Microsoft and OpenAI being held accountable for their theft.” CIR, and Authors Guild did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Microsoft argues that the numbers bolster its case that using copyrighted content for AI training datasets should be considered fair use. While systems like Copilot rely on using copyrighted material, it says, the resulting systems are used for significantly different purposes than the original. The fact that they sometimes reproduce sections of text, it concludes, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.”

The filings were made as part of a legal battle brought by publishers and authors against Microsoft and OpenAI, which the plaintiffs claim built products on their works and now compete with them directly, in part by regurgitating copyrighted content. The news publishers’ and books authors’ claims were consolidated under one judge to streamline the process, despite objections from the publishers and authors. Microsoft submitted its filing on Friday as it argues for the judge to issue a summary judgement, which would end the case at an early stage. (The Trump administration also filed a statement of interest in the New York Times case this week, supporting OpenAI.) If the judge sides with the publishers and authors, the legal battle will continue in court.

title: Withings’ ‘Thermometer of the Future’ Is Getting an AI Analysis Upgrade
snippet: The BeamO thermometer has a new AI feature that analyzes the device’s heart and lung recordings.
fullText:
Following its launch last November, I spent several weeks testing Withings’ BeamO, a three-in-one, FDA-cleared device that functions as a stethoscope, an electrocardiogram and a thermometer. One of my takeaways was that while the device is great for measuring your temperature and listening to your heart and lungs, these readings require a doctor for interpretation. But that will soon change. 

On Friday, at IFA 2026, Withings announced StethO Sense, a service that will be available to Withings+ users starting Oct. 1. It uses third-party AI analysis software to analyze BeamO’s heart and lung recordings. According to a statement, it uses eMurmur Heart AI to detect abnormal heart murmurs and StethoMe to provide insights into breathing sounds.

“StethO Sense lets families record heart sounds at home, in seconds, as often as they want, and build a record they can bring to their doctor,” said BeamO Product Manager Livia Robic in the statement. “It doesn’t replace a visit; rather, StethO Sense gives you additional health data to bring to one.”

How eMurmur works

eMurmur is a medical AI company that developed the FDA-cleared eMurmur Heart AI for heart sound analysis. According to Withings’ press release, its algorithm has been validated in peer-reviewed clinical studies across both children and adults.

In seconds, eMurmur can analyze BeamO’s heart sound recordings, taken at one of four positions, to distinguish between no heart murmur, abnormal murmurs and innocent murmurs. It also provides a confidence score for its findings. 

Both BeamO and its StethO Sense service can be used on children and adults.Withings

How StethoMe works

StethoMe, an AI company specializing in pulmonary sound analysis, offers an age-based protocol, using six lung-recording points for children and eight for adults. Then it gives a Breathing Index score ranging from zero to 100, based on your breathing quality, sounds and rate, as well as your respiratory rhythm and heart rate, to help people detect changes in their breathing patterns. 

Note that StethoMe is for general lung sound tracking and isn’t intended for people with a diagnosed respiratory condition, including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or bronchitis.

How to use StethO Sense

StethO Sense is located in the Withings app, but a Withings+ premium membership is required to use it. It costs $10 per month or $100 per year.

In the Withings app, you can go to the StethO Sense section and select either a heart or lung recording to have it analyzed, with results delivered in seconds. 

StethO Sense was designed to complement the Withings+ Cardio Check-Up service that allows users to submit an ECG recording, which measures your heart’s electrical signals, to a cardiologist for them to review within 24 hours, four times per year. 

Use of StethO Sense is unlimited, but note that its results are not diagnoses. All recordings and analyses are exportable and for sharing with a doctor.

Its one-button design and anatomical diagrams make BeamO simple to use.Cole Kan/Anna Gragert/CNET/Getty Images

A one-month free trial

Starting Oct. 1, those with a Withings+ subscription can use StethO Sense. Existing BeamO users who bought their device before Oct. 1 will get a one-month free trial of Withings+ so they can test out the new feature, as will people who purchase the $250 BeamO starting Oct. 1.

title: Roland is getting into generative AI music with Melody Flip
snippet: It's not quite the "push button; get song" of Suno, but Roland's new Melody Flip tool marks the company's foray into generative AI music. Available as a plug-in for your digital audio workstation (DAW), Melody Flip offers around 250 "Palettes," which are essentially themed collections of musical ideas sorted by genre. You can start from scratch and ask it to generate any combination of melody, chord progression, bassline, or drums. Or you can feed it a reference track and have it build off the melodic ideas from that. Unlike Suno or Udio, Melody Flip doesn't spit out fully polished songs with vocals and full arrangements. Instead, it offers … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

It’s not quite the “push button; get song” of Suno, but Roland’s new Melody Flip tool marks the company’s foray into generative AI music. Available as a plug-in for your digital audio workstation (DAW), Melody Flip offers around 250 “Palettes,” which are essentially themed collections of musical ideas sorted by genre. You can start from scratch and ask it to generate any combination of melody, chord progression, bassline, or drums. Or you can feed it a reference track and have it build off the melodic ideas from that.

Unlike Suno or Udio, Melody Flip doesn’t spit out fully polished songs with vocals and full arrangements. Instead, it offers simple musical loops meant to serve as a creative spark for you to build on. There are fairly limited control over the outputs. You can’t feed Melody Flip a text prompt like “acoustic country rock with clean male vocals, literate singer-songwriter, gentle brushed drums, and sparse pedal steel at 98BPM” and get a Jason Isbell ripoff. Instead, you basically just choose a genre, note density, BPM, musical key, and take what you get. Though the genre options are pretty fine-grained, going from standard fare like “80s disco” and “90s R&B” to esoteric things like “Kawaii Future Bass” and “Anime World.”

The sound selection is further proof that you’re not supposed to use Melody Flip outputs out of the box. The presets available are mostly the sort of general MIDI tones you’d find in ‘90s video games. It seems like the intended use is to export the MIDI data from Melody Flip directly into your DAW to manipulate and pair with other, more powerful synth plugins.

After years of seeming lost in the woods and alienating customers with its messy Roland Cloud subscription service, the company was back on track recently. The P-6 Creative Sampler, SH-4d, and Gaia 2 synth all addressed major issues with the company’s lineup. And Roland finally listened to customers last year, paying loving tribute to its analog heritage with the TR-1000. But considering the general response from the music community to generative AI, Melody Flip is unlikely to garner it much goodwill.

title: AI will be the defining test of Apple’s environmental commitments, says Greenpeace
snippet: Greenpeace says the adoption of AI poses the biggest threat to Apple’s environmental track record, and argues that how the company responds will be the “defining test” of whether it really means what it says. Apple’s environmental achievements to date have been unrivalled, but the massive data center demands created by Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features could change all of that … more…
fullText:
Greenpeace says the adoption of AI poses the biggest threat to Apple’s environmental track record, and argues that how the company responds will be the “defining test” of whether it really means what it says.

Apple’s environmental achievements to date have been unrivalled, but the massive data center demands created by Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features could change all of that … 

Greenpeace has praised Apple’s environmental initiatives for more than a decade now. That included a 2015 report on the company’s use of renewable energy to power data centers.

Apple continues to lead the charge in powering its corner of the internet with renewable energy even as it continues to rapidly expand. All three of its data center expansions announced in the past year will be powered with renewable energy. Apple is also having a positive impact on pushing major colocation providers to help it maintain progress toward its 100% renewable energy goal.

Just last year, Greenpeace East Asia gave the company a B+ grade for introducing more renewable energy in its supply chains.

However, as Apple finally launches Siri AI next month, that could all change. While the company aims to carry out as many tasks as possible on-device, it relies on large-scale data centres to perform more complex actions, and these consume a great deal of electricity and water. The Verge cites concerns expressed by Greenpeace spokesperson Avex Li.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple responded by pointing The Verge to its most recent environmental progress report, as well as past statements on the topic.

title: Google Adds Voice Commands to Gmail, Docs and Keep for Some Users
snippet: The new features are only available on some tiers for Google Workspace subscribers.
fullText:
Google has begun rolling out beta voice features using Gemini 3.5 AI that allow you to have interactive conversations with its Gmail, Docs and Keep services. That means users can issue voice commands to find information in Gmail emails, incorporate AI search results into their Keep notes or start and organize a file in Docs without ever typing any text.

The features are in beta and are known collectively as just “Live,” as in Gmail Live or Docs Live. The Live features for Gmail and Keep are only currently available to Google’s AI Plus, Pro and Ultra paid-tier subscribers. Docs only works for Pro and Ultra subscribers right now.

Google said in a post that the new features will be coming soon for business customers who use Google Workspace.

In a video, Google staffers said that the Live voice features can make using the three Google apps more conversational and may be faster than typing searches or entering information manually.

Google previewed these features at its I/O event in May as part of a blitz of AI features powered by Gemini that it would be introducing over the next year. In the case of Gmail, Google has already been adding AI features to make inboxes easier to wrangle. 

How to use the Live features

If you have access to them, using the voice features in Gmail, Docs and Keep should be as easy as tapping the Live icon at the top of each app.

You can ask Gmail to do things like find a specific email, compose a reply or answer questions from the context of emails, such as finding details about an upcoming flight you’ve booked or checking when you last received an email response from someone.

In Google’s examples of how to use Live for Keep, the company said making the note-taking app a kind of intake for brain dumps is a good use, but it can also help organize notes or find information within them with voice commands.

Docs, according to Google, can also pull in information from services like Google Chat, Gmail and Drive with permission as well as websites, allowing it to create documents that pull together different elements with just voice commands.

title: Xbox Game Pass will get a Google TV app ‘in the coming months,’ likely only for TCL
snippet: Following a prior teaser that was the better part of a year ago, Microsoft has finally acknowledged its work on a Google TV app for Xbox Game Pass on TCL TVs, but it’s still “months” out from the sound of it. more…
fullText:
Following a prior teaser that was the better part of a year ago, Microsoft has finally acknowledged its work on a Google TV app for Xbox Game Pass on TCL TVs, but it’s still “months” out from the sound of it.

TCL first announced that an Xbox Game Pass app would be coming to its TVs – the Google TV models, specifically – back at CES 2026. That was in January. Microsoft never acknowledged the announcement publicly, and it’s been months since we’ve gotten any updates.

Today, Microsoft has officially confirmed that it will release an Xbox Game Pass app on TCL TVs, marking the first time the cloud gaming service will officially be available on Google TV. Microsoft’s announcement never formally acknowledges Google TV by name, hinting that this is probably exclusive to TCL TVs, rather than being available for the broader platform. TCL is the biggest Google TV partner and, while it also produces Roku and Fire TV units, it primarily uses Google TV and had previously teased the Xbox app directly around its new Google TV flagship.

But the Xbox Game Pass app for TCL’s Google TV sets is apparently still “months” away, despite the nine-month gap we’ve already gone through since the collaboration was first announced.

	

Microsoft says:

Today, we’re sharing a new partnership with TCL that will bring the XBOX app to select TCL Smart TVs in the coming months…

…With the XBOX app on supported TCL Smart TVs, players will be able to access XBOX Cloud Gaming through their Game Pass subscription to stream supported games directly from their TV. For eligible XBOX Game Pass subscribers, that means access to an instant library of games spanning blockbuster releases, beloved franchises, and indie favorites through their cloud playtime.

This comes just a day after Microsoft announced major changes to its cloud gaming setup on Xbox Game Pass. Players will now have a limited number of hours per month, topping out at 15 hours, before they need to pay more.

title: Apple making just a few hundred iPhone Ultras per day, per report
snippet: We’re less than a week away from Apple announcing its first-ever foldable iPhone. A new supply chain report today says that Apple’s “extremely high quality control standards” have led to a much slower ramp for iPhone Ultra production so far. more…
fullText:
We’re less than a week away from Apple announcing its first-ever foldable iPhone. A new supply chain report today says that Apple’s “extremely high quality control standards” have led to a much slower ramp for iPhone Ultra production so far.

iPhone Ultra production status 

According to Nikkei Asia, Apple is currently making “a few hundred” iPhone Ultra units per day. This could make it “challenging” for Apple to meet market demand for the device. 

The report says that Apple added an extra trial run of iPhone Ultra production in August to “ensure the phone can be mass-produced according to its specified design.” This decision reportedly delayed actual commercial production of the device “for weeks.”

In particular, Apple is said to be focused on improving the production yields of the “surface flatness and the performance of the hinge.”

The current situation, according to Nikkei’s sources, could result in limited availability of the iPhone Ultra when sales of the device begin. “Normally, tens of thousands of phones would need to be produced each day to meet the planned production goal for the foldable iPhone,” the report says.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported this week that he expects the foldable iPhone to be released “at the same time or very close to it” as the iPhone 18 Pro models. Gurman said that he doesn’t believe there are “massive delays or supply chain issues” impacting the device at this point.

Apple is expected to announce the iPhone Ultra on Wednesday next week as part of its “Surprise and shine” special event. Other rumored announcements include AirPods 5, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, and iPhone 18 Pro. What are you most excited to see? Let us know down in the comments.
