title: Roborock Launched Its First-Ever Robot Pool Cleaner and We Saw It First
snippet: Roborock makes seriously impressive robot vacuums. With the launch of the RockAqua P1, it’s taking on pool care for the first time.
fullText:
Roborock, one of the flashiest home robot makers, is taking the plunge. The Beijing-based brand, known for its super-smart robot vacuums, including models with robotic grabbing arms and stair-climbing capabilities, has launched its first-ever robotic pool cleaner. 

We saw it first at IFA Berlin.

On a crowded showroom floor, we got a look at Roborock’s small and colorful new pool cleaner. Dubbed the RockAqua P1, this autonomous underwater vacuum is engineered to clean pool floors, walls, waterlines and shallow platforms. 

Its adaptive cleaning path, a feature prominent in Roborock’s indoor vacuums, allows the robot to navigate pools of different shapes and depths. Vision-based obstacle avoidance identifies obstacles such as drain covers and steps, helping reduce interruptions during cleaning.

Roborock has entered the pool-care conversation with the launch of the RockAqua P1 at IFA.

While obstacle avoidance is useful, the ability to track down debris in a pool using AI cognition, as our top-rated Aiper Scuba V3 does, is even more impressive. So far, it doesn’t look like Roborock’s entry into the pool-cleaner category offers a comparable debris-detection feature.

	

			

	

			

									

						8 Best Robot Pool Cleaners, All Tested by CNET					

							

		

What the RockAqua P1 lacks in proactive leaf, bug, and stone hunting, it makes up for with a lot of suction power. The robot delivers a suction rate of 6,800 gallons per hour, placing it in the same class as some of the most powerful pool-cleaning robots from well-established brands. Still, our lab testing shows that raw power doesn’t necessarily translate to better cleaning.

Roborock’s first-ever pool vac can adjust its suction strategically to better capture debris.Tara Brown/CNET

One particularly interesting feature is the robot’s ability to adjust its suction depending on the situation. According to Roborock, when it encounters larger debris, the robot reduces suction to prevent the water flow from disturbing the debris and pushing it out of the cleaning path. As it gets closer, it increases suction to capture the debris.

Roborock’s first pool cleaner runs for up to 3.5 hours on a full charge, which is average for high-end models. When a cleaning cycle is complete, the robot rests on the water’s surface. That’s a useful touch, since some pool cleaners remain at the bottom and have to be hauled out manually. The surface-resting design should make the RockAqua P1 easier to retrieve for emptying and recharging.

As of now, the RockAqua P1 is set for release in Europe only, with a rollout to the US market still in question.

title: OpenAI releasing major upgrade to ChatGPT and Codex with GPT-6 Astra, details here
snippet: Update: A day later, GPT-6 Astra is rolling out to Business and Pro customers on the $100/month or $200/month plan. This follows other new model releases before Plus customers on the $20/month plan gain access. Update #2: A few hours later, Plus users with the $20/month subscription now have Astra access as well. It’s been just over a year since OpenAI released the first GPT-5 models for ChatGPT. Now it’s time for GPT-6 Astra to upgrade ChatGPT and Codex capabilities. Details below. more…
fullText:
Update: A day later, GPT-6 Astra is rolling out to Business and Pro customers on the $100/month or $200/month plan. This follows other new model releases before Plus customers on the $20/month plan gain access.

Update #2: A few hours later, Plus users with the $20/month subscription now have Astra access as well. 

It’s been just over a year since OpenAI released the first GPT-5 models for ChatGPT. Now it’s time for GPT-6 Astra to upgrade ChatGPT and Codex capabilities. Details below.

GPT-6 Astra details

OpenAI has officially detailed its new model, GPT-6 Astra, which it calls “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.”

Here’s more from the official announcement today:

GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work. Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helped solve long-standing open problems⁠ in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment. 

OpenAI goes further on how GPT-6 improves computer use, which allows ChatGPT to use your Mac or other desktop, including in the background while you work:

GPT‑6 Astra pairs advances in computer use with targeted training for professional environments, to help tackle complex work tasks. It combines the intelligence required for complex problems with the ability to carry out multistep workflows and produce polished documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.

Additionally, GPT-6 Astra is “the best model for software engineering to date,” OpenAI says.

With Astra, ChatGPT is nearly 2x faster at computer use than before.

In addition to the amazing new model, we’ve optimized the harness to make computer use run much faster.

These optimizations work in existing models too, so tasks are sped up by ~60% in GPT-5.6 Sol. Try it! pic.twitter.com/2EXH5f0uZL

— Ari Weinstein (@AriX) September 4, 2026

In terms of Codex specifically, here’s something new about GPT-6:

With Astra, we’re introducing a new way for Codex to preserve and retrieve context when the context window fills. Historically, models have used compaction to summarize work during long sessions, such as when debugging complex issues or tackling large refactors. Each compaction can leave out details about why a fix failed or how a component behaves. In Codex, Astra can keep notes across context windows, preserving accumulated details without repeatedly compressing them into a single summary. Earlier context windows remain searchable, so Astra can find requirements or test results from previous messages and tool outputs—even if that information wasn’t captured in its notes. You can enable this experimental feature in your Codex, and it will become the default for Astra in the coming weeks.

we launched a thing…

it is best in class at computer use, scientific research, coding, math, professional work like making slides, and so much more.

it is superhuman at ingesting enormous amounts of context. so patient. so relentless. so good at context switching. and it will… https://t.co/l3yM1Sy68n

— Kundan Kumar (@kundan2510) September 3, 2026

OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra a “significant jump in cyber capabilities,” adding that it “meets the Critical threshold⁠ in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework.”

For that reason, the model is rolling out slowly to users.

“GPT‑6 Astra is rolling out today to a limited set of organizations and over the coming days will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS,” OpenAI says. 

“Astra usage is included within the existing subscription allowances—users and businesses will also be able to purchase credits for additional usage. Users on the Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans will also get access to GPT‑6 Astra Pro. Enterprise administrators can enable Astra for their workspace; access is off by default at launch.”

The road to GPT-6 Astra

GPT-5 launched August 7, 2025, replacing GPT-4o and several reasoning models as ChatGPT’s default. Its defining feature was automatic routing: ChatGPT could answer quickly or invoke deeper reasoning depending on the request. OpenAI also claimed fewer factual errors than GPT-4o.

Apple adopted the model with iOS 26, iPadOS 26, and macOS Tahoe 26. ChatGPT requests passed through Apple Intelligence, including Siri handoffs, Writing Tools, and visual intelligence, switched from GPT-4o to GPT-5.

GPT-5.1 promised warmer, more natural answers in November. December’s “code red” GPT-5.2 accelerated professional work in response to Gemini. GPT-5.3 Instant targeted ChatGPT’s “cringe” tone, followed two days later by GPT-5.4 Thinking with a million-token context window and built-in computer use.

OpenAI subsequently added GPT-5.4 mini and nano, the restricted GPT-5.4-Cyber, GPT-5.5 for more autonomous work, GPT-5.5 Instant, and July’s GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna models.

From the Codex Mac app to a new ChatGPT

The software around those models transformed too. OpenAI launched a dedicated Codex Mac app in February as a hub for running multiple coding agents, reviewing changes, and scheduling work.

In July, Codex effectively became the new ChatGPT desktop app, combining Chat, Work, and Codex while the previous native client was renamed ChatGPT Classic.

For me, Codex has changed how I work with ChatGPT the most. I’m able to offload a lot more work that doesn’t require critical thinking and even build tools on my Mac that I couldn’t put together otherwise.

GPT-6 availability

OpenAI says its new GPT-6 models will only be available to its cyber security-focused Daybreak program members to start. This echoes a similar release cadence with the previous model release, GPT-5.6. 

Here’s what OpenAI says about availability, specifically:

GPT‑6 Astra is rolling out today to a limited set of organizations and over the coming days will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API and AWS.

You can learn much more about OpenAI’s latest frontier model here.

title: Lenovo’s first RTX Spark laptops can have up to 128GB of RAM
snippet: IFA 2026 is underway with Lenovo’s Innovation World event seeing the debut of the company’s first RTX Spark laptops as well as a flagship Android tablet and more. more…
fullText:
IFA 2026 is underway with Lenovo’s Innovation World event seeing the debut of the company’s first RTX Spark laptops as well as a flagship Android tablet and more.

Starting off with laptops, Lenovo is using Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip in new Yoga machines – and they sound nuts.

The Lenovo Yoga Pro 9n is a 15-inch with a 2560×1600 OLED display, up to 128GB of RAM, two SSD slots and up to 4TB of storage, and a 92.5Whr battery with 140W charging and a “Rapid Charge Express” mode that buys 3 hours of battery life in 15 minutes. For ports, it has two USB-C (40GBps) and two USB-A ports on either side, as well as HDMI and a full-size SD card slot. That’s all in a machine that’s “as thin as” 16.7mm and weighs 3.64lbs. It also has a haptic trackpad which has pen support.

Again, it sounds nuts.

	

The other option is the Yoga 9n 2-in-1 with a 16-inch display. It has a 2880×1800 OLED display, the same Nvidia RTX Spark chip, but is a bit tamer throughout the rest of the package. Up to 64GB of RAM, up to 2TB of SSD storage, but the same ports. Battery life is powered by a 99.9Whr battery with the same fast-charging setup, but this one is thicker at 17.5mm and weighs in at 4.28lbs.

Lenovo is directly positioning these machines at professional creators, with a focus on raw power for video editing, 3D rendering, and local AI applications. 

As you might imagine in the midst of RAMageddon, Lenovo isn’t confirming prices for either of these machines just yet, and there’s no release window either.

Data center developer Crusoe, which counts Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI as its customers, has raised a new $3 billion round at a $30 billion valuation, Bloomberg reported.

title: Apple Vision Pro was just used in a first-of-its-kind surgery
snippet: We’ve seen several stories about Apple Vision Pro being used in healthcare settings. This week, Stryker announced the completion of the first surgical procedure using an innovative new app on Vision Pro. more…
fullText:
We’ve seen several stories about Apple Vision Pro being used in healthcare settings. This week, Stryker announced the completion of the first surgical procedure using an innovative new app on Vision Pro.

The surgery, a hip arthroscopy, was completed using SportSuite Vision, an app that brings “critical digital content into a surgeon’s virtual space.” This includes things like arthroscopic video, HipCheck, HipMap, and CT imaging.

Here’s how Stryker describes the app:

SportSuite Vision brings critical digital content into a surgeon’s visual space, allowing them to see physical objects in the OR alongside digital tools such as arthroscopic images, HipCheck, HipMap and CT imaging.

During arthroscopic procedures, surgeons often rely on multiple displays positioned throughout the OR to access visualization and procedural data. By bringing multiple data sources into the surgeon’s field of view, the technology can reduce reliance on traditional monitors and support a more streamlined, ergonomic surgical workflow.

SportSuite Vision received FDA De Novo authorization on July 17. Stryker says this makes it the first app the FDA has authorized for intraoperative use with Vision Pro.

The hip arthroscopy was completed at Duke Health. Chad Mather III, the orthopedic surgeon who performed the operation, praised Vision Pro and SportSuite Vision:

“Using spatial computing enabled me to customize the placement of key clinical information to fit my workflow and access it within the sterile field. This helped create a more comfortable, streamlined OR setup while keeping the information I needed in view.”

You can learn more about SportSuite Vision on the Stryker website.

Also this week, Pfizer announced it is using Apple Vision Pro “to create an unforgettable, immersive experience” to “illustrate” its commitment to “outdo cancer.”

Pfizer’s bold mission is clear: Outdo cancer through relentless innovation and hope. To vividly illustrate this commitment for patients, healthcare providers, and internal stakeholders, Pfizer collaborated with Groove Jones to craft an immersive mixed reality experience that inspires as much as it informs. Apple Vision Pro’s ability to seamlessly blend digital and real worlds provided the perfect canvas to emotionally connect audiences and showcase Pfizer’s oncology leadership.

You can get a closer look at the experience on the Groove Jones website.

fullText:
As AI continues to be a bigger and bigger part of Google Search, the company is making AI Overviews bigger on some searches.

Already placed above traditional search results, Google’s AI Overviews provide an AI-generated answer to your query, pulling that information from links around the web and placing some of those links within the answer. 

Now, those are getting bigger.

In some search queries, Google will automatically fully expand AI Overviews, effectively turning the whole page into an AI response rather than just taking up the very top of the page. For some queries, AI Overviews may dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it’s most useful for people. Our research has shown that with this dynamic experience, users find Search more helpful and engage deeper in follow-up exploration.

One example of where this happens consistently is with definitions, where AI Overviews take up the entire screen.

title: Gemini 3.8 Flash rolling out three weeks after last release
snippet: After the last model release three weeks ago, Google today is rolling out Gemini 3.8 Flash. This marks the third Flash update in three months. more…
fullText:
After the last model release three weeks ago, Google today is rolling out Gemini 3.8 Flash. This marks the third Flash update in three months.

…our most intelligent workhorse model, delivering significant improvements from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and critical, multi-step reasoning in specialized domains.

Gemini 3.8 Flash “delivers substantial gains” over its predecessor in various benchmarks, with Google also noting how it is “often approaching the performance of higher-cost frontier models.”

On DeepSWE v1.1 (Long-Horizon Software Engineering) 3.8 Flash outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, only at a fraction of the cost.

In quantitative and professional fields that require advanced analysis and reporting, 3.8 Flash outperforms 3.7 Flash and other frontier models in benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark. 

3.8 Flash also achieves a 54.9% on HLE-Verified, demonstrating its ability to handle multi-step reasoning across STEM, humanities, and professional fields.

Google says these “performance gains stem from a core design choice: 3.8 Flash works harder.”

On complex tasks, it exhibits greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively. At times, the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels.

Note: Updated DeepSWE v1.1 score

	

Similar to the previous model, Gemini 3.8 Flash’s knowledge cutoff date is March 2026 “for some domains while in others [users] may experience the model’s knowledge is limited to January 2025.”

Google is once again offering an introductory price of $0.75/1M input tokens and $3.75/1M output tokens until December 31.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is already live in the Gemini app for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, AI Mode, and Gemini in Google Sheets. It’s also available for developers in Google Antigravity, AI Studio, and the Gemini API.

Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber

Google today also announced Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber (replacing 3.5) for trusted testers — via a new Fairwind Program — with “frontier-level performance in autonomous vulnerability discovery.”

The Chrome Security team found that 3.8 Flash Cyber produced 2.6 times more correct patches to vulnerabilities in Chrome than the best commercial models that are much larger.

Wiz found that Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber achieves +7.5-9.7% higher recall on their internal penetration testing benchmark for a 2.3-5.2x lower cost compared to other leading frontier models.

Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research team leveraged the 3.8 Flash Cyber model to find a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours, a vulnerability for which research and discovery usually takes months.

title: Google stops selling ‘Certified Refurbished’ Pixel 7 series, still no Pixel 9 yet
snippet: Google has pulled refurbished Pixel 7 devices from its store, with the Pixel 9 yet to make its debut. more…
fullText:
Google has pulled refurbished Pixel 7 devices from its store, with the Pixel 9 yet to make its debut.

On the Google Store you can buy a “Certified Refurbished” Pixel smartphone at a lower price, usually hundreds off of the original retail price. While it’s not always the best deal compared to a used device on the private market, there’s considerable peace of mind in buying a refurbished device directly from Google seeing as every device comes with a one-year warranty, gets a full inspection with replacement parts, and is sold unlocked for use with any carrier. These devices are also available on Amazon.

But the options have now shrunk.

Google now only has the Pixel 8 series – 8, Pro, and 8a – available alongside the Pixel 7a, with prices ranging from $289 to $649. The Pixel 7 series has been removed in the past few days, with its final appearance on the Wayback Machine in late August. Google was running a promotion where refurbished Pixel 7 devices included a free Pixel Watch 2 from July up until the past week or so.

	

This doesn’t come as a huge surprise. The Pixel 7 series launched in 2022 and will stop getting updates in the latter half of 2027. What’s more of a surprise is that the Pixel 9 series has yet to arrive in Google’s refurbished program. With Pixel 11 now available, it’s likely the Pixel 9 will arrive in the coming weeks. Pixel 8 was added in October 2025, roughly two months after the Pixel 10’s debut.

title: Google Pixel adding ‘Battery usage summaries,’ rolling out on Pixel 10 and newer
snippet: Google is rolling out a new AI-generated feature on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices called “Battery usage summaries” which translate battery use stats into natural language. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out a new AI-generated feature on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices called “Battery usage summaries” which translate battery use stats into natural language.

Rolling out via an AI Core update on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices, “Battery usage summaries” deliver on a rather simple premise. On your battery usage page, a new AI-generated overview summarizes your battery usage, pulling in recent history and calling out more powerful apps. 

On a support page, Google explains:

At the top of the Battery usage page, you can get a personalized summary of your battery usage. It summarizes these analyses, which are performed in the background:

Identifies apps that consume the most battery.

Monitors app background activity.

Compares the overall and app-specific battery consumption between your selected period and recent average.

The feature is enabled by default on supported Pixels, but can be turned off via Settings > Battery & charging > Battery Usage > Battery usage summaries (overflow menu). A screenshot sent to Android Authority shows an example of what the summary might say beyond the “you’ve barely used your phone” vibes our unused-for-the-day Pixel 11 Pro Fold shows. Google says that “outputs vary and highlight the most important info only.”

	

Google’s support page mentions that the latest AI Core update is needed to enable the feature, but it’s unclear if there are any additional requirements. While we’re seeing the feature live on both a Pixel 11 Pro Fold and a Pixel 11 Pro XL, it’s not yet showing on Pixel 10 or Pixel 10a devices we’ve updated and tested.

If you’re seeing “Battery usage summaries” on your Pixel, let us know in the comments below.

title: FBI investigates as hackers sell digital scans of 153M drivers licenses
snippet: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more. The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … more…
fullText:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more.

The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … 

Krebs on Security was able to confirm the authenticity of the claim made by the cybercriminals as they were able to provide a scan of his own driving license, with other victims likewise confirming their scans were correct.

A new identity theft service [dubbed Nexus] launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada […] The people behind Nexus claim the license images are coming from an active breach at “a major identity verification company” whose customers include multiple Fortune 500 companies.

KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

The report says that the ID verification company appears to be one based in Louisiana. The criminals claim that they still have access to the source of these scans, a claim supported by their adding almost 400,000 new ones within the past 24 hours.

There are indications suggesting that at least some of the data was stolen from a verification service used by rental car company Hertz. The report points to a New Orleans-based company as a potential source, and that company’s client list includes Hertz, Target, Fedex, Motorola Solutions, Jack Henry, and Caesars Entertainment. There are many more details in the full report.

9to5Mac’s Take

The irony of criminals being able to hack an identity verification service in order to provide documents that can be used for identity theft would be amusing if it weren’t so serious. This type of breach is depressingly common.

It was recently estimated that online scams cost Americans almost $150 billion last year as the number of cyber scams continue to increase dramatically.

title: Qualcomm’s upcoming premium chip has Adreno ‘Neural Fusion’ GPU
snippet: Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. more…
fullText:
Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU.

Qualcomm’s next SoC will be the first chipset to feature dedicated AI GPU cores in the graphics pipeline. These so-called “Matrix Cores” sit snugly in each of the three 1.45GHz GPU slices on the new Adreno GPU. Qualcomm says they act as dedicated local hardware to “run advanced AI models directly inside the graphics pipeline.”

The Snapdragon chip’s Adreno GPU will also feature a dedicated 18MB HPM (High Performance Memory) cache. That capacity sounds humble, but Qualcomm says its HPM “provides large, low-latency memory directly to the GPU, allowing tile-based rendering,

frame buffers, and compute workloads to remain local to the graphics subsystem.”

Both components in the new core architecture help make up the entirety of the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. For the end user, it means a 40% power improvement with the technology enabled. The company detailed in its press release how developing an SoC with AI processing done in closer proximity to the GPU means less latency and better efficiency.

	

The trick is keeping the work close to the silicon. Adreno Matrix Cores handle AI models right where the graphics happen, and the 18MB of Adreno High Performance Memory holds the heavy data—tiles, frame buffers, compute—on-chip so it isn’t constantly shuffling back and forth to system memory. Less movement means lower latency and better efficiency, which translates into gaming sessions that last longer.

For the time being, Unity and Unreal Engine have already integrated Qualcomm’s Neural Fusion stack.

The end result should be improved graphics quality with “upscaled images, stable frame rates, and improved efficiency through AI-enhanced rendering built directly into the Snapdragon

graphics pipeline,” as Qualcomm puts it.

Snapdragon Summit is scheduled for September 22-24, and more is set to be announced regarding the new chip’s NPU.

Adobe is bringing its creative and productivity tools directly into Slack, letting teams create and edit images, videos, designs and PDFs without leaving the conversations where projects already take shape.

The new Adobe for Slack MCP app launches today with more than 70 pro-grade tools spanning Firefly, Adobe Express, Photoshop, Premiere, Acrobat, InDesign, Illustrator, Stock, Lightroom and more.

It works through Slackbot, Slack’s built-in AI assistant. Slackbot can pull context from messages, files, channels and Canvases before calling the appropriate Adobe tools.

Context is the heart of the integration. A user could ask Slackbot to summarize a project brief, then turn the information into a PDF, image or video.

The app can also search Creative Cloud assets by subject, style or mood and bring the results into a Slack workflow for further editing.

Other examples include resizing approved campaign creative for different social platforms, transforming spreadsheet data into a shareable visual and refining batches of photos.

Adobe says users can remove backgrounds and distractions, adjust lighting and tone, crop images and produce multiple variations from Slack.

Availability 

Adobe for Slack is available globally to Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ customers across desktop, web and mobile starting today.

People can start without an Adobe account, while signing in unlocks more tools, generative AI features, Creative Cloud files and continuity across sessions.

The launch expands Adobe’s push to bring its tools into AI chatbots. Adobe already supports ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot, with Gemini integration coming soon.

title: Mammotion Luba 3 changed my mind about robot lawnmowers
snippet: Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models. more…
fullText:
Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models.

I’m all for smart home advancements, but a robot lawnmower was one I was never really a fan of. I like mowing my lawn, crazy as that sounds, and leaving that to a robot felt like more set up and maintain than it was going to be worth. Inevitably, though, curiosity won over. When Mammotion sent over the Luba 3 AWD mower, my attitude flipped.

The main reason for that boils down to how this mower operates. Unlike many others, which require the use of a boundary perimeter or RTK base station, the Mammotion Luba 3 operates with what’s called a “NetRTK,” which is effectively just a highly accurate satellite positioning system combined with LiDAR.

The results here really blew me away. 

	

After mapping the robot to the areas of my yard I wanted it to work on, it stayed nearly perfectly within those lines, to the point where I actually had to go back and redo the lines. Initially, I’d set up several feet of buffer zone between the mower and the fairly-busy road in front of my lawn for fear that, if the positioning shifted, the mower might risk getting run over. The first two runs showed how misplaced that fear was. It hit its lines almost perfectly, which left plenty of room for me to adjust those lines much closer to the road. There’s still a small buffer, but I now know I can trust that Luba 3 isn’t going to go rogue into the road. It’s not without hiccups. Another part of the yard with a ditch left the mower stuck a couple of times when the positioning was off by a few inches, and a tough-to-access area of the property also proved tricky. But in most cases, it goes off without a hitch.

It’s all managed through the app, where you use a virtual joystick to set up a map and the pathways the mower can use to get to various zones, including crossing over driveways or perhaps portions of your neighbor’s lawn. The same app can be used to set schedules, view progress, and even watch a first-person-view of the mower’s main camera as it runs through your yard.

Taking a step back, the initial setup is an absolute breeze. Assembly and setup took around 30 minutes, with the included tools making it easy to attach the front bumper and side covers. 

Luba 3 has a docking station in the box that just needs a power outlet in the vicinity, with a generous length of cable included. You want a fairly level location for this, but I’ve found that even my slightly uneven and unstable mulch base works well enough. I’ve only had one occasion where it didn’t fully seat for charging in several weeks of use. You do get a physical RTK base station in the box but, really, you don’t need it unless you’re in some very specific circumstances. 

Like most robot mowers, grass is cut using some fairly small blades underneath, and this also makes the whole thing feel safer. Not only is there a giant “STOP” button at the top, but the blades themselves won’t be able to do nearly as much damage as a real mower would.

The physical hardware is huge, easily 2-3x the size of a robot vacuum, and it turns heads. My dogs still go crazy every time they see this in the yard, and I always see neighbors and drivers passing by turn to look when Luba 3 is out in the front. But it’s not an eyesore either. The white finish shows all dirt and dust that’s kicked up – most of the pictures in this post are after about two weeks without a wipedown – but it’s a sensible color choice as it rejects heat. It is heavy at 41lbs, but that’s totally managable for the rare occasions where you need to move it manually.

How’s the actual mowing performance? 

Good, but not perfect.

Luba 3 thankfully cuts at up to 3.9-inches in height, which matters to me. Overly short grass is how you kill a lawn in a hot summer, so it was nice to see Mammotion offers the right amount of height to keep everything fairly healthy. Whether sending it off into a thick lawn or one that’s mostly been scorched by the heat and drought of the North Carolina summer I’ve been living in, Luba 3 gets the job done well. The cut is fairly even with only the occasional straggler blade left behind, particularly when cutting at maximum height or when running it less frequently. This benefits great from running on a regular basis rather than the “as needed” schedule you’d use with a traditional mower.

It also handles slopes like a champ, with it able to cover my steep front lawn and some other raised portions of the yard without skipping a beat. Mammotion says it can handle a slope of up to 38.6-degrees with its all-wheel-drive setup. There are a couple of spots in my lawn where I can tell there’s some dead grass from Luba’s tracks, but I’ll mostly blame that on the local conditions. In some particularly uneven parts of my lawn, I do need to go back with my push mower or weed-eater, but Luba 3 really takes the bulk of the work off of my plate – complete with stripes in the finished yard.

I do think that’s an important note to make. Mammotion’s Luba 3, and really any robot lawnmower, isn’t going to fully end your yard work. There are certain sections you’ll need to do yourself, especially with regard to weeds and edging along the sides. There are options that aim to solve this, but you’ll still inevitably need to do cleanup here and there. 

But most weeks, this cuts my mowing time from an hour or two to just a few minutes – a couple of passes along the road, checking for spots it might have missed, and then weed-eating around the driveway and fence.

As for battery life, the 0.75-acre model I’ve been testing can run for about two hours before it takes a break to recharge, but that’s largely due to the hills it has to deal with. Mammotion says that, under ideal conditions, it can run for up to 215 minutes (about 3.5 hours).

Another point in favor of its navigation, too, is that it can easily handle jumping around to different portions of the yard. Zones are easy to set up and can make it easy to mow different areas at different times, or juggle things like fences. Part of my yard is gated, so having a specific zone I can run just when the gate is open is a really handy option.

All-in-all, Mammotion really changed my mind about robot lawnmowers. Luba 3 works like a charm and addresses every complaint I thought I’d have about setup, navigation, and cutting performance. 

Really, the only tough part left is price.

Mammotion Luba 3 AWD starts at $2,399 in the US, which is not cheap. But this is also on the bleeding edge and, in a world where time is money, might be worthwhile for anyone who just can’t seem to keep up with their lawn. It saves so much time.

title: John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO: Here’s the latest
snippet: Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make. more…
fullText:
Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make.

Luca Maestri

Bloomberg reports that Luca Maestri is stepping down as Apple’s “Corporate Services” leader. Maestri served as Apple CFO until January 2025, when he stepped down to take on a smaller role. As head of Corporate Services, Maestri oversaw information systems and technology, information security, and real estate and development.

According to today’s report, Maestri left that job “in recent weeks.” He is, however, still on Apple’s payroll. His only remaining responsibility is “hosting a popular class at Apple University, an in-house program for teaching Apple’s ways to rising executives and employees.”

Bloomberg says that Maestri’s Corporate Services tasks have been shifted to CFO Kevan Parekh.

Adrian Perica

Mark Gurman points out that Apple’s new Leadership page excludes Adrian Perica, its head of mergers and acquisitions.

Apple’s new leadership page also excludes Adrian Perica, the company’s head of mergers and acquisitions. It remains unclear where he will shift within Apple. Bloomberg reported on Sunday that he would likely be dropped by Ternus as a direct report and could split his responsibilities across Apple’s services and finance teams.

It’s possible this signals a change to Apple’s strategy for mergers and acquisitions. Some analysts expect Ternus to be more aggressive in making bigger acquisitions.

A change to how Apple manages outgoing executives

Gurman also says that “people in and around Apple” expect Ternus to change how the company handles outgoing executives. While Cook made a habit of retaining executives in smaller roles, like Maestri, Gurman says “Ternus may be less likely to continue using this approach.”

More tidbits

Ternus officially joined X today, and his first tweet was an all-lowercase “hello” with no punctuation. The post was quoted by marketing exec Greg Joswiak, who wrote: “Hello, indeed. More to say September 9.”

Gurman says Apple is hosting an event at Apple Park today “to introduce John Ternus as its new CEO to employees and to again celebrate Tim Cook’s tenure.”

Laura Legros, a former Apple VP who Ternus recruited out of retirement last month, will reportedly serve in a “Chief of Staff” style role. Cook did not have a person like this around him, according to Gurman.

title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
snippet: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API. more…
fullText:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour. 

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

Introducing Muse Voice Transcribe! 🗣️

This is our first real-time audio perception model from @AIatMeta. It's trained on 70+ languages and delivers diarization with 20+ speakers. A truly fantastic model.

fullText:
Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users.

Here are four new ‘Sonos 27’ features launching this fall

Sonos has launched Sonos Ace Ultra headphones today alongside a Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar. And in addition to the new hardware introductions, the company has rebranded its software.

‘Sonos 27’ is the official name of the Sonos software platform that already exists, but is getting a proper name starting today. More than just a rebrand though, Sonos announced four new software features coming this fall to Sonos users:

Portable surrounds

Personal listening

Sonos 27voice

Sonos MCP

Portable surrounds

Turn two compatible portable speakers into wireless rear surrounds for movie night — then move them right back to wherever they usually live when the credits roll. No wires, no permanent setup, no rearranging furniture.

Personal listening, without missing a beat

Headphone linking which is available in Early Access, allows you to seamlessly move audio between Sonos Ace Ultra and a compatible Sonos speaker or group streaming over the same WiFi connection with just the press of a button. You will also be able to pick and control your music on your headphones directly in the Sonos app while on your home network. For more information, read our support article here.

The new Sonos voice experience

Sonos 27voice is a new way to ask for music, built specifically for that purpose in the home, and the shortest path from wanting a song to hearing it. Instead of remembering exact commands, you can ask the way you’d talk to someone in the room with you. Say things like “Play that song I had on in the kitchen last night,” or “Put on something downstairs that the kids will like.” The system works out the rest.

Control Sonos with the AI you already use

Sonos has always been an open platform. Sonos MCP expands it. Sonos MCP connects your system to frontier large language models (LLMs), so you can control Sonos from familiar chatbot interfaces and mix advanced dialog and reasoning with out-loud listening on your speakers.

title: John Ternus just revealed his priorities in first introduction as Apple CEO
snippet: John Ternus is officially Apple’s CEO starting today, and his new bio page on Apple’s website reveals some of Ternus’s key priorities, as noted by Myke Hurley. more…
fullText:
John Ternus is officially Apple’s CEO starting today, and his new bio page on Apple’s website reveals some of Ternus’s key priorities, as noted by Myke Hurley.

John Ternus’s new Apple bio signals his priorities on day one as CEO

Today Apple updated its leadership page with John Ternus’s new title as CEO.

Alongside the leadership refresh, Ternus’s official bio has been updated and expanded too.

As noted by Myke Hurley at The Enthusiast, the new bio highlights three key narratives around Ternus’s time at Apple and the work that he cares deeply about. And two of those narratives are based on an all-new bio addition.

While the bio partly carries over details that were there before, there’s one brand new paragraph quoted below. From Apple’s website:

John has led much of the company’s focus in areas like reliability and durability, introducing new techniques that have made Apple products remarkably resilient. He has also driven much of Apple’s innovation in materials and hardware design that have reduced the carbon footprint of its products, including the creation of a new recycled aluminum compound that has been introduced across multiple product lines, the use of 3D-printed titanium in Apple Watch Ultra, and advancements in reparability that have increased the life spans of several Apple products.

This is the only entirely new paragraph. The rest of the bio either remains the same as before, or has been reworded but with the core message unchanged.

The new paragraph takes up nearly half the length of the whole bio, which is relatively brief overall.

As a result, this one paragraph is a strong indicator of priorities that matter a lot to Ternus, and that he wants to specifically highlight as he starts his CEO role.

To sum up the paragraph, Ternus cares about hardware “reliability and durability,” and “innovation in materials and hardware design,” with the goal of a reduced carbon footprint and increased product lifespans.

We’re seen a big emphasis from Tim Cook on reducing Apple’s carbon footprint. Ternus is clearly signaling that will continue under his leadership. But this paragraph also emphasizes that Ternus is an innovator in hardware design, and aims to create products that last for many years.

title: YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required
snippet: Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube. more…
fullText:
Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube.

As described in an announcement post on the YouTube support forums, Google is rolling out some big changes to how YouTube on your smartphone interacts with your television. The company is describing your device as a “companion” now, even ditching the classic Cast icon for something a little more generic. It’s a change that, based on Reddit threads, seemingly entered testing earlier in 2026, and is now ready for a full rollout. 

It’s not just a new way to describe pairing your devices, though. With this refresh, casting videos from your phone to a television now sounds like it has a whole lot less friction, thanks in part to a shift on completely relying on account-based management. These changes include:

No longer requiring both devices to be on a shared Wi-Fi network to cast. Instead, users will need to be signed in on the same account on both devices.

The ability to like videos, leave comments, and subscribe to channels while the video plays in the background.

The option to consume YouTube Shorts content on your phone while a different, full-length video plays on your television.

A built-in “Play on different device” option found within the menu button on every video listed in your homepage feed.

There are, of course, some caveats to these upgrades, and it primarily revolves around the shift to forcing account-based pairing between devices. While this should work wonders for private viewing sessions — i.e., casting a video from your own phone to your own television to watch either independently or with someone else in the room — it’s unclear if this completely removes the ability to cast over Wi-Fi, something that’s genuinely useful in larger gatherings with multiple participants. That’s a pretty common use case for watching YouTube on a television, so I’m hoping generic Cast support continues to exist in this format. Otherwise, this feels like a particularly anti-social change from Google.

	

Generally, though, these are all steps in the right direction, taking a lot of the existing Cast elements and simply streamlining them for a more modern second-screen experience. That “Play on different device” option, for example, appears to be pretty similar to the current casting menu, but won’t require you to begin playing a video on your phone prior to beaming it to your TV. Personally, browsing Shorts while watching a full-length video on your television sounds pretty overwhelming to me, but it’s certainly Google meeting modern viewers where they’re already at.

Today’s announcement did not include a specific rollout window, but it does sound like it’ll be coming to a mobile device near you very, very soon.

title: US military disabled ad tracking on troops’ devices following reports of targeted attacks
snippet: A senator's letter confirms the U.S. military moved to prevent the tracking after foreign adversaries used location data to target troops.
fullText:
Image Credits:AFP (opens in a new window) / Getty Images	

	

						

6:21 AM PDT · September 4, 2026

											

			

The U.S. Department of Defense has disabled advertising tracking on troops’ phones and computers as part of an effort to protect them from threats that target their locations, according to a letter shared with Senator Ron Wyden.

Per a letter shared with the senior Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, Wyden said that the U.S. Army, Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps, and Special Operations Command have all disabled advertising tracking across their government-issued devices.

This includes the departments’ iPhones and Android devices, and Windows computers managed across the federal military enterprise network, the letter said.

Reuters, which first reported the news and the letters, said the military rolled out the protections earlier this year. The Air Force told Wyden it implemented its changes more recently in July.

The aim is to prevent adversaries, including hostile governments, from using location data derived from the apps on troops’ phones to target them on the battlefield or on their bases. Location data collected from phone apps is commonly shared with third-party companies and data brokers, which then sell the information on the commercial market. Disabling the advertising ID makes the person far more difficult to identify as the location data blends in with everyone else whose advertising ID is also disabled.

Wyden raised the issue earlier this year in a letter to U.S. military leaders after finding that unnamed foreign adversaries had targeted U.S. troops in the Middle East using their commercially obtained location data. The senator, a known privacy hawk on Capitol Hill, said that while the move to reduce the advertising tracking was commendable, he warned that the personal devices of troops and contractors brought onto military bases could still expose service members and facilities to attacks.

While the U.S. government has acknowledged that its troops face a risk from this data, the U.S. intelligence community and the FBI have confirmed that they buy this data for surveillance and intelligence collection without a warrant.

fullText:
In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade.

Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 arrive today

In Anthropic’s world, Fable is Claude’s most capable model. Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus are the small, medium, and large models below Fable. 

“Claude Fable 5.1 sets a new standard on coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks,” Anthropic says. The company says the new model has a higher level of performance compared to Fable 5.

Anthropic also says Fable 5.1 “achieves similar or better results than Fable 5 at a much lower cost” when set to low or medium effort.

More from Anthropic below:

Fable 5.1 avoids shortcuts that result in poorer-quality work, and it’s smart enough to fix the root causes of software issues. For example, in testing by the investment firm Millennium, Fable 5.1 found the cause of a rare crash on their internal systems that none of their engineers (or any other model) had been able to explain after several years of trying.

In addition to Fable 5.1, Anthropic is also releasing Mythos 5.1 for users with Mythos access.

“Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but with different levels of safeguards,” Anthropic explains. “Fable 5.1 is generally available, while Mythos 5.1 is available only through our trusted access programs; its safeguards are specifically designed to support work in cybersecurity and the life sciences.”

Here’s pricing data for Fable 5.1:

Fable 5.1 will cost an estimated 25% less than Fable 5 for typical workloads, wherever usage is billed by token. This is because we’re reducing our pricing on cache reads (where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored). For highly agentic work, the savings will often be much larger—up to approximately 45%.

In terms of pricing, Anthropic says it has “reduced the price of Fable 5.1’s cache reads (where the model reuses context it has already processed) wherever usage is billed by token, such as on our API.” The company says this “leads to a substantial reduction in the overall cost of running the model.” Pricing is otherwise unchanged from Fable 5.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 11th digital state ID, first addition in 10 months
snippet: After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android.

Open the Google Wallet app, tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom, IDs & personal info, and then Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Ohio as the 12th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the Northern Cardinal, which is Ohio’s state bird.

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the OH BMV. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

title: Tesla’s Cybercab Opened Up to Riders — and the Feds Opened an Investigation
snippet: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is examining whether the self-driving vehicle meets federal safety standards.
fullText:
On Thursday, Tesla made its Cybercab robotaxi available to riders in Austin, Texas. Soon after, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it was investigating the launch.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled the Cybercab in October 2024, noting the vehicle would go into production “before 2027.” Production indeed kicked off in April 2026, though Musk noted that scaling would be “very slow” due to supply chain and validation timelines.  

Tesla’s robotaxi service initially launched with Model Y vehicles in Austin last year, though the goal is to eventually make the Cybercab the main autonomous vehicle in the company’s network. This week marks the first time customers, rather than just employees and early testers, can climb aboard the fully autonomous Cybercab via the Robotaxi app. There are currently 45 Cybercabs operating commercially in Texas.

Unlike robotaxis from Alphabet-owned Waymo, which is currently the leader in the autonomous ride-hailing space, Tesla’s Cybercab doesn’t have a steering wheel or pedals. It shares that characteristic with Amazon-owned Zoox, which has deployed its boxy, purpose-built robotaxis in a handful of cities so far.

The Cybercab’s lack of manual controls prompted NHTSA to investigate, with the agency noting the lack of “a brake pedal, gas pedal, steering wheel and mirrors” in its filing. Given that Tesla self-certified its Cybercab, NHTSA now plans to “examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.” NHTSA said earlier this year that it’s exploring removing the requirement for manual controls in autonomous vehicles.

“NHTSA fully supports the safe development and deployment of automated vehicles. But as the federal regulator, we need to ensure that all of our laws are followed,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in a Friday statement. “Our approach of balancing innovation with safety oversight will allow the United States to maintain its global leadership in AV innovation.”

	

			

As noted by TechCrunch, NHTSA also probed Zoox’s autonomous efforts during its testing phase due to the lack of traditional controls, like a steering wheel and pedals. Zoox eventually launched its ride-hailing service for members of the general public in September 2025, beginning in Las Vegas. It obtained federal regulatory approval to start charging for rides in July. Along with invite-only robotaxi rides in San Francisco, Zoox has also deployed its robotaxis for limited service in Austin and Miami.

A key aspect that sets Tesla’s robotaxi apart from competitors is that it relies solely on cameras for navigation, rather than the more standard combination of cameras, radar and lidar. That could make some riders uneasy, especially with 71% of US adults saying they wouldn’t be comfortable riding in a driverless car, according to a Pew Research Center survey from July. Tesla’s self-driving vehicles — as well as those from competitors — have been involved in a handful of crashes since hitting public roads.

Musk has also said that individuals will eventually be able to own a Cybercab, which could be used to earn passive ride-hailing income by joining the robotaxi network. He’s stated the car will cost “below $30,000,” but hasn’t shared any recent updates on that strategy. Tesla released an interest form for anyone who’d like to be “considered for future Robotaxi opportunities,”  which includes an option for “Cybercab fleet vehicle purchasing.”

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: The Memoket Gem is an 11g AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch in a co-wear band. Press once to capture a conversation, and Gem connects it to what you discussed weeks ago — surfacing the earlier thread with a source link. From $179, shipping August 2026.

In 2023, early adopters were just getting to know ChatGPT and AI chatbot tech. Three years later, OpenAI’s Codex agent, now part of the ChatGPT desktop app, has brought about a similar season of learning. Here’s how I’m using ChatGPT, Codex, and more on my Mac.

The summer I turned Codex

Like a billion other people, ChatGPT has become a regular part of my tech stack. But I’m a writer, not a programmer, so Codex as an agentic coding app didn’t immediately appeal to me.

That started to change in April when Codex for Mac added Computer Use.

First, a brief history lesson. 

Back in December 2014, Ari Weinstein and friends launched a new iOS 8 app for mobile automation. Here’s my 9to5Mac coverage of Workflow’s launch, a friendlier version of OS X’s Automator made for iPhone and iPad.

In March 2017, Apple bought Workflow. Workflow gained system integration and became Apple Shortcuts with iOS 12 in 2018.

Weinstein and other Workflow veterans later left Apple to create Software Applications Incorporated. The startup previewed Sky, a modern AI assistant on the Mac, before being acquired by OpenAI.

Sky never publicly launched. Instead, Codex for Mac delivered the technology in April in the form of the Computer Use plugin. 

So excited to share that we're bringing Computer Use to Codex. Computer Use lets Codex see, click, and type into your Mac apps, with its own cursor.

It's a magical feeling to have agents using your apps in the background, and still get to use your computer at the same time. pic.twitter.com/wdgxiHAKyX

— Ari Weinstein (@AriX) April 16, 2026

Trusting an AI with using your Mac, especially in the background, requires a level of trust. I don’t know what my adoption of Codex and Computer Use would be like without the history behind it.

I just know that, for me, there was a great level of inherited trust and continuity that gave me confidence in the system.

Here’s where I admit that Workflow and Shortcuts never super clicked for me. I’ve used both systems with tools that others built, but I haven’t been a builder myself.

Codex has completely changed that, but not overnight.

ChatGPT to Codex to ChatGPT … a journey

I initially found Codex to be too intimidating and outside my comfort zone compared to ChatGPT. Now ChatGPT without Codex feels like a toy. 

I’ve mentioned before that it was actually a toy-like feature inside Codex called Pets that served as the training wheels for me. (The real Codex pets are the personal projects you hatch along the way.)

I started using Codex daily in May. The first project I started with Codex is a Mac app called Flow — because it helps my story writing flow. It’s mostly a way to monitor app releases and updates. 

In my early 9to5Mac days, I used iTunes on the Mac for this purpose. It required local (and otherwise unusable) iPhone app files. More recently, I’ve used iPhone Mirroring to check the App Store on my iPhone for app updates as part of my work routine.

Describing this “workflow” to Codex started the process of building Flow. Being able to describe every little feature and change that I wanted, as if I was messaging a colleague, made it feel natural.

Because it’s my first project and built just for me, the icon is my first initial, handwritten by me (Apple Pencil, iPad Pro, Procreate), made with Apple’s Icon Composer Mac app.

Closing the loop

Because you can iterate forever, I’ve found it’s important to “close the loop” and consider a project mostly complete.

With Flow, I’ve definitely moved to the stage where I can measure the number of my 9to5Mac posts that originate from using the tool. This is an important distinction from measuring the amount of time spent invested into building the tool itself.

But because building with Codex has been such a joy, there are naturally other projects that have followed. You can just make your own Mac apps, specific to your very particular needs.

In my case, I’ve made more modern versions of apps I’ve used for years, tailored to my specific needs, right down to very specific narrow column widths.

This is very specific, but it’s very cool to me. I have a column view for social media, and a column view for RSS, on either side of my Mac display. Both are 275 pixels wide (and made for macOS 27 Golden Gate specifically). This is much narrower than the solutions I previously used, which weren’t even optimized for macOS 26.

Using X2 and Flume, I’m able to open up a significant amount of screen real estate in the middle without overlapping windows.

Social media and RSS are also mostly passive viewing apps for me. By default, toolbar button accent colors turn gray for non-active windows. But because these apps are made for me, I’m able to express that I prefer the touch of color to stay active, just desaturate a step, adding a splash of joy to my Mac.

But wait, there’s more 

At this point, if you’re still reading, this post is probably starting to feel like the guy who just discovered going to the gym and can’t stop telling everyone about how great it makes them feel. 

For that reason, I’ll just flag a few more hobby projects that Codex has unlocked for me.

First, Better Remote. It’s on the Mac App Store. If you’re already using your Mac, it makes tvOS feel like just another Mac app. Here’s a look at the update currently in the queue.

Outside of work (and spending more time outside), iterating on Better Remote has been my main side project this summer. The project started in June.

Second, Better Battery. I adore the look of macOS 27 Golden Gate, but I can’t read the battery indicator with the percentage displayed as well.

Prior to Codex, I’d probably write a blog post as a feature request to flag the issue. Instead, I’ve been able to make my own solution — during the beta period — which others can use for free.

I’ve also been testing ChatGPT Sites with a custom domain to make sharing all of this easier. I initially thought OpenAI’s Sites feature wasn’t really for me.

Publishing Better Remote on the Mac App Store required a web presence, though, which gave me a reason to test the ChatGPT/Codex feature.

Now I’m pretty excited to see where ChatGPT Sites can go from here. OpenAI recently added shared site management tools, and there’s a big opportunity for a more defined interface — like a modern Apple iWeb.

It’s still very early days for these tools, but I find it all very promising and exciting. I haven’t had this much fun using my Mac to make things since GarageBand two decades ago.

Every day, important conversations happen in meetings, on calls, over coffee, and on the go. By the time you sit down at your desk, half the details are gone. And AI tools are only as smart as the context you feed them.

Your iPhone stops recording the moment a call comes in. Your Apple Watch can’t capture what’s happening across the table. Neither connects what was said today to a decision made three weeks ago.

Memoket Gem was built for exactly that gap. An 11g AI wearable that captures conversations with one press and connects them across time. When a topic comes up that you discussed weeks ago, Gem surfaces it automatically with a source link. Everything flows directly into ChatGPT, Claude, Slack, and Notion.

For Apple Watch users, Gem slots into a custom co-wear band alongside your Watch on the same wrist. Two devices, completely unobtrusive.

At 0.4 oz with 20 hours of battery and 153 languages supported, Gem disappears into your day while capturing everything that matters.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro Max Could Start at $1,300, an Analyst Predicts. You Can Thank RAMageddon for That
snippet: Since when did smartphones cost a month’s rent?
fullText:
We’re days away from Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event, where we expect the tech giant to unveil its first foldable iPhone (which could be called the iPhone Ultra), along with the premium models of the iPhone 18. You can expect better battery life and a variable aperture camera. But that’s not what everyone really wants. 

When we asked CNET readers one thing they’d change about the iPhone in our Big Guessing Game, 16% said they want it to cost less. But that’s wishful thinking. 

TrendForce, a global market research firm, released a report on Thursday suggesting you can expect higher prices instead of steep discounts. The firm expects the iPhone 18 series to cost 10 to 20% more due to the ongoing RAM shortage and higher hardware costs. 

“For the 256GB Pro model, memory costs in [the third quarter of 2026] are expected to be nearly 400% higher than a year earlier,” TrendForce said. “Despite Apple’s efforts to negotiate lower prices for other components, these savings are unlikely to offset the resulting pressure on overall [materials] costs.”

Apple raised prices on select products in June due to the RAM shortage, but excluded iPhones from the price hikes. Now there’s a chance that Apple could release some iPhone 18 models with higher prices at the September event. TrendForce said it expects Apple to absorb some of the costs to keep prices for the new models as part of a “relatively moderate” pricing strategy. 

So exactly how much more are we talking about? Some analysts believe the foldable iPhone Ultra could cost between $2,000 and $2,500. TrendForce predicts the starting price will be slightly higher — between $2,099 and $2,299. The phone could go up to $3,000. 

As for the premium models of the iPhone 18, TrendForce expects the iPhone 18 Pro to start between $1,199 and $1,299, and $1,299 to $1,399 for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. 

A TrendForce representative said in an email to CNET that even though upgrades to the processor and optical system are part of the reason for higher costs, the “sharp surge in memory component prices is indeed the single biggest factor driving this price adjustment.”

But higher costs aren’t equivalent to big improvements. 

TrendForce says we shouldn’t expect major performance upgrades from Apple’s upcoming iPhone lineup. Instead, we should expect a more powerful processor for AI features and power efficiency, better chip cooling technology and power-efficient displays. And the iPhone 18 Pro models’ main camera could have a “mechanical variable aperture” to improve depth-of-field control and dynamic range for different lighting settings. 

The really big upgrade is the potential release of the folding iPhone Ultra and bigger batteries for premium iPhone 18 models, TrendForce predicts. The iPhone 18 Pro Max could see the biggest upgrade due to a larger chassis. CNET’s Patrick Holland tested smartphone batteries last year and found that the iPhone 17 Pro Max was the best for battery life, so iPhone 18’s premium models could be an even bigger upgrade from the current model.

title: Alienware’s refurbished 16 Aurora is almost $200 off at Woot
snippet: Gaming laptop deals aren’t what they used to be (stares daggers at RAMageddon), which is why I consider Woot’s deal on a refurbished Alienware 16 Aurora gaming laptop with Nvidia’s RTX 5050 a pretty good deal at $927 for new Woot customers (with code WOOTALIEN used at checkout). It costs $1,029 for returning Woot shoppers, which is a decent discount off the new $1,099.99 price at Alienware’s site. Notably, this refurb unit includes a one-year Alienware warranty. Alienware 16 Aurora Where to Buy: $1099.99 $927.99 at Woot (refurbished, with code WOOTALIEN) These days, most configurations with Nvidia’s RTX 5060 GPU sail well over the $1,200 mark, which is just too much if you ask me. If you’re in the market for a relatively speedy and well-designed machine, perhaps this one will be a good fit for your needs and budget. The Aurora has a 1600p 120Hz 16-inch screen, Intel’s capable Core 7 240H processor, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 512GB SSD. Its RTX 5050 GPU likely won’t be able to play most games at max settings, especially at its native 1600p resolution, but you should be able to get respectable frame rates and visual fidelity with some tweaking. As for its condition, the company says “it’s as close to new as you can get without technically being “new.” The 16 Aurora features two M.2 slots, letting you greatly boost its included 512GB SSD with other drives. It also has two SO-DIMM slots, so you can upgrade the 8GB x 2 (DDR5 5,600MHz) down the line to 16GB x 2 (it tops out at 32GB RAM). If you have other specs you want to dig into, check out Dell’s comprehensive spec sheet within its support site. Other great Verge-approved deals Live in a really small space? Perhaps, an RV or a van equipped with power to run appliances? The Loch Capsule dishwasher that my colleague Thomas Ricker tested is 20 percent off for a limited time through Labor Day. Normally $459.99 for the skinny dishwasher, it’s down to $367.99 with free shipping at Loch’s site. Now, folks with setups large enough to accommodate a bigger dishwasher shouldn’t consider the Loch Capsule. But it might be just what some are looking for. It can clean and dry (even sanitize) dishes and pans in a 20-minute cycle. It doesn’t require plumbing, and its design isn’t an eye sore. If you can look past its flaws (mainly that it’s sort of loud), it’s worth considering during the sale. There are no other speakers that look like the Bowers & Wilkin’s Zeppelin. Its Zeppelin Pro is 29 percent off at Amazon in the black color option, costing $639 (originally $899). We haven’t tested this particular model, but it seems impressive, featuring five drivers (one being a six-inch subwoofer), plus Bluetooth, AirPlay 2 and Spotify Connect. It also has an optional downward-firing light that gives it a unique presence in the room. You can tell that Samsung is trying to get rid of monitors when it’s selling a whopping 49-inch OLED gaming monitor for $999.99 (originally $1,699.99). That’s how much its ultrawide Odyssey OLED G93SD costs now at Best Buy. Its width is roughly equivalent to sticking two 25-inch 1440p monitors next to other, then curving them inward slightly for a more immersive viewing experience. The full resolution is 5,210 x 1,440 and it features a 240Hz refresh rate. The screen has a 110 pixels per inch density, which isn’t great, though it’s the standard for most QHD OLED gaming monitors. The monitor includes a three-year warranty protecting against defects, however, Samsung’s warranty page doesn’t explicitly mention burn-in.

fullText:
While not as big as the last release, Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 is a sizable update ahead of the stable December release.

Private Compute Core log

Private Compute Core is a “secure environment that is isolated from the rest of the operating system and apps” that Google first launched in 2021. This on-device processing powers Now Playing, Smart Reply, Live Translate, Live Caption, Google Messages Spam Detection, and Cough & Snore Detection.

Pixel 11 support is coming

Platform stability milestone

Bug fixes

Enabling the “render apps below the cutout area” developer setting caused a transparent status bar on the launcher after exiting fullscreen video playback. (Issue #295747911)

title: Gemini Spark rolling out Google Photos control for automated editing, sharing, & more
snippet: The latest first-party app that Gemini Spark can control is Google Photos. The personal agent can “handle complex, multi-stage workflows” with your library. more…
fullText:
The latest first-party app that Gemini Spark can control is Google Photos. The personal agent can “handle complex, multi-stage workflows” with your library.

Available Google Photos actions that Gemini Spark can perform include:

Search & curate: Find specific photos and videos by subject, location, date, or event. Ask Gemini for the best shots and to filter duplicates.

title: Startup ARR is less secure than ever, new research shows
snippet: The AI era has completely broken enterprise buying patterns, and startups haven't yet figured out how to navigate.
fullText:
AI has ushered in a lot of never-happened-before moments, but one of the most transformative is its impact on enterprise IT. Companies that have historically been cautious and committed long-term to what they buy are on pace to spend $4.25 trillion on technology in 2026, market researcher IDC predicts. It’s almost all driven by AI.

New research from venture capital firm Madrona shows that 74% of 150 enterprise IT professionals it surveyed plan to expand their AI budgets in the next 12 months, and the rest plan to hold spending steady. Yet these same enterprises say that fewer than half of their AI pilots ever make it into full production.

That’s actually an improvement. Last year, MIT famously reported that 95% of enterprise AI projects had failed in terms of ROI. Fewer than half succeeding is a pretty low bar, but it’s better than a 5% success rate.

But the most telling finding from Madrona’s report is that, even when an enterprise does roll out the AI tech, it doesn’t commit to it long term.

Some 77% of enterprises reevaluate their AI vendors every six months or even on a rolling basis. “This creates a ‘fast in, fast out’ dynamic that is fundamentally different from traditional enterprise SaaS, where multi-year contracts provided a moat of inertia,” Madrona writes in the report. “In enterprise AI, switching costs are lower and the re-evaluation cadence is relentless.”

This has widespread implications for all those fast-growing annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers startups report. Enterprise trial budgets are what fueled the initial AI boom of 2025. This year was supposed to be the year these big customers settled in and started committing long term to AI startups. Enterprise contracts are what allow so many AI startups to claim astronomically fast revenue growth — think the phenomenon of startups going from $0-$10 million in three months.

Yet, for the first time ever, enterprise revenue remains insecure, even after a startup’s AI product graduates out of a pilot phase and gets adopted by a company.

Part of the issue is that many AI startups haven’t fully landed on a good way to price their AI wares for enterprises. New research from VC firm Andreessen Horowitz that surveyed 50 technical AI buyers found that more than half of them want AI fees tied to the work produced or other outcomes, rather than to usage like the number of tokens consumed.

Charging for usage like tokens is basically a SaaS-era business model. Once an enterprise knows it needs email, or HR software, or cloud storage, it’s merely a matter of how many employees or how much data it must pay for.

For AI, pricing “around the recognizable work” is what helps the startup prove its worth to the customer. When the fees revolve around, say, how many reports are processed, or tickets closed, or leads generated, this makes the product “economically valuable to both sides,” writes a16z partners Tugce Erten and Sarah Wang.

All of this means that AI has potentially ushered in a new era of enterprise experimentation. That opens doors to startups — enterprises are more willing to try their tech — but it also means an enterprise contract no longer secures long-term revenue. When or if enterprises will revert to their long-term buying habits remains to be seen.
