title: Accel reportedly in talks to lead $1B round for Thinking Machines at $40B valuation
snippet: The high-profile startup's annual revenue run rate stands at over $100 million.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:36 PM PDT · September 3, 2026

Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Thinking Machines, the AI lab founded early last year by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, is in discussions to raise $1 billion at a valuation of at least $40 billion, The Information reported Thursday. Existing backer Accel is in talks to lead the fundraise, according to our source and The Information’s reporting.

The new round, if it is completed, would value the company below the $50 billion valuation that Thinking Machines reportedly sought to secure late last year.

Thinking Machines’ annual revenue run rate stands at over $100 million, according to a source with knowledge of the company’s financials. At that revenue figure, a $40 billion valuation reflects an extraordinarily high revenue multiple.

Accel and Thinking Machines didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In July, the company introduced Inkling, an open-weight model that generates revenue by charging usage-based compute fees for adapting models on proprietary data on its Tinker platform.

The startup’s prior fundraise — a $2 billion round that stands among the largest seed financings in history — valued the company at $12 billion. Andreessen Horowitz led the investment, joined by Nvidia, GV, Lightspeed, and Conviction Partners. Investors backed the round largely on the pedigree of Murati and the former OpenAI researchers who joined her.

Thinking Machines has since had several high-profile departures, with some of the co-founders, including Lilian Weng and Luke Metz, going back to OpenAI.

fullText:
Siri AI on Apple Watch arrived two cycles late for watchOS 27 beta this summer. I had high hopes for how new Siri could transform Apple Watch into an AI wearable.

What actually happened in July and August is that Siri has been remarkably unusable in watchOS 27 beta. Like “hold off on updating” bad.

This week, I half-expected Apple to remove “Siri AI” from watchOS 27 beta 8 and revert to the previous version of Siri. Instead, I think Siri AI on Apple Watch actually got good?

Siri AI on Apple Watch has been a major regression this summer

The issues that plagued Siri AI on Apple Watch all summer were clear.

Siri has been slow and unresponsive. At times, Siri has been unable to do tasks like set alarms and create reminders.

Setting a timer while cooking? Go ahead and subtract at least 30 seconds from the timer to give Siri time to get it together.

Controlling HomeKit accessories with Siri on Apple Watch has also been terribly slow with watchOS 27 beta. Really, just any normal Siri task on Apple Watch: starting a workout, sending a text, you name it.

Based on two months of pre-release betas without signs of improvement, I thought Apple might need to delay Siri AI on Apple Watch. At least for existing hardware… or maybe they were just going to mess up Siri for everyone who updates? 

watchOS 27 beta 8 appears to shape things up just in time

Well, it’s been a few days since watchOS 27 beta 8 arrived, and I think all of my summer beta issues with Siri AI are just fixed now.

	

I’m always cautious to declare something resolved that could still be an issue for others. But at least in my experience, it’s a night-and-day difference with Siri AI on Apple Watch this week. I hope that’s true for everyone.

I’ve really enjoyed Siri AI for easily getting answers to the kind of knowledge questions that my curious 8-year-old son asks me. It’s especially great to do this without needing my phone. AI on Apple Watch has been a pretty big gap for the last couple of years, and Siri AI solves it — as long as it actually works.

I’m optimistic for the first time since Siri AI arrived in beta that it actually does work now. Are you testing Siri AI on Apple Watch yet? How has your experience been this summer and this week? 

(Now my one watchOS 27 complaint is that double-clicking the Digital Crown no longer jumps between recent apps… maybe watchOS 27.1 will do something with the double-click gesture. For a device so button-constrained that only the Ultra gets an Action button, it’s odd to see a double-click gesture replaced with … nothing.)

title: Apple faces yet another lawsuit over App Tracking Transparency, with a twist [U]
snippet: While Apple has long used privacy as a selling point for both its hardware and services, I do wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT). For something with rather limited scope, it sometimes feels like scarcely a month goes by without a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator challenging it. fullText:
While Apple has long used privacy as a selling point for both its hardware and services, I do wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

For something with rather limited scope, it sometimes feels like scarcely a month goes by without a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator challenging it. A third ATT lawsuit is being brought in the UK – this one with a twist.

This piece has been updated with a response by Apple at the end of the piece …

Personalized advertising has been one of the hot button tech topics for many years now. Instead of seeing random ads for products that may or may not interest us, we are shown ads based on our interests, as gleaned from the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win for all parties. Consumers are shown ads that may genuinely interest them; advertisers get better results from their ad spend because it is targeted; while free apps and websites funded by ads get higher payments for the same reason.

Although the data used to serve personalised ads is collected in an anonymised form, the practice has led to a widespread perception of it as an invasion of privacy. Even when Apple specifically developed a technology to ensure that this data was anonymous, many consumers remained suspicious.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple’s App Tracking Transparency was designed to solve the problem by letting consumers choose whether or not their data could be used to serve personalized ads. Developers who wish to collect this data must ask consumers for permission.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, this has led to a whole slew of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, mostly based around the fact that Apple’s own apps don’t seek this permission. The company has on numerous occasions pointed out that its rules are in fact consistent: Apple’s own apps don’t present the ATT prompt because they don’t collect the data it references. Third-party apps that don’t collect this data are also exempted from the need to present the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints to the UK’s relevant antitrust regulator, the Competition Appeal Tribunal. Apple lost the first of these – though is currently appealing – and the second one is still ongoing.

Reuters reports on the third, which was filed today.

Apple is facing a £2 billion ($2.7 billion) London lawsuit brought on behalf of app developers over its app tracking rules, with the ​iPhone maker accused of abusing its power to unfairly impose ‌greater restrictions on third parties. The lawsuit, filed at London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal on Thursday, follows years of regulatory scrutiny over Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature.

With a twist

The latest lawsuit has an interesting twist: it’s being brought by Ann Pope, who was previously a senior official with the regulator behind today’s case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official with Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority who ​is leading the lawsuit, said Apple’s policy “resulted in very significant harm ​to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper”.

“This action is important to protect ‌the ⁠rights of British businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure that the rules that Apple applies are fair, and to compensate the losses that British companies have suffered,” Pope said in a statement.

Apple recently agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU following an investigation by the German antitrust regulator. In respect of this lawsuit, the company told us:

At Apple, we believe privacy is a fundamental human right, and we created App Tracking Transparency to give users a simple way to control whether apps have permission to track their activity across other companies’ apps and websites. Apple is bound by the exact same requirements as all developers under ATT, and this feature has been embraced by our customers and praised by privacy advocates and data protection authorities around the world, including in the UK. We disagree with these claims, and will continue to defend strong privacy protections for our users.

A number of privacy advocates have spoken up in support of ATT over the years.

title: Ford explains why it chose Apple Maps over Google for its new EVs
snippet: Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom.

In a new interview, Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced vehicle projects, elaborated on the decision to use Apple Maps instead of Google Maps and what this means for CarPlay Ultra.

In an interview with GreenCars, Clarke said Ford spoke with Apple, Google, and others about mapping for the Fathom. Ultimately, the company turned to Apple:

“We had to optimize for performance capabilities cost, quality, you name it. We spent time determining which was the best solution.

A couple of things about Apple Maps.

One is that it has gotten so much better over the last few years. It’s a really great solution. The team that we worked with at Apple was very flexible to ensure that we get the absolute best customer experience.”

Clarke said Ford wanted a close working relationship with the Apple Maps team. There are a lot of factors that go into mapping for an EV, including things like range, charger availability, weather, and more. Taking all of those things into account, Ford determined Apple offers “the best solution.” 

“We wanted to make sure that we had really tight integration with that team when we’re talking about the things that have to happen on a vehicle: range estimation and determining how much range you have and how you want to precondition the batteries and how you charge.

You need a great maps provider that has the capability to get elevation, weather, and the maps data to have accurate updated information about chargers.

I think we thought that Apple was the best solution for this vehicle in order to get the customer the best solution.

It’s amazing to be first as well. Apple Maps looks beautiful, and having a large display to be able to put it on we think will be a really big wow factor for our customers when they get to see it.”

Clarke also confirmed that this is Ford integrating Apple Maps into its native, in-car software platform. The automaker is not adopting CarPlay Ultra in the Fathom. Instead, it will offer native Apple Maps, plus standard CarPlay and Android Auto.

With CarPlay support, Ford drivers can choose between Apple Maps, Google Maps, Waze, and other mapping solutions. They can also easily access many excellent third-party CarPlay apps.

fullText:
As the impact of RAMageddon continues, a couple of this week’s key stories have had me thinking – is the somewhat-boring nature of Samsung’s year-over-year Galaxy flagship refreshes the exact thing making these devices a hit?

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Outside of the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s wider new form factor, 2026 has been a pretty boring year for Samsung Galaxy devices. The Galaxy S26 series is nothing more than a chipset refresh and the Ultra’s Privacy Display, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Flip 8 were both refinements, the latter feeling like it’s on its last legs. Then the Galaxy S26 FE launched this week, which might as well be a poster child (right next to the Pixel 11 series) for the impacts of RAMageddon with its barely-updated package that costs more than last year.

Yet, it’s working.

	

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is, as of the latest update, the world’s most popular Android phone. A $1,300 flagship is outselling Samsung’s uber-cheap budget phones that the company’s success is built on. That’s wild, and it’s also the first time that’s ever happened. It comes alongside foldables as a whole being the one segment of the smartphone market that isn’t shrinking back right now – it’s actually growing steadily. New forecasts from the IDC this week claim that the “cheap smartphone era is over” and that price hikes are essentially never going away, and it’s just looking so bleak.

So how is Samsung actually pulling it off?

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a hit, and that’s probably in large part because not only is it new, but it directly addresses feedback from users. Thin and light, media-centric designs have been among the biggest requests from foldables right up there alongside ditching the crease – which the Fold 8 also more or less does. The Galaxy S26 Ultra manages this in far less exciting fashion. There was nothing especially new or groundbreaking about the latest Samsung flagship – Privacy Display rules, but it’s not exactly a game-changer – but it proved incredibly popular. I suspect that comes down largely to the simple fact that, if you’re looking for a new smartphone, the Galaxy S26 Ultra is an incredibly safe bet. For the millions on older Galaxy flagships, it’s a no-brainer, especially with trade-in deals thrown up on top.

The strategy is working. No one has to like it, but it is working. On that note, the other thing on my mind was an opinion post asking if Samsung is actually the problem, or if slab smartphone design as a whole has “peaked.” On the one hand, yes, smartphone design has pretty much peaked. On the other, yes, Samsung is the problem. As we’ve discussed repeatedly at this point, Samsung’s existing Galaxy design is an actual problem for users and for the future of smartphone accessories. The market is moving in a direction that Samsung’s phones are incompatible with, and Samsung’s answer to that is apparently to make changes on its highest-end designs and leave the base models stubbornly in the same place. Yes, Samsung is the problem.

But as RAMageddon continues and Samsung’s devices remain a steady rock in the turbulent market, I can’t blame anyone for going for a Galaxy flagship. Boring or not, it checks all of the boxes, and that’s really all that matters for the time being.

title: WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking
snippet: A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. more…
fullText:
A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. 

First spotted by @VBarraquito on Twitter/X and further confirmed by “Mobile Hacker” and NotebookCheck, a very straightforward flaw exists within WhatsApp for Android that allows someone to access a user’s private photos before the device is unlocked. 

This works by first having a WhatsApp call pop up and be answered – this doesn’t require the phone to be unlocked, just like a standard phone call – at which point the user can tap a button to use filters and effects on their video feed, including Meta’s AI to edit a photo – you can see where this is going. Instead of preventing access to photos, the preview is shown clearly before the phone ever asks to be unlocked with a PIN or biometrics.

This isn’t universal, though. NotebookCheck found that a Galaxy device does force the lockscreen to be unlocked before reaching this step, while Pixel and Oppo devices both allowed the full bypass. The loophole doesn’t exist on iPhone, where WhatsApp is forced to use the native iOS calling UI.

	

The plastic piece here has nothing to do with the exploit, and is presumably only for covering a contact name

The good news: this doesn’t seem to bypass the lockscreen fully, as accessing any other part of the device is still blocked. There’s also not much that can be done with the photos beyond physically seeing them – though a malicious party could use this to take photos of those images with a second device. 

WhatsApp should be able to patch this with an update, but no such update has been announced at this time. The loophole has been reported to both WhatsApp and Google. 

In the meantime, a temporary workaround is to set WhatsApp’s photo/video access to “limited” in Android’s permissions, which breaks the loophole.

title: Philips Hue adds HDMI-free Sync and new 4K Box, Nanoleaf integration, and more app upgrades
snippet: To kick off IFA 2026, Philips Hue announced a new set of sync boxes for its Play lighting. The company also teased a few new app long-awaited changes to the app, and a Nanoleaf partnership that makes your light-up triangles compatible with Philips Hue’s products. more…
fullText:
To kick off IFA 2026, Philips Hue announced a new set of sync boxes for its Play lighting. The company also teased a few new app long-awaited changes to the app, and a Nanoleaf partnership that makes your light-up triangles compatible with Philips Hue’s products.

Philips Hue’s Play Sync Box 8K is an incredible addition to any home theater or living room, but it’s expensive. At around $385, you can connect your TV’s visuals with compatible Philips Hue lights, but that isn’t a feasible option for a lot of users.

Camera-based light kits have become popular for users who want the experience without spending the money on Philips’ good-but-pricey hardware. Options from companies like Govee fill that gap for much less.

Today, though, Philips Hue announced that it’s going to offer a couple of more affordable options for users, starting with its own camera-based sync box. The Philips Hue Play Screen Sync is made up of a single fisheye camera that sits on the top of your TV. It captures colors displayed by your TV, so not only is it more affordable, but it’s input-agnostic. Unlike the 8K Sync Box, this model will work with native TV apps because it isn’t pulling from select HDMI feeds.

	

The Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box 4K sits in the middle of three, with a similar experience and compatibility to the higher resolution version. It only has one HDMI connection, which might make it ideal for those that just need a connection to an AVR, instead of media players and consoles.

Both new models can also opt to sync to devices through Bluetooth instead of using a Hue Bridge. That makes the setup simpler. The Hue Bridge and Hue Bridge Pro allow connections to expand to 10 lights, as opposed to a single light strip.

With that, new gradient strip lights were announced for entertainment spaces. Philips Hue says these strips will be available for TVs up to 100 inches.

The IFA announcement continues with an announcement regarding a new partnership with Nanoleaf. The company says compatible Nanoleaf shapes can be integrated into the Philips Hue ecosystem with the Wall Light Module. Those devices will work with Hue’s scenes and automations within app control.

The app itself is also getting a couple of changes. First, Philips Hue on Android and iOS will get backup and restore functionality, so users don’t lose their scenes and automations if the app is deleted or they switch phones. The app will also introduce Custom AI Behaviors, which use natural-language instructions to create more sophisticated and personalized automations by combining triggers, conditions, and lighting actions.

Both of those upgrades will roll out “beginning in fall 2026.”

The new Philips Hue Play Screen Sync will start at $119, while the Play HDMI sync box will be available for $149. Both are now available on Philips Hue’s website and retailers like Amazon.

title: Siri AI won’t be your friend, and here’s why that really matters
snippet: Elon University has partnered with The Washington Post to conduct what turned out to be a worrying survey about Americans viewing AI chatbots as virtual friends or therapists. The results very much vindicate Apple’s careful decision to ensure that Siri AI doesn’t encourage such pseudo-relationships … more…
fullText:
Elon University has partnered with The Washington Post to conduct what turned out to be a worrying survey about Americans viewing AI chatbots as virtual friends or therapists.

The results very much vindicate Apple’s careful decision to ensure that Siri AI doesn’t encourage such pseudo-relationships … 

The AI friendship findings

More than a quarter of Americans view AI chatbots in much the same way they might a close friend or therapist, according to The Washington Post.

Many talk to AI apps as they might a close friend or therapist […] 27% of Americans turn to AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini with personal, emotional or social queries, according to a new poll [including] seeking entertainment, relationship advice, romantic chats, or connection when alone.

Among the people who said they used chatbots for personal or emotional queries or discussions, nearly 4 in 10 strongly or somewhat agreed that they sometimes talked to AI to feel less alone. Nearly a third said they consider the chatbot they use most often to be a friend.

While some of this usage may serve positive purposes, the concern is that having chatbots act as an emotional substitute for friendship and romance reduces the incentives to invest time and effort in establishing genuine human connections. It may lead to a downward spiral of increasing social isolation.

Siri AI does not encourage this

Apple execs Craig Federighi and Greg Joswiak said earlier this year that Siri AI will not act in this way.

Q: “So just to confirm, there are no AI girlfriends or boyfriends being created with the updated Siri AI?”

A: No, no, no. Quite the opposite. Because as you may know, if you use many of the existing chatbots, they’re really focused on engagement to a large degree. And sycophantic, right? They kind of want to pull you in. They might encourage you to reveal things about yourself and then use that as a basis to establish a connection.

And we view it quite the opposite. I mean, the way that we have designed Siri, Siri really wants to say, listen, that’s not what I’m here for, right? I’m here to help you. I can help you get things done. I can help you learn about the world. But if you try to engage Siri as a romantic partner, Siri is not up for that.

9to5Mac’s Take

I found the survey results extremely alarming, especially after listening to the excellent Suspicious Minds: Al and the Apocalypse podcast about AI-fueled delusions. The stance Apple is taking here is absolutely the right one.

title: Samsung is randomly deactivating some accounts for ‘security reasons’
snippet: A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.” more…
fullText:
A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.”

Over the past 24 hours or so, a number of Samsung Galaxy users have taken to the web with reports of being locked out of their Samsung accounts. A message appears saying that the account is “deactivated.”

Can’t sign in. Account deactivated for security reasons.

Dozens of users have reported the issue across Reddit threads and Samsung’s Community forums. Samsung hasn’t directly provided an explanation for the issue. This can have a pretty big impact on using a Galaxy device, especially if a user is invested in Samsung’s software ecosystem including apps like SmartThings, Wallet, and Find. 

Some users appear to have had success getting back into their account with the help of support, but it’s very hit or miss. 

	

While there’s no clear problem at play here, it does appear that alias email addresses may play a role – adding “+” or “.” to an address. One support representative apparently mentioned this and a number of those affected mentioned that they do indeed use an alias of their email address for their Samsung account. But not everyone affected uses an alias, so this is likely not the sole cause.

Samsung has yet to confirm the issue or comment on a fix beyond generic troubleshooting. We’ve reached out to Samsung for more information and will update this article when we hear back.

If you’re running into this problem, let us know in the comments below.

Thanks Evan!

title: XDOF, just three months out of stealth, is in talks for a Series B at a $1.2B valuation
snippet: The round is being raised just months after the robot data startup exited from stealth.
fullText:
Less than three months after emerging from stealth, XDOF, a startup that collects real-world teleoperation data for training general-purpose robots, is in late-stage talks to raise a Series B at a valuation of about $1.2 billion valuation led by 8VC, several people with knowledge of the deal said.

XDOF was co-founded by UC Berkeley researchers Philipp Wu (CEO) and Fred Shentu (CTO) in 2024. TechCrunch reported on the startup’s $70 million Series A in June, with participation from Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Lux, and Spark Capital. XDOF wasn’t planning to raise again so soon after that round. But the company’s rapid growth — with annualized revenue approaching $50 million — prompted VCs to approach it about a new round, the people said.

TechCrunch was unable to learn the total capital being raised or whether the valuation includes the new funding. The terms of the deal are not final and could still change.

XDOF and 8VC didn’t respond to our request for comment. 

The startup aims to build the data pipelines, collection tools, and annotation systems that frontier AI labs and robotics companies can’t easily build themselves, essentially acting as an outsourced data-supply chain for the robotics industry.

As a PhD student, Wu was studying how robots learn from large datasets. One big impediment to his research was the lack of “large-scale data to work with,” he told TechCrunch in June.

So he teamed up with Shentu on a project called GELLO, a low-cost teleoperation system that allows a human operator to control a robotic arm remotely in order to generate training data. Their work led to an influential paper in robotics.

That research formed the foundation for XDOF, which investors now describe as the Scale AI or Mercor for physical robotics, a reference to the data-labeling giants that helped fuel the AI boom. Unlike LLMs, which initially trained on the entirety of the internet, physical robots don’t have an equivalent real-world dataset to draw from, making data collection a critical bottleneck to building general-purpose machines.

XDOF is partnering with UC Berkeley’s AI Research lab to release what it believes is the largest collection of high-quality robot training data ever assembled, dubbed ABC. 

To capture this data, XDOF combines remote robot teleoperation with human collectors who wear sensors to record everyday tasks like folding clothes and flattening boxes.

The startup plans to hire and train teams of data collectors worldwide, including teleoperators who steer robots remotely and egocentric operators who wear body sensors to capture movement data.  

XDOF previously told TechCrunch that it is already working with 20 customers, including several frontier AI labs.

Other startups attempting to collect real-world data for robot training include Mecka AI, as well as human-data platforms expanding beyond LLMs, such as Scale AI and Micro1.

title: Google Meet hardware dropping ChromeOS for Android
snippet: As we wait for consumer Googlebooks to launch, Google shared today that it is “transitioning [its] Google Meet hardware portfolio from ChromeOS to Android.” more…
fullText:
As we wait for consumer Googlebooks to launch, Google shared today that it is “transitioning [its] Google Meet hardware portfolio from ChromeOS to Android.”

Existing Google Meet hardware consists of touchscreen controllers, cameras, microphones, speakers, and what’s essentially a Chromebox to run scheduling software and the actual video conferencing suite.

Google is replacing ChromeOS with Android going forward. That said, “existing investments in ChromeOS devices are protected,” with full software support: “We will continue delivering security patches, stability updates, and ChromeOS releases for all Google Meet hardware running ChromeOS.” There are no changes to support timelines, with hardware continuing to work until 2030 for recent models. 

Hardware partners like Logitech, CTL, and Asus will “gradually end manufacturing and sales for ChromeOS-based hardware according to the following timelines.”

	

Logitech / CTL Google Meet Compute System: February 2027

ASUS Google Meet Compute System: April 2027

For customers looking to purchase ChromeOS devices to complement their existing fleet, particularly for large event spaces, we encourage you to purchase devices as soon as possible.

Google says Android for Google Meet hardware “provides several benefits”:

Device variety: Android-based room hardware offers a broader range of form factors, including compact all-in-one devices, video bars, and integrated room solutions. Whether equipping a focus room, collaborative huddle space, or boardroom, you have options to find the right fit.

Enterprise stability: Android-based devices deliver the performance, responsiveness, and stability you rely on with ChromeOS.

Hardware flexibility: Certified AOSP devices can run multiple video conferencing solutions, protecting your investment by allowing rooms to be repurposed without replacing equipment.

Long lifecycles: Devices certified for Google Meet are engineered for long-term reliability and predictable software support.

The company teases “several exciting Android devices intended for large-format spaces planned for 2027.”

title: Razer Prio is an Android and iPhone game controller that folds down to roughly the size of a credit card
snippet: Razer has just launched its new Prio game controller, a USB-C controller for your smartphone that folds down to the footprint of a credit card. more…
fullText:
Razer has just launched its new Prio game controller, a USB-C controller for your smartphone that folds down to the footprint of a credit card.

Available now, the Razer Prio’s claim to fame is that it’s very compact. 

Like countless other mobile game controllers, it attaches to either side of your phone and plugs in via USB-C, but when you’re not actively using it, the controller folds down into a size that’s roughly the same footprint as a credit card – around 10-15mm wider and taller. It’s obviously a lot thicker, but it’s still a much smaller footprint in your pocket or bag. It weighs 101g. 

Despite the size, it still features tactile low-profile thumbsticks and dual bumpers and triggers, as well as a D-Pad and ABXY buttons. The thumbsticks avoid drift issues by using contactless sensors. 

	

Razer Prio is available today for $99.99 from the company’s online store, the same price as Kishi V3. Prio is also already available and shipping via Amazon.

title: watchOS 27 removes three features that Apple Watch users might miss after updating
snippet: When watchOS 27 is released later this month, Apple Watch users may notice that some things work a bit differently. The upcoming software update removes three features that users may miss after updating. more…
fullText:
When watchOS 27 is released later this month, Apple Watch users may notice that some things work a bit differently. The upcoming software update removes three features that users may miss after updating.

Walkie-Talkie removed from Apple Watch

First up is Walkie-Talkie, Apple’s real-time voice communication app that only works between Apple Watches. 

Personally, Walkie-Talkie never clicked for me, especially because leaving it on meant having the yellow app icon on your watch face. Others who use it in real-world situations are already missing it, and more people will notice this month (and on new Apple Watches).

I don’t think a third-party app can replicate exactly what Apple offered with Walkie-Talkie on Apple Watch. Still, a version that works on both iPhone and Apple Watch would be better received, I think.

Multitasking shortcut is missing

Next, there’s the Digital Crown double-click multitasking gesture that now does … the same thing as single-clicking the Digital Crown. I wrote about this in my watchOS 27 public beta preview and again yesterday. 

I don’t know if double-clicking the Digital Crown will be the way forward on multitasking in watchOS. Still, a way to quickly jump between two apps or an app and the watch face has always been useful. I hope a solution returns. 

As for the double-click button shortcut, I think the Apple Watch is so button-limited that there should be something that happens with a double-click, even if it’s not multitasking. I’m thinking about this as two separate possibilities now.

Dynamic app grid always comes first

Lastly, there’s what happens when you just click the Digital Crown a single time.

Since watchOS 1 (when it was called Watch OS 1), clicking the Digital Crown from the watch face or inside an app has invoked the full app launcher. Before now, the biggest change to this system was when Apple removed the first click centering the app grid before returning to the watch face. 

watchOS 27 replaces it with the dynamic app grid: five intelligently suggested apps, the Siri app, and an icon for the full app grid. You can tap the app grid icon, or scroll the Digital Crown up to see your full grid or list of apps.

I get it. Apps aren’t super popular on the Apple Watch. The new dynamic app grid has larger tap targets with fewer icons to navigate. It also puts the Siri app in your face, which is a common theme of Apple’s OS 27 updates in general. 

If given the option, I’d probably turn off the dynamic app grid. I think it’s a fine default, but it feels cumbersome compared to just viewing the app launcher.

Anyway, change of any kind always takes a period of adjustment before it just becomes how things work. Still, I’ve been running watchOS 27 since the first day of beta 1 in June. For me, losing Walkie-Talkie isn’t something I notice, losing the multitasking shortcut feels temporary, and the dynamic app grid is a fine default, but cumbersome for speedier users.

Of course, I’d trade it all if we could get the Explorer watch face back. Removing features and changing how things work is par for the course, but removing Apple Watch faces when they’re already pretty user-removable still doesn’t make sense.

title: OpenAI calls trade secret dispute ‘a mess of Apple’s own making’
snippet: Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more. The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” … more…
fullText:
Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more.

The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” …

The ongoing lawsuit is to determine whether Liu and Tang Tan stole confidential information acquired from their employment at Apple in order to help OpenAI develop an AI hardware device. In particular, it alleges that both engineers downloaded confidential engineering files after leaving the iPhone maker.

Apple was granted access to a MacBook belonging to Liu in order to carry out a forensic analysis to determine whether it held evidence of unlawful access to the company’s intellectual property. The firm yesterday submitted a court filing claiming it had found four “shocking” pieces of evidence backing its allegations.

In its own filing made the same day, Reuters reports that OpenAI doesn’t hold back.

Employees “can leave a company like Apple that has struggled to ⁠adopt ​AI and move to an exciting startup that builds innovative products,” ​OpenAI wrote. “Apple may not like those choices. But it cannot claim those choices are unlawful, and it cannot use its own sloppy ​procedures to blame others for its own mess.”

	

Specifically, it says the problems were caused by three issues:

Apple encourages employees to use personal iCloud accounts to access Apple documents

Departing employees aren’t given enough time to return company devices, transfer files back to the company, and hand over responsibilities

Former employees are contacted by their erstwhile team members for assistance after they have left, requiring them to access company information

9to5Mac’s Take

On the face of it, the evidence Apple provided yesterday does appear damning. OpenAI doesn’t seem to be denying that confidential Apple information was used by the company, but rather claiming that the iPhone maker failed to properly protect it.

However, while I’m not a lawyer, my understanding is that this could become a crucial argument – since companies can only claim information comprises a trade secret if they have taken appropriate steps to protect it. If OpenAI can show that Apple did not do so, then the AI company could prevail even if use of the information is proven.

snippet: Samsung is expanding its Android 17 / One UI 9 beta program to several new Galaxy smartphones this month, signaling that the stable release isn’t too far away. more…
fullText:
Samsung is expanding its Android 17 / One UI 9 beta program to several new Galaxy smartphones this month, signaling that the stable release isn’t too far away.

The update will be available as an opt-in beta through the Samsung Members app in India, Korea, the US, and the UK “in September.” While there’s no concrete timeline, it’s likely to be sooner than later based on past releases.

title: iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad
snippet: Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order. Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad. iOS 27 is currently in beta, and the behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, eight developer betas so far show this change will ship this month — even if I’d change it. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is currently in beta, and the behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, eight developer betas so far show this change will ship this month — even if I’d change it.

Siri AI takes over the swipe gesture for a lot of the iPhone and iPad top edge

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Notifications now live in the top left corner

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

	

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri. 

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

iOS 27 is currently available as a developer and public beta. The official release is expected this month.

title: Google’s Gemini Spark can now manage your Google Photos library
snippet: Gemini Spark can edit and curate photo albums, create shared collections, turn photos into calendar events, and handle other Google Photos tasks for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.
fullText:
Google is integrating more of its services with AI, as the company announced that its personal agent, Gemini Spark, can now manage your Google Photos library. That means you can ask Gemini Spark to execute tasks in Google Photos, like editing images, curating albums, automatically creating shared albums with your favorite shots, turning concert flyer photos into calendar appointments, running workflows, and more. 

On Thursday evening, Google Photos lead Shimrit Ben-Yair shared the new capabilities in a post on X, noting that the new capabilities would roll out over the next few weeks to eligible Gemini AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the U.S. in English.

The company didn’t say if or when it would roll out more broadly to international markets.

For a while now, I’ve relied on @GeminiApp and @antigravity agents across a wide range of use cases—spanning creativity, productivity, and analysis. But I’ve always dreamed of having a power agent to help me get the most out of my 143,206 photos and videos. And that day has come!… pic.twitter.com/WbnkYpattQ

— shimrit ben-yair (@shimritby) September 3, 2026

The addition is yet another example of Google attempting to find product-market fit in terms of making AI appealing to consumers — in this case, by automating tedious tasks and helping people manage what are now often sizable photo libraries.

The move comes at a time when the AI industry is reckoning with the fact that it hasn’t properly sold the promise of AI to consumers. This week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Bloomberg that the industry has “done a terrible job” communicating the benefits of technology, which has led to backlash from communities around the world.

Announcements like this from Google are part of the problem. While they may make certain tasks easier, on their own, such features don’t seem revolutionary or even, really, necessary. (It’s not that difficult to make a photo album after all.) But the competitive nature of the AI industry is pushing companies to promote every AI-infused upgrade, no matter how small, instead of waiting until the company can tell a broader story about how AI has shaped its software for the better. 

To use Gemini Spark with Google Photos, you’ll need to first connect Google Photos to Gemini, then toggle on Spark in the top corner of the Gemini app, and enter your prompt.

title: Motorola is finally making a new Wear OS watch and it’s not called the Moto 360
snippet: It’s finally happening. Motorola is making a new Wear OS smartwatch, but it’s not a new Moto 360 – this is the Moto Watch Ultra. more…
fullText:
It’s finally happening. Motorola is making a new Wear OS smartwatch, but it’s not a new Moto 360 – this is the Moto Watch Ultra.

Rewinding the clock, the Moto 360 is perhaps still the most iconic Android smartwatch of all time. It was the poster child for the early days of “Android Wear,” but Motorola threw in the towel after a couple of generations. There was a brief revival of the Moto 360 name in 2020, but even that faded away – and the licensing deal behind it is likely why Motorola isn’t using that name now.

Motorola hasn’t stopped making smartwatches in that time, but they’ve all been based on an RTOS, making them fall into the category of smartwatches that are focused on health tracking and battery life at the expense of more useful notifications and access to a proper app ecosystem. The most recent attempt ended up cloning Wear OS’ design, despite the limitations.

Now, Motorola has a new smartwatch – the Moto Watch Ultra.

	

The $349 smartwatch offers up a Snapdragon W5+ Gen 1 chipset, 2GB of RAM, and 32GB of storage, all used to power Wear OS 6. We’ll have to wait and see if Motorola has made any customizations to the UI here, but re-entering the Wear OS ecosystem is a pretty big deal. Motorola does note that its Qira AI assistant is on board.

The Ultra has a 1.5-inch pOLED display in a 46mm chassis that’s 12.1mm thick – though Motorola’s images make it seem a lot thicker. The display is covered in Gorilla Glass 3 and the body is stainless steel with a brushed finish in silver or gunmetal finishes. There are four strap options, including both silicone and leather, but you can use any 22mm band as there are no fancy connectors, just a traditional spring pin. There’s NFC support for Google Wallet, IP68 + 5ATM dust/water resistance, and LTE support too. Motorola claims 2 days of use from the 550 mAh battery inside – Pixel Watch 5 (45mm) has a 465 mAh battery, for comparison. Charging is handled by a magnetic dock that connects over USB-C.

On the fitness side, Motorola is working with Polar – another brand that tried and has since left the Wear OS market – with features including activity goals, scores, and intensity zones, as well as inactivity alerts, energy sources, and wellness features around breathing and sleep. 

The Moto Watch Ultra will be available unlocked starting on September 10 for $349, with a debut on Verizon on September 24. Other carriers including T-Mobile, Metro, and AT&T will follow later on. 

Beyond the Watch Ultra, Motorola is today also launching a Swarovski version of the base Razr (2026). This special release has the same specs, but with a new dark grey case that has Crystals by Swarovski embedded in the back. It also costs $100 more at $899 and is also launching on September 10.

title: MapQuest Acts Fast With Its Revived Fame, Adding Android Auto Support
snippet: The map navigator is the most downloaded app in the US after it refused to relabel Lake Ontario.
fullText:
MapQuest, who knew? A week ago, the app seemed like just another long-forgotten relic from the dotcom glory days. Now, it’s surged to the top of app download charts after the company ignored an executive order from President Donald Trump by refusing to relabel Lake Ontario as Lake America. And the company apparently is going to keep riding the wave.

The 30-year-old app announced that it was bringing its navigation service to Android Auto in an experimental phase. Thus, drivers can use MapQuest on their dashboard infotainment screens rather than Google Maps if they have Android Auto enabled.

MapQuest announced the new integration on X, saying simply, “Android Gang, dinner is served.”

Android Auto is a software system that allows Android phone apps to display on a dashboard screen, which basically performs like a computer monitor. By connecting your phone to the vehicle’s Android Auto system, you can use map apps such as Google, Waze and now MapQuest, as well as stream music and listen to podcasts or use AI programs like Google Assistant or Gemini to send texts and make calls.

What about Apple users? A message on MapQuest’s help center noted that “CarPlay is coming to the MapQuest iOS app soon!”

In addition to basic navigation, the MapQuest app is trying out a crowdsourcing feature on Android Auto. Drivers and passengers can report accidents, road closures and activity by police and other first-responders on the app so that other drivers might know what’s coming up for them on the roads.

As a comparison, MapQuest and Google Maps both have the basics — planning a route from Point A to Point B with an estimated travel time, a computer voice telling when and where to turn and search functionality to find businesses and other locations. But Google Maps also has public transit directions, indoor maps for malls and airports and user reviews of businesses through its integration with Google Search.

Read more: Google’s In-Car Gemini Dimmed the Sunroof, Ordered Dinner and Became My Tour Guide

MapQuest did not say if all Android Auto users would be able to use it or how long the beta testing would last. A representative for MapQuest did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

MapQuest back in the spotlight

It’s been a while since “MapQuest” rolled off the tongue of many Americans. The company launched on Feb. 5, 1996, and within a few years, it controlled nearly all of the market share for online mapping, with 2 million page views per day in 1999. But the company began to decline after Google launched its maps app in 2005.

That changed earlier this week. MapQuest refused to change Lake Ontario to Lake America on its maps, as Trump called for with an executive order on Aug. 27. Google and Apple complied, but MapQuest and Microsoft haven’t.

Within days, MapQuest became the No. 1 most-downloaded app in the US, with more than 1.5 million downloads since Trump’s order. The company also created a widget that lets you name the lake whatever you want.

MapQuest General Manager Doug Berger told CNN’s Erin Burnett, “We were absolutely blown away by the response,” he said. “It’s completely shocking.”

title: No little kids allowed, and other new info about Tesla’s Cybercab
snippet: The company says no children under 13 can ride -- even with a parent. That's more restrictive than the Model Y SUVs it's using as robotaxis.
fullText:
Tesla’s private Cybercab event has come and gone, and it was very different from the large, loud, livestreamed events the company usually puts on — an odd choice for the launch of a product CEO Elon Musk has spent years building toward.  

In fact, it doesn’t even appear that Musk spoke at the event, the keynote of which, by all accounts, only lasted around 15 minutes.

The promise of the Cybercab is massive: a fully autonomous vehicle that uses only cameras and AI to drive itself, all for much less than a Waymo. But Tesla scattered a lot of the details. Some are in PDFs the company released on Thursday, as well as in updated terms of service in its “Robotaxi” app. The rest were left for a select few die-hard fans to disseminate online.  

The company now has to prove that these vehicles are safe — to the public, to local governments, and to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which has already opened an investigation into Tesla’s Cybercab rollout.  

In the meantime, here are some of the most interesting new details that caught our attention: 

No Cybercab for kiddos

One of the more interesting details in the Cybercab fine print is that Tesla does not allow minors under the age of 13 to ride in the vehicle “at this time.”  

Minors between the ages of 8 and 17 are allowed to ride in Tesla’s “Robotaxi” Model Y SUVs, and Tesla does have guidelines on how to use child seats in both vehicles. 

Curiously, the Cybercab does not have the standard LATCH anchors for child seats. Instead, they can only be attached using the seat belt. Tesla executives, including Musk, have talked a lot about how much they focus on taking out unnecessary parts to cut down on costs, though I’ll admit I wasn’t expecting the company to ditch child seat anchors — especially given Musk’s obsession with making more babies. 

All children under 18 must be accompanied by an adult in both vehicles, according to Tesla. But something is making Tesla hesitate on allowing young children in the Cybercab for now. 

What happens in a crash? 

While the goal of an autonomous vehicle is to avoid crashing, even the most capable ones on the road today do wind up in collisions. 

Here’s what happens when the Cybercab gets in a crash: The airbags will inflate, the doors will unlock, the hazard warning lights and interior lights will turn on, the high voltage battery is disabled, the windows go to the “vent” position, the Cybercab will apply the brakes to come to a stop and park, and the infotainment system will start up a two-way connection with Tesla’s rider support team. 

Unlocking the doors is notable because Tesla has come under fire for its reliance on electronic door latches, both in its home market of the United States and in its largest market, China. Just last month, Tesla agreed to recall 3 million cars in China, alongside a number of other automakers, as a result of an investigation into electronic door latches that could trap people following a crash.  

Manual door releases

Speaking of doors, another recent criticism of Tesla is that its interior manual door releases are too hard to find in an emergency. These are necessary because the electronic door latches are the main method of getting in and out of the company’s vehicles, activated either by pushing a button or using a smartphone.  

The Cybercab uses electronic door latches, which allow the doors to open automatically at the start or end of a ride. There is also a small button on the exterior of the car that riders can use to open the doors. But inside, the manual release is thankfully in a very obvious spot on the armrest of each door.  

Brake-by-wire

Tesla is using a brake-by-wire system in the Cybercab, again largely (it seems) for the purposes of cutting costs. Instead of using a hydraulic system that pumps fluid through lines to control brake pressure, Tesla has electronic actuators controlling the brake calipers. 

“Having electric brakes avoids the complexity of a hydraulic system: no need to rout [sic] plumbing all around the car,” Musk wrote in a post. 

The company was already the first major automaker to use steer-by-wire on its Cybertruck, severing the physical connection between the steering wheel and the front wheels.

A little fresh air

For some reason, the windows of the Cybercab “cannot be fully opened at this time.” Tesla doesn’t explain why in the documentation it released this week. 

USB-C power

According to influencer Jeremy Judkins, the USB-C outlets in the Cybercab put out 90W of power — roughly four times more than you’d typically find inside a car.

title: Dyson Went Bonkers During IFA 2026: Here Are all 10 of Its New Products
snippet: Dyson popped off at a launch event in Berlin, introducing a whopping 10 new products.
fullText:
Gone are the days when Dyson, one of the biggest names in home and beauty tech, let new products trickle out to the masses. 

It was a slow burn at first, and for years, the brand made only vacuums, fans and air purifiers. In 2016, beauty tech, including cult-favorite hair care tools like the Supersonic hair dryer and Airwrap, was folded into the lineup. Still, we’d be lucky to see a handful of new stuff released each year.

Those days are over.

This year during IFA, the massive Euro tech showcase, Dyson has gone off, as the kids say, releasing a whopping 10 new products at its counterprogramming event in Berlin — dubbed “Dyson Unveiled.” From floorcare and air purifiers to first-ever beauty tech, including its first-ever toothbrush, Dyson’s eye-popping launch is matched only by last year when the brand introduced 11 new products.

Dyson is tackling oral care with the release of a camera-equipped toothbrush and a water flosser.Dyson

Dyson isn’t just churning out products at a faster rate, as Dyson’s Chief Engineer Jake Dyson explained. 

“The latest innovations combine Dyson’s decades of mechanical engineering with AI, vision systems and machine learning to create products that can see, understand and respond to the environments around them.”

Our team on the ground got a close-up look at everything the brand has coming to market, and the list is long. Here’s what’s new from Dyson in 2026.

CameraJet toothbrush 

At IFA 2026, we’re seeing all the upgraded, AI-powered, repairable, camera-equipped tech. And then some.Tara Brown/CNET

This is Dyson’s first toothbrush, and it houses a tiny camera for the most detailed possible cleaning. According to the brand, it’s the first oral care tool to use AI-powered vision to detect and target gaps between teeth. It brushes, liquid flosses and even dispenses mouthwash. 

The toothbrush costs $499 and is available now.

HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+ Formaldehyde air purifier

Dyson’s most powerful purifier, engineered for long-range air projection and multi-room purification, with a three-stage filtration system that captures particulates and gases and destroys formaldehyde. 

This model will cost a whopping $1,099 and hits retailers in the fall.

HushJet Pure Cool+ Formaldehyde air purifier

Dyson’s new HushJet air purifiers are a total redesign.Tara Brown/CNET

This new compact high-performance purifier and fan is designed for large spaces. The brand says it delivers three times the power of its predecessors. 

You can grab this model in the fall for $599.

HushJet Hot Cool Pure+ air purifier

Dyson’s most powerful 3-in-1 purifier, combining purification, heating and personal cooling in one machine for year-round home comfort. This also launches in the fall and retails for $599.

Read our full coverage of Dyson’s new HushJet lineup here.

R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV 

Dyson is calling the R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV its most advanced robot vacuum to date.Dyson

The brand is calling this its most advanced wet-and-dry robot vacuum to date. It features UV enhancement and, you guessed it, AI elements to help identify up to 200 types of stains and substances. The self-cleaning wet roller uses a 12-point system that continuously applies water heated to 158°F to simultaneously lift and remove stubborn stains. 

The robot vac costs $1,199 and is available starting Sept. 15.

R1 Nurovi Dry

Dyson R1 Nurovi Dry robot vacuum cleaner

The Dyson R1 Nurovi Dry is engineered for deep cleaning on hard floors and carpets. It uses Dyson’s Twin-capture technology and intelligent floor and dust sensing. 

This simpler robot vac will be available sometime in September for $549.

R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry 

Another robot vac is joining the lineup; this one has triangular cleaning pads to clean those pesky room corners. 

The Wash+Dry is now available exclusively at Costco for $699.

W1 PencilWash + Dok

The PencilWash weighs less than 5 pounds and is just as thin as the PencilVac.

Dyson

The new handheld cleaner is slimmer and lighter than the older model, includes a more absorbent roller, a hygienic waste system, and self-cleaning features built into the dock. 

It will cost $349 and will be available in the fall. 

Dyson Airsmooth dryer brush

Dyson has unveiled its first-ever dryer brush.Tara Brown/CNET

Dyson’s releases aren’t limited to air care and cleaning. The brand released its first-ever dedicated dryer brush, which uses smart heat control and novel dual-bristle technology to dry, smooth and lift hair all in one motion. 

The Airsmooth will retail for $249 starting on Sept. 8.

Dyson Corrale CoolShine straightener

Tara Brown/CNET

The success of Dyson’s cult-favorite Airwrap inspired this next-generation straightening tool, featuring flexing plates with active cooling that dries hair without exposing it to as much heat, which can damage it. 

The Corrale CoolShine costs $329 and hits shelves on Sept. 15.

title: Instagram cracking down on accounts that feature AI-generated influencers
snippet: As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach. more…
fullText:
As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach.

In a blog post, Instagram details that its “AI creator” label for accounts is now going to say “AI-generated profile,” better reflecting that the account is not just using AI, but that viewers are interacting with an influencer that is entirely AI-generated. 

Accounts that were using the “AI creator” label will have a chance to review the status and have it removed if it no longer fits their content. 

The bigger change, though, is that Instagram will actively crack down on accounts that don’t use the label at all if they are using “AI-generated influencers.” This includes not showing content in recommendations such as the “For You” page. 

	

Instagram explains:

For unlabeled profiles that feature an AI-generated person, creators can and should apply the label by editing their profile and toggling on AI-generated profile. The label will then begin to appear on their profile and alongside their content if their specific media doesn’t already have a label indicating that it was created or edited with AI. Creators who proactively add the AI-generated profile label will not see a change to their profile’s reach.

Adding the label or appealing the decision can reverse the impact, but this is a considerable change on Instagram’s part, especially as AI-generated content has become incredibly prevelant on both Instagram and Facebook, both Meta-operated platforms.

fullText:
The doors to Europe’s largest consumer tech show officially opened to the public today following a week of news coming out of IFA 2026 in Berlin, Germany. If you’re struggling to keep up with what has been announced, here are some of the best new gadgets and upgrades from the show — including a smartphone that attempts to finally rid the world of screen bezels and a powerful robovac that carries a smaller sidekick for cleaning spaces it can’t squeeze into.

To catch up on everything announced at IFA 2026 you can follow The Verge’s complete coverage right here.

Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge

By tucking the edges of its 6.78-inch, 144Hz OLED panel underneath the phone’s thin metal frame, Tecno managed to create a smartphone that nearly entirely eliminates a visible bezel, maximizing screen real estate. The aptly-named Bezelless made its debut at IFA with a MediaTek Dimensity 7400e chipset paired with 8GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, a 6,000mAh battery, and a trio of front and back cameras including a 50-megapixel main shooter. The company hasn’t announced any plans to put the concept into production, but its unique design could eventually inspire other devices.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Why build one robovac that can do it all when you can split the work between a pair of them? That’s the idea behind iRobot’s Roomba Duo concept. The main vacuum is the most powerful robovac the brand has ever made. It can suck up messes like spilled pasta, steam-mop hard floors, and vacuum and wash carpeting while navigating a home using a combination of lidar and cameras. But it’s big, so to reach and clean tighter spaces, the Roomba Duo carries a Roomba Plus 757 on top in a small garage it can raise and lower to deploy its robovac sidekick.

Image: Aurzen

One of the most portable projectors on the market is getting some welcome upgrades. The $579.99 Aurzen Zip Pro carries forward the same tri-fold design of the original including features like autofocus and automatic keystone adjustments but is getting a bump in brightness from 100 to 200 ANSI lumens and an increase in resolution to 1080P. It’s a bit bigger than its predecessor thanks in part to a battery that now offers up to 2.5 hours of runtime and added connectivity, including the ability to tether to the Nintendo Switch using only a USB-C cable.

Image: RugOne

First announced at MWC 2026 earlier this year, the RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro is an extra durable $999 Android 16 smartphone with dust and water protection, a beefy 9,300mAh battery, a 6.67-inch 120Hz AMOLED screen, and four cameras. The three on the back include a 64MP night vision camera assisted by infrared LEDs and one that can be removed and used as a standalone action camera capable of capturing video at up to 2.7K/30fps. The pop-out camera module has a battery good for up to 40 minutes and 64GB of built-in storage. When either are depleted, you can reattach to the camera module to the phone where its battery will recharge and the footage will be copied over automatically.

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Lenovo continues to experiment with ways for laptops to take advantage of flexible OLED displays, but its latest concept feels a bit tame compared to the Legion Pro Rollable gaming laptop it debuted at CES 2026. The 14-inch Project Swan concept is much smaller by comparison with a display that unfurls horizontally to grow to 17 inches with a 16:9 aspect ratio. It keeps the laptop compact while boosting productivity with extra screen real estate, but accommodating the OLED panel and motors leaves the laptop’s lid feeling unusually heavy with a design that limits how far back it can be tilted.

Image: Lexar

At its thickest point, the Muse measures around 3.8mm and will be available in 512GB or 1TB capacities with read and write speeds topping out at 1,050MB/s and 1,000MB/s, respectively. There’s not much compromise on performance, but there is with connectivity. To slim down the drive, Lexar skipped a standard USB-C port in favor of a magnetic pogo-pin connector and a proprietary USB-C cable. Not only do you have to keep tabs on a special cable, if you want to stick the Muse to the back of your smartphone while recording video you’ll need to use an included magnetic sleeve that negates the drive’s slim design.

Image: Anker

There are two new versions of Anker’s sleepbuds that can help quiet a snoring roommate, but the $349.99 Soundcore Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro introduce a new charging case with a round OLED display on the case. Without having to reach for your phone you can select a preset soundscape, browse your recent sleep stats, and set alarms. The sleepbuds also feature in-ear PPG sensors, so while you doze, they can keep tabs on the quality of your sleep, heart rate, HRV, and other health metrics that may provide insights if you wake up exhausted each morning.

Image: Oukitel

Borrowing an idea that Lenovo proposed in a laptop concept last year, Oukitel’s RG14-P features a solar panel on the lid that can recharge the laptop’s battery at up to 10W under “optimal sunlight conditions.” It would take approximately six hours to bring a dead battery up to a 50 percent charge, but you won’t have to be scrambling to find a power outlet. It’s expected to launch in November with a 14th gen Intel Core i7 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage.

Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

With most rope lighting solutions you can easily see the individual LEDs illuminating it from within, but Philips Hue’s new Liane 360-degree Rope Lights emit an even diffuse light in all directions using the company’s OmniGlow technology with the ability to adjust their color. The ropes can be used to line and illuminate architectural features, simply hung from a ceiling, or shaped using clear clips and mounts. But they’re not cheap. A 3-meter version is $399.99 while a 5-meter option is $549.99.

Image: Awol Vision

At $5,999 when it launches later this year, Awol Vision’s latest ultra-short throw projector will strain budgets, but at a distance of just 7.5 inches from a wall it can project a 4K/120Hz image with 6,000 ISO Lumens of brightness up to 120 inches in size, so it’s actually more affordable than a comparably sized flat panel TV. The LuxVision can be customized with various finishes and colors to match a room’s decor or furniture, but its most appealing feature is the projector’s ability to physically shift its lens so you can adjust and reposition the image on a wall or screen without having to rely on digital image corrections.

Image: TCL

TCL’s Nxtpaper technology is one of the better ways to merge the functionality of a modern smartphone with the benefits of a dedicated e-reader. A push of a button activates a Max Ink Mode with a paperlike monochromatic display and a streamlined version of the Android UI that reduces distractions and boosts battery life. What sets the new P80 Ultra apart is that it’s the first Nxtpaper phone to feature a 6.83-inch, 120Hz OLED screen with a 1.5K resolution and 3,200 nits of peak brightness with an anti-glare coating you won’t find on other devices.

Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge

Packard Bell dates back to 1933, but most remember the brand from when it was resurrected in 1986 and used for a line of popular and affordable home PCs in the 90s. Acer is bringing it back again for its new 14.5-inch DotBook laptop as well as a bunch of other colorful accessories including keyboards, speakers, a 4G feature phone, audio glasses, and a record player.

Image: Dreame

The smart home long ago expanded to include devices that can help care for cats and dogs, but Dreame’s LumaTempo is one of the first to help fish thrive. The smart tank can be controlled using a mobile phone on your app letting you use and schedule its build-in feeder, see a history of when your fish last ate, and keep tabs on the water temperature. It’s expected to launch next year, but pricing isn’t known yet.

Image: Acer

Flipping the gaming laptop script, Acer’s latest concept is a Windows-based gaming handheld, similar to its Predator Atlas 8, that can transform into a tiny portable PC thanks to a swiveling design that repositions its screen atop a mini keyboard. The DualPlay Mini’s display is just 8-inches in size, which could make productivity a challenge if work involves sprawling spreadsheets, but the concept could be used for answering emails during a daily commute and then connected to a larger display at work for more demanding tasks.

Image: Dell

The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or light as its recently launched XPS 13, but the company is looking to make this model even more accessible for students or others on a tighter budget. The laptop starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and those specs can be bumped to 16GB/1TB. It features a 1080P webcam with face unlock support, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and like Apple’s MacBook Neo, will be available in four bright color options: linen, dusty rose, washed denim, and velvet green.

Image: iRobot

The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is iRobot’s latest flagship floor cleaner and introduces a new feature the company calls “SealForce.” When it detects it’s cleaning carpeting, the robovac lowers a skirt around the cleaning head to create a better seal that increases suction for a deeper clean. The Max 875 also offers up to 35,000 Pa of suction power, mopping capabilities, lidar and camera-based autonomous navigation, and the ability to climb over obstacles and thresholds up to 3.5cm tall.

Image: Jsaux

Released under Jsaux’s new Voidjoy brand, the $49.99 SkyLark S1 Pro is a compact portable controller that appears to do a lot of things right. It’s got drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks that are recessed so they won’t get snagged on other devices in your bag, a pair of analog triggers ideal for racing games, and three different ways to connect to devices and consoles: Bluetooth, USB-C, and 2.4GHz. If you opt for a 2.4GHz connection, you can also pair two S1 Pros to a single transmitter and swap back-and-forth between what character you’re controlling in a multiplayer game, making it useful for parents playing with a kid who may struggle with some challenges.

Image: Acer

Is Framework’s approach to easily repairable and upgradeable laptops finally rubbing off on other companies? Acer’s 16-inch Vero 16 offers tool-free access to several internal components including its user-replaceable SSD and battery. The company says the laptop’s processor can also be upgraded down the line, but that will require it to be sent in to an Acer service center. Pricing is still unknown, but the Vero 16 is expected to launch early next year outside North America.

Image: Jsaux

If you’re lucky enough to have an original Nintendo Switch Pro controller that hasn’t succumbed to joystick drift and want to expand its capabilities, Jsaux’s new Elite Extender is an easy aftermarket upgrade. For $39.99 it attaches to the back of the controller and adds four mappable buttons that can be programmed to reproduce multiple button presses. It’s got its own rechargeable battery, but does hinder Amiibo functionality while it’s piggybacking.

title: Tesla is asking people if they want to buy and run Cybercab fleets
snippet: The company published a form on its website Thursday soliciting info from people who are interested in "Cybercab fleet vehicle purchasing."
fullText:
Tesla published a form on Thursday for businesses interested in buying Cybercab fleets or providing infrastructure for its network, the latest sign that the company’s aspirations for its gold-hued autonomous vehicle stretch beyond being a robotaxi operator.

The robotaxi interest form, which was released ahead of the company’s Cybercab event in Austin, is not definitive proof that Tesla will sell its autonomous vehicles to third-party operators. But it’s certainly an indicator of where the company’s longer-term plans lie. Tesla wants to scale and it doesn’t seem to want to do it alone.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has talked often, and for years, about building a massive fleet of low-cost robotaxis. But in the early days, those dreams centered on personally owned Tesla vehicles. As early as 2016, Musk spoke publicly about a future in which Tesla owners, equipped with self-driving software, would be able to earn money by renting out their vehicles. He stuck with that Tesla network idea for years, noting at the company’s Autonomy Day in 2019 that it would allow owners to add their autonomous vehicles to its ride-sharing app, similar to how Uber’s business model works.

“I feel very confident predicting that there will be autonomous robotaxis from Tesla next year — not in all jurisdictions because we won’t have regulatory approval everywhere,” Musk said in 2020.

That vision never materialized. Instead, the company has focused on testing, and now operating, its own fleet of robotaxis — first with Tesla Model Y vehicles and now the purpose-built Cybercab. 

Until now, Tesla seemed committed to keeping its robotaxi business in-house. The interest form, which says “helps us build our robotaxi network,” suggests the company sees promise and profits in widening the circle to include third-party companies.

What that might look like, though, isn’t defined. The company asks interested parties to pick one of several possible options, including Cybercab fleet purchasing, mobility hubs and infrastructure, event collaboration, and “other.”

There are a growing number of companies jumping into the robotaxi fleet management business. For instance, Moove, an African fintech startup that initially focused vehicle financing for ride-hailing drivers, is scaling up an autonomous fleet management business. The startup, which raised $250 million last month at a $2.1 billion valuation, is the fleet operator for Waymo in Phoenix, Miami, and Las Vegas, and in the future, London. The company doesn’t own the Waymo vehicles, but its CEO told TechCrunch that it plans to.

Other autonomous fleet management companies, which Uber has partnered with in its bid to own a piece of the robotaxi market, include Avomo and New Horizon as well as larger more traditional rental car giants like Avis and Hertz.

Tesla’s welcome mat to fleet operators could encourage more small players to open up shop — helping the company saturate markets faster.

title: The White House is making arcade games racist
snippet: Trump’s racist new “Build the Wall” game. | Image: The White House The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed "arcade" games, some of which are racist - and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be associated with the MAGA agenda.
