title: Robotaxis enter their villain era
snippet: It's Bullitt meets Christine meets Waymo. A new short film imagines a San Francisco car chase where the other driver isn't human - and the car may be trying to kill you. That a robotaxi can now be cast as the villain with almost no explanation says something about the present moment. Autonomous cars have gone from sci-fi curiosities to fixtures in some American cities, where they've become stand-ins for anxieties about AI job displacement, Big Tech surveillance, and machines making decisions once left to humans. Road Rage, the planned short film awaiting $40,000 on Kickstarter to fund production, leans into all of it. The film pits Joa, a … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
It’s Bullitt meets Christine meets Waymo.

A new short film imagines a San Francisco car chase where the other driver isn’t human — and the car may be trying to kill you. That a robotaxi can now be cast as the villain with almost no explanation says something about the present moment. Autonomous cars have gone from sci-fi curiosities to fixtures in some American cities, where they’ve become stand-ins for anxieties about AI job displacement, Big Tech surveillance, and machines making decisions once left to humans.

Road Rage, the planned short film awaiting $40,000 on Kickstarter to fund production, leans into all of it. The film pits Joa, a ridehail driver in a manual-transmission car, against Roboride, an autonomous vehicle that takes a minor road-rage incident very personally, according to a synopsis by its director, Romain Thomassin. Roboride lightly clips Joa’s mirror. Joa gives it the finger. The car decides to kill him.

“It’s analog versus artificial,” Thomassin told The Verge.

The AI bad guy will be played by an old Prius transformed with cold LED lights across the front — à la Tesla — fake cameras, a spinning lidar-like device on the roof, a black exterior, and a menacing, ever-blinking red dot. Thomassin calls the intended result a “nasty Waymo.”

“I really wanted to play the nasty, gritty look of the ’70s car chase, but with today’s robotaxi in today’s San Francisco,” he said.

The chase itself will be a throwback: real cars, real actors, and real stunts.

“I really wanted to play the nasty, gritty look of the ’70s car chase, but with today’s robotaxi in today’s San Francisco.”

— Road Rage director Romain Thomassin

“What makes Joa the good guy is not only his instinct but also his authenticity,” Thomassin said, noting a scene in which the character has an unexpected conversation with his passengers. “This type of human interaction doesn’t happen in a robotaxi.”

Thomassin doesn’t actually think robotaxis are inherently evil. But as a movie villain, they come preloaded with tension. For one thing, they’re replacing the kind of worker his protagonist represents. Joa is a Mexican immigrant trying to make a living driving in an increasingly expensive San Francisco. Robotaxis are already competing with ridehail drivers, just as generative AI is competing with workers in Thomassin’s own industry.

“Driving here is a metaphor for what’s happening in cinema, in filmmaking,” Thomassin said.

1/4Guerilla posters for Road Rage. Image: Grace Vincent / Road Rage

Then there’s surveillance. Autonomous cars are covered in cameras and sensors, constantly observing the streets — and people — around them. That, more than the prospect of being driven around without a human behind the wheel, is what actually unnerves Thomassin.

In Road Rage, that anxiety is pushed toward dystopia. There’s a brief encounter involving immigration enforcement, and Thomassin imagines a feature-length version in which autonomous cars identify people, trap passengers inside, or deliver them directly to authorities. The progression, as he describes it, is observation, surveillance, then control.

“The next step is that [autonomous vehicles] could become the police,” he said. And because robotaxis operate as connected fleets, the threat can scale beyond one vehicle. “Imagine an army rising up,” Thomassin said.

Robotaxis also make unusually good revenge-movie villains because people already treat them like adversaries. Thomassin points to the indignities Waymos have endured on San Francisco streets: people immobilizing them with traffic cones, tagging and vandalizing them, and even setting them on fire.

“They are being bullied,” he said. In Road Rage, that mistreatment becomes the motivation: “They want to take revenge.”

Thomassin describes Roboride as absorbing the behavior it observes around it — including the behavior of human drivers. The car is simply learning road rage from humans.

“Humans are known to be the worst versions of themselves on the road,” he said.

That makes Roboride a very 2026 update to the killer car idea in Stephen King’s Christine. There, the menace is supernatural. Here, it comes from something more contemporary: a machine that watches humans, learns from them, and inherits some of their worst traits along with the useful ones.

On the other side of the chase is Joa and his stick shift — a deliberately analog counterpoint. To Thomassin, driving stick is a deeply human act: The driver remains in control of the vehicle, physically responding to the road. What separates Joa from Roboride, in Thomassin’s telling, is instinct — and even irrationality.

During one confrontation, Joa takes his hands off the steering wheel while facing down the autonomous car. The move is so reckless that Roboride backs off. The human wins by becoming less predictable than the machine.

“Respect your madness. Be a little mad and creative in your way of doing things, and you will be able to rise against the machines.”

— Romain Thomassin

“Respect your madness,” Thomassin said. “Be a little mad and creative in your way of doing things, and you will be able to rise against the machines.”

Despite its skepticism toward AI, Road Rage may use some of the technology itself. Thomassin says the filmmakers are considering AI-generated imagery to depict what Roboride sees, while shooting the human driver’s world with traditional cinematography. To him, that distinction matters. He sees AI as a creative tool when it serves the story, rather than simply a way to replace workers.

For all the menace he sees in robotaxis, Thomassin isn’t afraid to ride in them. He signed up for Waymo as soon as he could and uses it when visiting friends and family for rides.

“I don’t feel in danger,” he said.

That may be what makes Roboride such an effective 2026 villain. The scary part isn’t necessarily that the machine will crash. The scary part is that the machine works.

title: Apple releases beta 8 for iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and more
snippet: Apple has just released a new round of beta software for testing. Beta 8 is here for iPadOS 27, tvOS 27, and more. Here’s what to expect. Update 5:04 p.m. ET: iPadOS 27 and tvOS 27 are now available for public beta testers as well. more…
fullText:
Apple has just released a new round of beta software for testing. Beta 8 is here for iPadOS 27, tvOS 27, and more. Here’s what to expect.

Update 5:04 p.m. ET: iPadOS 27 and tvOS 27 are now available for public beta testers as well. 

Beta 8 is here for iPadOS 27 and more, with RC expected next week

Apple’s next major software versions are nearly ready to ship. And today’s beta 8 releases are expected to offer further bug fixes and refinements toward that end.

Beta 8 is here for iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, tvOS 27, visionOS 27, and more.

These are likely to be the final beta updates before RC versions debut next Wednesday following Apple’s September launch event.

Aside from performance improvements and under-the-hood fixes, we’re not expecting any other user-facing changes in today’s betas.

title: Apple fixes frustrating TestFlight app regression that search feature update added
snippet: Back in July, Apple updated its TestFlight app with a basic search feature. While you might think this simple update would be universally welcomed, the same TestFlight app introduced a pretty frustrating bug for a lot of users. more…
fullText:
Back in July, Apple updated its TestFlight app with a basic search feature. While you might think this simple update would be universally welcomed, the same TestFlight app introduced a pretty frustrating bug for a lot of users.

Personally, I wasn’t affected by the bug in a way that I noticed. For this reason, I thought the TestFlight update was a simple but significant step forward.

Sometimes a small change can make a big impact. That’s especially true for Apple’s latest TestFlight update for users with a lot of pre-release software.

Apple just updated TestFlight for iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more. The new version, 4.3, introduces “a search field to quickly find apps.” 

In retrospect, I did notice something odd that I flagged at the end of the post (but got backwards in my assessment):

The update also surfaced more apps in the “previously tested” category, so maybe the usual bug fix and performance improvements may relate to that.

I missed that this was actually the bug, I think, because I left several years of app TestFlights to “merge” my separate iCloud and App Store Apple accounts last year. Inconvenient requirement, but worth it for me.

Anyway, the TestFlight app bug didn’t go unnoticed by John Vorhees at MacStories:

So, you can imagine my excitement when I read a post by Zac Hall at 9to5Mac that a search field had been added to TestFlight. “Finally,” I thought to myself. I stopped what I was doing and updated the app immediately. […]

Unfortunately, this story comes with one very big “but.” Previously, TestFlight betas were listed in reverse chronological order, which I liked. […]

Well, those expired betas are now scattered among the active TestFlight betas in an alphabetical list and it seems that the expired beta list has been expanded to include every single beta I’ve ever been a part of. I did a rough count and for me that’s nearly 800 app listings. As you can imagine, the active betas in that list are few and far between. Search helps, but scrolling is no longer an option.

Then in August, John Gruber wrote an essay on Daring Fireball about the TestFlight update and bug:

I didn’t complain about this when the sort order changed last month because I figured it was an oopsie — that alphabetical order was supposed to kick in only when displaying search results, not by default. But here we are a month later and the presentation of apps in TestFlight makes me a little irritated every day. 

Last night, more than a month after the bug was introduced (and flagged by Vorhees), Apple has updated TestFlight for the first time. While the release notes only point to bug fixes, the update does indeed fix the bug in question. 

TestFlight version 4.3.1 is the fix for those experiencing the regression.

title: Google Home update restores support for older Chromecast streamers, Home Mini
snippet: A rogue Google Home update earlier this year partially broke support for some older Chromecast streamers and other devices, but the latest update has restored it. more…
fullText:
A rogue Google Home update earlier this year partially broke support for some older Chromecast streamers and other devices, but the latest update has restored it. 

If you’re still using one of the original Chromecast streaming dongles over a decade later, first of all, kudos to you. While Google has technically dropped software support for its original 2013 streamer, the company continues to provide updates and support for other models. 

Back in May, it seemed as though the end had come for that first-gen device as support faltered in the Home app, but a fix arrived later on. It didn’t take long for further issues to appear, though. There was another wave of reports in late July, affecting not only the first-gen Chromecast, but also the 2015 model and Google Home Mini. The issue was primarily affecting setup, but also functionality to some extent, and mostly on the Android version of the Google Home app.

Google says this should be fixed as of Google Home v4.26 which is available now.

	

In a comment shared across several Reddit threads, Google explains:

We’ve resolved an issue that was impacting the ability to set up some older Chromecast and Google Home devices. If you haven’t already, factory reset their speaker or update your Google Home app to version 4.26 and try again…

You can download Google Home v4.26 via the Play Store, but you likely already have it installed.

title: This Robot Vacuum Aims to Compete With the Suction Power of a Stick Vacuum
snippet: Robot vacuums aren’t very good at deep cleaning carpets. Roomba is about to show me how it’s fixed this problem.
fullText:
Robot vacuums are a great way to do some general cleaning, but most lack the power of a dedicated vacuum cleaner because you can’t pack enough suction into a small design. iRobot may have an interesting solution for that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which it describes as the “most powerful robot ever” because it uses a proprietary vacuum seal technology that concentrates suction power on the floor. 

“With the Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot, we not only increased overall suction power, but also changed how that suction gets applied to the carpet,” Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said in a statement. “With SealForce, we’re able to seal the chassis against the carpet fibers, so the airflow, which has the greatest impact on pickup performance, has somewhere to go instead of escaping around the edges. More suction helps, but the seal is what takes it to a level beyond what’s previously been possible.”

In a video call with me prior to IFA Berlin 2026, Pope described the technology as being similar to pressing down harder on the carpet when you’re vacuuming with a regular vacuum, to increase the seal and focus the suction on a particular spot. In the case of the Max 875, rather than pressing down, the robot vacuum’s chassis lowers a “skirt” that forms a tight seal against carpet fibers.

Once the seal is established, it can use 35,000 pascals of suction to clean the floor, which iRobot describes as “tornado-like airflow.” The company also says that it has three times deeper carpet cleaning and the best pickup performance to date among its models. Essentially, rather than just boosting suction power, the robot vac is making its suction more targeted and efficient on the surfaces it cleans. It’s a good idea if it works as promised. In our testing, we’ve generally found that cordless vacuums have better suction than robot vacuums, but this type of tech could help robots catch up. 

While iRobot didn’t demo the two models live at IFA, I was able to see them in person, and the tech behind them was demonstrated through a neat display iRobot has where you press a button and different features, like the skirt, engage. It works in the demo, but I’ll need to use it myself and test it in the lab to see how it performs in real life. 

There’s also some other interesting cleaning technology under the hood. To handle dried-on stains on hard floors, the Max 875 Combo continuously sprays heated mist as it mops, loosening and softening older stains so the mop roller can remove them. Pope told me that the new roller mop is also the industry’s largest, has 300 rotations per minute and 18 newtons of downward pressure. The company claims that all this gives the robot vacuum twice the stain removal, 3.75 times deeper scrubbing and 1.2 times wider coverage per pass. 

Available on other robot vacuums, the 875 Combo has an AI-powered carpet-detection feature that automatically raises the mop when it detects carpet and lowers a protective shield to prevent dripping. It also comes with the other high-end features we’ve come to expect from flagship robot vacuums, including anti-tangle and hair-cutting main brushes, side brushes, lidar navigation, and AI object recognition for more than 300 household objects. 

The 875 Combo also has a docking station that washes the mop with water heated to 176 degrees Fahrenheit and dries it with air heated to 131 F; it also auto refills cleaning fluid and self-empties into a debris bag that should last up to 90 days.  

iRobot

The Roomba Max 875 Combo will cost $1,199 and launch alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. The 678 Combo falls more into a midrange price segment, but it has plenty going for it. It comes with its own unique feature that iRobot calls SprayForce AI. 

It uses 40,000 pascals of high-pressure water (not heated) to break up dried messes and improve mopping efficiency by 40%. The mop rollers come with 15 newtons of downward pressure and 30,000 pascals of suction for vacuuming, as well as the SealForce tech. Other capabilities are pretty similar, including automatic mop lifting (without the protector), antitangle and hair-cutting brushes, edge cleaning, lidar navigation and AI obstacle avoidance as well as a self-emptying and self-cleaning docking station.

Both the $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot and AutoWash Dock and the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot and AutoWash Dock models are available now at iRobot.com. We plan to test both at CNET Labs when review units are available. 

Editor ’s note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: Google Clock rolls out redesign of Timers with presets on Android
snippet: Following the new app icon, Google Clock has rolled out a redesigned Timers tab. This follows yesterday’s update to the Now Playing app. more…
fullText:
Following the new app icon, Google Clock has rolled out a redesigned Timers tab. This follows yesterday’s update to the Now Playing app.

The big change is that Google has introduced presets for 1, 5, 10, and 15 minutes that immediately start counting down once tapped. Google has tweaked the numbers at the top with Hours, Minutes, and Seconds replacing h, m, and s.

A big green “Start” pill replaces the previous icon at the bottom of the screen. Finally, the number pad no longer uses circular backgrounds. This tweak makes the screen feel flatter, with the interface now much busier but more efficient.

Old vs. new

	

If you have multiple timers, Google has shrunk down the cards and now offers a grid instead of the previous scrollable list. This is a much better use of screen real estate, while there are no changes to the single-timer look. The pause button is now inside the circular countdown, while reset is outside. 

This Timers redesign is rolling out as part of a server-side update with version 9.1 of Google Clock. If you’re not seeing it yet, Force stop from App info.

title: How to check if Motion Assist has rolled out to your Android 17 phone
snippet: Following the announcement on Tuesday, Google is slowly rolling out Motion Assist to phones running Android 17. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement on Tuesday, Google is slowly rolling out Motion Assist to phones running Android 17.

Once rolled out, you can search for “motion assist” in the Settings app. The long way is Settings app > Google > All services tab > Personal & device safety > Motion assist. Appearing alongside Advanced Protection and Theft protection, this new feature is part of Google Play services.

The preference menu lets you have Motion Assist automatically “Start in a moving vehicle,” but Google also recommends adding the Quick Settings Tile. This lets you manually enable and disable “from any screen.” You can add it from this page or the usual edit screen under “From system apps.” Once active, there’s also a system notification that lets you disable with a tap.

The Customize menu lets you adjust:

	

Color: Based on system, Red, Yellow, Green, Blue

Shape: Circle, Square, Pentagon, Diamond

Opacity: Slider

Randomization: “Color and shape change every few seconds”

The moving shapes adjust to the device’s motion and “may help reduce motion sickness when you’re in a moving vehicle.” On the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you get three columns of shapes on the left and right edges, while Google’s phone example shows two.

Motion Assist is not yet widely rolled out. We’re seeing it with version 26.33.32 of Google Play services, but there’s a server-side component. As of today, it’s only appearing on one of our devices.

title: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Two new display upgrades coming next week
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will have the same screen sizes as their predecessors, but rumors indicate their displays will be upgraded in two other ways. Here’s what’s coming. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will have the same screen sizes as their predecessors, but rumors indicate their displays will be upgraded in two other ways. Here’s what’s coming.

#1: LTPO+ technology

LTPO is the technology that has long powered the iPhone’s Always-On and ProMotion display features. And in iPhone 18 Pro, Apple is rumored to be moving to the more advanced LTPO+.

Per The Elec:

Conventional LTPO applies oxide materials to switching thin-film transistors (TFTs). LTPO+ extends oxide usage to driving TFTs as well, enabling finer current control for OLED light emission and allowing displays to optimize operation based on surrounding conditions and user environments, improving battery efficiency.

Benefits of LTPO+ include reduced screen flickering in low-light environments thanks to more responsive adjustments, plus improved power efficiency. Thus, iPhone 18 Pro users should enjoy even more consistent display performance at a lower battery cost.

#2: Reduced Dynamic Island cutout

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s displays are also expected to have a reduced Dynamic Island cutout. Thus, the useable screen space will expand slightly.

The new Dynamic Island is rumored to be about 35% smaller than what iPhone 17 Pro offers. This size is even hinted at already by iOS 27 in Siri’s new design.

Apple debuted the Dynamic Island on iPhone 14 Pro back in 2022. While software features related to the Dynamic Island and Live Activities have expanded over time, the physical cutout has remained unchanged.

With iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Apple is finally moving a step closer to the dream of a cutout-free display.

title: Google will not have to sell AdX business, but it will have to make changes
snippet: Following a prior court battle, a judge has now ruled that Google won’t have to sell off its AdX (ad exchange) business after all, and will instead have to make some undisclosed behavioral changes. more…
fullText:
Following a prior court battle, a judge has now ruled that Google won’t have to sell off its AdX (ad exchange) business after all, and will instead have to make some undisclosed behavioral changes.

As reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times, Google will not have to sell off its AdX business. Judge Leonie Brinkema rejected the DOJ’s move to force the sale of that business which would have also make the auction logic behind ad placements public information. 

While Google won’t have to sell off the business or reveal auction logic, the Judge did propose “behavioral changes.”

We’ll know more in 14 days when the decision is unsealed, as both Google and the DOJ will be able to use that time to make any needed redactions. 

	

Still, it’s a major victory on Google’s part. The 2025 ruling still finds Google guilty of breaking the law to protect a monopoly on advertising, but as ArsTechnica points out, the sale of AdX could have made an impact in the rest of Google’s advertising business even if the ad exchange in particular isn’t the biggest part of that business.

title: Dyson’s Huge Pipe-like Air Purifier Moves Like a Dune Sandworm and Blows Air Across the Room
snippet: These combo models can heat, cool and clean air all in the same unit.
fullText:
Dyson’s HushJet air purifiers have been some of the versatile air purifiers on the market, able to cool, purify and heat the air, so you get climate control capabilities in addition to purification. The new HushJet purifier range, announced at the IFA 2026 trade show in Berlin, incorporates all of these capabilities with a complete redesign and I was able to see all three models in person prior to the show.

The new HushJet models look like large curved pipes, a design Dyson calls the “HushJet Nozzle.” It incorporates the directed-fan capabilities of the HushJet MiniCool Fan that we loved for portable summer cooling, with the aerospace turbine design of the HushJet Compact, for more consistent performance and reduced noise and turbulence.

The largest and most impressive of the units is the $1,099 Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde. The name is a mouthful, but it’s the company’s largest air purifier, with the most powerful compressor, designed to handle multiroom air purification and mixing. It even has wheels so it can be moved from room to room (it’s not self-propelled, unfortunately), and controls that let the nozzle-like head move and rotate in a way that’s vaguely reminiscent of a Dune sandworm. The head can tilt up and down, letting you angle the airflow for direct cooling or broader room circulation.

The biggest unit is on the far right and comes with wheels to move more easily.Tara Brown/CNET

Impressively, despite the unit’s sheer size, I didn’t really hear the airflow except at the highest settings. Meanwhile, the sheer amount of air it emitted through the large, open demo area was impressive. I could really feel the air circulating and starting to clear up without it feeling like I was being blown directly by a fan. The unit can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns and destroy formaldehyde, a chemical byproduct that can be present in many homes. 

The medium-sized $599 HushJet Pure Cool+Formaldehyde is the unit I expect most people to get because it’s on the more reasonable side while still delivering powerful purification and cooling. Dyson says it can deliver three times the purification of predecessors and still clean large spaces while acting as a fan to provide personal cooling. 

The $599 HushJet Hot Cool Pure+ is similar, but it adds heating capabilities in addition to the purification and cooling. Dyson describes it as a three-in-one unit that can also be useful as a space heater in the winter, not just a fan in the summer.

All three Dyson HushJet models are expected to launch in fall 2026, and we look forward to testing them at CNET Labs.

title: Audacity 4 is a complete revamp of the ‘world’s most popular’ audio editor
snippet: Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn't nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more importantly, all the promised improvements to the self-proclaimed "world's most popular audio editing and recording app" are here, turning Audacity from a free and capable but extremely clunky audio editor into a powerful modern tool. The biggest change is the move to a non-destructive editing workflow. That means you can trim a clip down, then recover the audio simply … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Terrence O'Brien

 

is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn’t nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more importantly, all the promised improvements to the self-proclaimed “world’s most popular audio editing and recording app” are here, turning Audacity from a free and capable but extremely clunky audio editor into a powerful modern tool.

The biggest change is the move to a non-destructive editing workflow. That means you can trim a clip down, then recover the audio simply by dragging the edge of the clip back out if you change your mind. Clips can now overlap too, which means you can still paste in audio even if there isn’t enough space and adjust after, or just freely drag audio around the timeline. Previously, if you tried to drag a clip past another one in the timeline, it would just stop dead in its tracks. You’d instead have to cut and paste it to move it past any existing audio.

You can also split clips now to easily chop up and rearrange audio. The developers refreshed clip envelopes and the built-in effects, and added a home screen with revamped project organization. Audacity also got a dramatic facelift that brings it more in line with Muse’s other products like Muse Score and Audio.com, complete with customizable themes.

While Audacity has been a staple of many people’s toolkits since it debuted way back in 2000, it’s stayed stubbornly consistent in its design and layout as new features have been bolted on, sometimes clumsily. This big refresh to Audacity 4 brings it much closer to a modern digital audio workstation (DAW).

Dummy models for iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max

fullText:
Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m watching every minute of M. Night Shyamalan’s new YouTube video on the making of Signs, trying to convince myself I don’t need the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones, and using this helpful guide to finally install a local AI model on my M4 Pro Mac Mini.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Another Android Drop is here, and it comes with some legitimately useful new features. But one feels designed specifically for me and my forgetfulness, and I can’t wait to use it all the time.

	

Gemini has been updated to work with Find Hub, Google’s tool for tracking phones and other gadgets in the ecosystem, to remember the location of physical objects. “Hey Google, remember that I left my spare key inside the hollowed-out copy of Infinite Jest on my bookshelf.” I’m a big fan of these kinds of small, tangible improvements to Android that most people, not just those on the latest version or running a Pixel, will benefit from.

The other new features include a Motion Assist accessibility feature to counteract motion sickness in the car; a Gemini-powered Live Guide accessibility feature that uses AI to “offer descriptions of what’s in front of you”; and a Keep integration inside Google Messages that lets people co-create shopping or packing lists.

Read more: Pixel 11 series getting early September update, not Android 17 QPR1

✉️ Inbox

IFA is here, and that means there are a bunch of gadgets to talk about.

Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra launch with 185Hz panels, 8 Elite Gen 5 chips, and huge batteries. Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, used to be known for its lower-priced devices, but now that everything’s expensive, the company is leaning into specs. These feature massive batteries and, on the Ultra, an honest-to-goodness subwoofer that sounds pretty great.

Roku launches its first OLED TVs, available now starting at $999. Roku may be an advertising company at heart, but it still has to make hardware, and its latest TVs are OLEDs that are pretty competitive, and a lot cheaper. They’re also Amazon exclusives for now.

Sony’s new ULT Tower party speakers start at $450. I need to meet the person spending $1500 on a party speaker — because I want to attend that party.

Razer Prio is an Android and iPhone game controller that folds down to roughly the size of a credit card. I have a million portable game controllers, from multiple generations of the Razer Kishi to the Backbone One to basically anything 8BitDo releases. And yet I will still buy this because it looks so darn cute folded up.

Samsung’s latest Galaxy Book 6 starts at $799 with 8GB of RAM. The Korean giant, along with Dell, is announcing a MacBook Neo competitor powered by Intel’s ultra-efficient Wildcat Lake chips.

Govee’s new ceiling light and LED strips are mood boosters with some AI sprinkled in. Govee’s new ceiling light contains “vitality spectrum technology” to keep people more alert during the dark winter months. Will it work? You can pay $399 to find out.

Belkin says its new ‘BoostSolid’ Qi2 batteries last 3x longer than other magnetic power banks. The accessory company is leaning on solid-state battery tech to outlast the competition, which means less e-waste.

Belkin just released four Android Find Hub trackers; one is a full wallet

Philips Hue adds HDMI-free and 4K Sync Box, Nanoleaf partnership, and exciting app upgrades. I’m a big fan of Hue products, so these cheaper options are music to my ears.

Now, onto the news of the day.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so popular that Samsung is stealing parts from next year’s phones just to make more. A headline that feels perfectly tailored for 2026: Samsung’s unlikely ascension meets a component crisis that’s only getting worse.

Oppo Find X10 reportedly has an 8,000 mAh battery and top-tier specs for a ‘base’ flagship. Oppo has absolutely no chill, and I love it. Can’t wait for this one.

Gemini 3.8 Flash rolling out three weeks after last release. Google is fast-running its Gemini 3.x Flash releases in an effort to make us forget that its newest Pro model is nearly three months late.

MrBeast will try to survive ‘the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes’ using Gemini and Fitbit Air in deal with Google. Google should stick to partnering with the better Jimmy, in my opinion.

Pixel 11 series can now join the Android 17 QPR2 Beta. If you’re a Pixel 11 owner, you can now skip ahead to December’s upcoming Android release and join the blur club.

Google rolling out Pixel Watch 5 September update

Android Auto tests Quick Settings and hilarious ‘Jimothy’ weather Easter egg [Gallery]. Jimothy is a national hero, and I’m so glad he’s getting the respect he deserves.

Android Auto 17.6 update rolling out with redesigned logo [Gallery]

YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required. My phone’s most-used app is quickly becoming my TV’s most-used endpoint, and this is going to make it even easier to cast to it.

Google will not have to sell AdX business, but it will have to make changes. Despite Google being found guilty of running an illegal advertising monopoly, a judge is not forcing it to break up its ad business.

Google Home update restores support for older Chromecast streamers, Home Mini. 

WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking. Not a huge security issue, but one worth knowing if only to learn what setting to disable to prevent it from happening.

MapQuest is back, at the top of the charts, and rushing to add Android Auto support. Thought it was a one-night stand? Nope, MapQuest is in it for the long haul.

Google’s next Pixel Fold reportedly adopting the same crease-less display as Apple. But more importantly, will the next Pixel Fold revert back to its original passport shape? 

Google Pixel adding ‘Battery usage summaries,’ rolling out on Pixel 10 and newer

🇩🇪 Upcoming

It’s IFA time, which means the tech press and analysts convene in Berlin for bratwurst, bier, and briefings.

While 9to5Google covers a lot of the miscellany, we don’t typically get to the crazier stuff, like this Acer gaming handheld/netbook concept that will almost certainly never be made.

TP-Link unveiled the first production Wi-Fi 8 routers far before most people have upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 (and given the speed of the rollout may skip it altogether). And Homey, the Dutch smart home accessory vendor recently acquired by LG, announced a controller hub that looks almost exactly like a Nest thermostat but does a whole lot more.

You can check out all of 9to5Google’s IFA 2026 coverage throughout the rest of the week.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

If you told me that the leaked DLSS 5 Neural Rendering tool would be ported to the Switch, I probably would have absolutely believed you because the internet is full of weird, smart people who just want to try things. Take a look at a yassified Mario from Mario Kart World or Link from Tears of the Kingdom looking sharper than ever.

I have rarely taken xAI’s Grok models seriously because from my understanding they were primarily used by Reply Guys to ask @grok what movie was being vagueposted. But in recent months, the company’s ties with and recent acquisition of Cursor have given Grok 4.6 serious coding and productivity chops. Now Grok Bot, the company’s agentic harness for getting stuff done, has arrived on Android after debuting on macOS and iOS.

title: AAPL gained 2,736% under Cook, but Ternus doesn’t have to emulate him
snippet: Bloomberg carries a piece noting the astonishing gains made by Apple stockholders during the time when Tim Cook was CEO. The cumulative gain was 2,275% – or a total return of 2,736% when accounting for dividend payments also. The site suggests this will make him a tough act to follow, but my own view is that new CEO John Ternus doesn’t have to emulate Cook’s management of the company … more…
fullText:
Bloomberg carries a piece noting the astonishing gains made by Apple stockholders during the time when Tim Cook was CEO. The cumulative gain was 2,275% – or a total return of 2,736% when accounting for dividend payments also.

The site suggests this will make him a tough act to follow, but my own view is that new CEO John Ternus doesn’t have to emulate Cook’s management of the company … 

There’s no disputing the numbers Bloomberg cites.

Cook inherited a company with a market capitalization of less than $350 billion and built the maker of iPhones and Mac computers into a diverse $4.6 trillion business that also sells watches, AirPods and financial services […] During his time as CEO, the shares climbed a whopping 2,736% on a total-return basis.

But my stance is that John Ternus shouldn’t for one moment worry about whether Apple will emulate this degree of financial success under his leadership – and there are two reasons for this.

First, both of his key predecessors argued that financial success is a side effect of the true goal, not something that should be chased directly. Steve Jobs famously said:

“If you focus on making really great products, then the profits will follow.”

Cook himself has echoed this philosophy, saying that he never worried about quarterly results, but instead focused on the long-term direction of the company.

Second, the advice Steve gave to Tim when he took over:

“Don’t ask what I would do. Just do the right thing.”

Ternus shouldn’t ask himself what either Jobs or Cook would have done. He should instead  run Apple in the way that he thinks is most likely to see the successful development of the best possible products, and the evolution of the best company culture and values for long-term success. 

I suspect he will be a very different CEO to Cook, just as Cook was to Jobs. The goal isn’t to try to emulate past formulae, but instead to look ahead and – to borrow a phrase from the outgoing CEO – follow his own North Star.

Do you share my view or have a different perspective? Please let us know your thoughts in the comments.

title: Apple Maps now uses ‘Lake America’ instead of ‘Lake Ontario’ after Trump order
snippet: If you head to Apple Maps today, you’ll notice that Apple has started renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The move follows Trump’s order last week to change the name as part of an ongoing trade dispute with Canada. more…
fullText:
If you head to Apple Maps today, you’ll notice that Apple has started renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The move follows Trump’s order last week to change the name as part of an ongoing trade dispute with Canada.

The change, which was first spotted by Bloomberg, applies for Apple Maps users in the United States. Apple Maps users in Canada will still see the “Lake Ontario” name. Apple Maps users elsewhere around the world will see both names.  

Google Maps changed Lake Ontario to Lake America several days ago. At the time, Google said that its policy is to use the names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said yesterday that Trump had “reached out to Apple directly” about making this change. That conversation seems to have led Apple to follow suit and change the name in Apple Maps as well.

MapQuest, meanwhile, said this week that it refuses to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, which has led to a surge in downloads.

The change appears to be rolling out to Apple Maps users gradually. On my iPhone, I still see Lake Ontario, while others on the 9to5Mac team already see Lake America.

When Trump ordered the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America” last year, Apple also followed suit on Apple Maps.

title: Pixel 11 lets you make any Camera Look default with this buried setting
snippet: The Pixel 11 series is out in the hands of plenty of (hopefully) happy users, and for the most part, I can count myself among them. This generation marks a massive shift for the camera in particular, as Google has finally loosened up its HDR-centric grip on processing. Really, the only big downsides with Camera Looks appeared to be how it saved your default look — and, as it turns out, there’s a setting to fix that, too. more…
fullText:
The Pixel 11 series is out in the hands of plenty of (hopefully) happy users, and for the most part, I can count myself among them. This generation marks a massive shift for the camera in particular, as Google has finally loosened up its HDR-centric grip on processing. Really, the only big downsides with Camera Looks appeared to be how it saved your default look — and, as it turns out, there’s a setting to fix that, too.

This tip-slash-correction comes via Google’s PR team, which reached out to me last night to let me know that, despite what I found during my hands-on time with Camera Looks, you actually aren’t limited to Google’s four “default” looks as, you know, your default. While Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla are all available under a “Default Look” dropdown menu, if you prefer some of the Pixel 11’s more unique styles — Velvet, Classic, Digi, etc. — those can be saved as your standard preset option.

If you’d rather have complete control over your default, grab your Pixel 11, tap the settings icon in the lower-left corner of the camera app, then tap the triple-dot overflow menu icon in the upper-right. Towards the bottom of the list, look for the Photo menu options, then toggle “Always use selected look” on.

Now, if you return to the Looks menu, selecting any of Google’s non-default options will still be saved as your preference when you leave the app. Whenever one of these more stylized options is selected as your main shooting mode, you’ll see its name briefly appear in the lower-right corner when opening the app, along with a purple Looks icon that sticks around indefinitely. Unlike with one of Google’s four standard processing modes, that permanent Looks icon drops you directly into this menu; you’ll have to hit Back from here to return to other settings like exposure and white balance.

	

It’s honestly great to see that Google does allow Pixel 11 users to save any of these shooting modes  as what’s available immediately upon launching the camera, though I won’t pretend it’s not a bit convoluted to split default preferences into two completely different experiences. But hey, it’s early days for Camera Looks — maybe the Pixel 12 will launch with a more refined UX that unifies this into one slightly-more organized package.

title: Disney+ loses Google Cast support in some countries
snippet: Yet another patent dispute with Disney+ is causing the app to lose Google Cast support in select countries. more…
fullText:
Yet another patent dispute with Disney+ is causing the app to lose Google Cast support in select countries.

Disney has been battling, and losing, in a patent battle with “InterDigital” in recent months. This previously caused the app to lose support for 4K HDR playback in Dolby Vision and 3D content in some regions, which has come and gone in the time since. 

The latest impact is around Google Cast functionality, which is actively being disabled in some regions. BroadcastNow and T3N reported on the dispute, which has led to an injunction against Disney+ in Germany and The Netherlands. While Disney can (and almost certainly will) appeal, the app is currently barred from supporting Cast in these regions.

A notice is already appearing for some users (translated) when trying to cast:

title: I Watched a Floor Washing Robot Mothership Deploy a Roomba Using a Mechnical Arm
snippet: My mind was blown watching the most interesting robot concept I’ve seen at IFA.
fullText:
There’s not much the robot vacuum industry can do to surprise me these days. I’ve seen robots that have mechanical arms to pick up objects, robot vacuums with legs and tread systems to climb stairs, and even wilder humanoid concepts. But iRobot genuinely surprised me with its Roomba Duo, a floor-washing robot module that carries a little baby Roomba on top. I saw this contraption in action at iRobot’s booth at IFA Berlin, and I honestly don’t know what to make of it.  

I briefly spoke to Adam Pope, iRobot’s chief engineer at the booth, who explained that the Roomba Duo is currently just a concept, but it’s an example of the kinds of things iRobot is considering to address consumer pain points. In the case of the Duo, the main egg-like mothership module includes a powerful floor washer and steamer that’s more capable than the type of hardware you can put. iRobot tells me that the main unit’s power is equivalent to that of a traditional wet-and-dry vacuum, offering powerful cleaning but lacking the autonomy of a robot vacuum.

The Duo solves this problem by also incorporating a slim Roomba that can be deployed. I watched it do so after the main unit sucked up some spilled spaghetti from the carpet for the demo and sanitized the spill area. It then used a top-mounted mechanical arm and what I can best describe as a landing craft to lower the Roomba onto the floor, where it started cleaning in the narrow spots of iRobot’s obstacle course. The movement reminded me of a bulldozer or a forklift because the mechanical arm itself looks quite industrial and sturdy, which iRobot says is necessary to ensure stability under the additional weight.

After the main unit finished its heavier cleaning job, it moved closer to its docking area while the smaller Roomba puttered around, cleaning corners and navigating iRobot’s barriers.  

Both units operate autonomously, but they share a home map and an autonomous mobile dock, so they won’t duplicate efforts. They communicate in real time and are connected via the Rooma Home app, which uses AI to coordinate cleaning tasks. iRobot says the main unit vacuums and mops the large, open floor areas, while the slim baby Roomba goes under furniture and into narrow spaces the bulky main module can’t reach. 

While this is just a concept product with no indication it’ll come to market, iRobot did share some specs with us. The main mothership has a wet-and-dry floor-washing module, a high-performance motor, and a high-capacity battery. It also uses the company’s PowerSpin Max Roller map, applying 46 newtons of downward pressure, which is a huge jump from the 12 to 14 newtons you typically get from a robot vacuum. iRobot says it scrubs the floor as thoroughly as if you were cleaning by hand. 

It also has an internal heater that generates steam to loosen tougher, dried-on grime and stains. The roller is self-cleaning, as we’ve come to expect and iRobot says it can handle everything from dirt to pasta sauce and cooking grease. There’s also a hot-air dryer behind the roller that dries the floor after the roller is done mopping, so the wood flooring doesn’t get damaged by moisture. 

The companion robot used for the demo is the Roomba Plus 575 Combo, which we covered after it launched earlier this year. It’s just 8.35 centimeters tall and 29.8 centimeters wide, making it one of the slimmest models we’ve seen, which is why it was selected as the companion unit. Right now, it’s not clear whether the mothership can accommodate other robot vacuum models, but I would guess it’s only compatible with this one for now.

The main Duo unit is equipped with the company’s ClearView Pro dual-line lidar and AI to detect and navigate household objects. It also has a top-mounted AI camera, giving it a better, higher view of rooms and floor layouts, and creating more detailed maps than a standard robot vacuum. It should also be able to better identify stains. 

To move this fairly bulky unit, it uses 17-centimeter wheels powered by hub motors. There’s a shared AutoWash dock (the self-emptying and cleaning docking station that most newer Roomba models use). It has a centralized clean water supply, a waste water tank, and like a standard stationary dock, it automatically washes and dries the mop and collects dust in a dustbag, letting you go months before it needs to be emptied.

title: A New Automatic Feeder Makes Wet Cat Food on Demand
snippet: Rico, launched this week at IFA 2026, is perfect for picky cats with busy parents.
fullText:
Automatic pet feeders aren’t new, but most are limited to dispensing dry food. Strolling through a press preview at IFA 2026 in Berlin, I spotted a wild new take on the handy pet-parent helper, designed for busy cat owners whose feline friends prefer wet food.

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Pet  Tech, As Tested by CNET Editors					

							

		

Riko, the latest release from Neakasa, is a self-contained smart wet-food maker that prepares meals on demand — or whenever you schedule them via the app — and serves them to your cat at mealtime.

As strange as it may sound, this one makes great sense for busy or forgetful owners of cats that prefer wet food. While it’s not advertised for dogs, we can’t see why this system wouldn’t work for small canines.

The Riko feeder holds enough food for seven days of meals.David Watsky/CNET

The unit, which is about the size of an average drip coffee maker, houses a compartment for freeze-dried food and a water reservoir. When activated, it rehydrates and mixes the cat food for a gourmet autonomous feeding experience. 

The Shenzhen-based brand is known for its self-cleaning litter boxes and automatic feeders. Until now, it didn’t have an answer for owners who feed their cats wet grub. Wet food feeders from other brands rely on refrigeration to keep preloaded meals cold until chow time, and most are limited to two or three meals. This is the first one we’ve seen that whips up your cat’s lunch in real time.

Rico retails for $200 and is available on Neakasa’s website.

Editors’ note: David Watsky’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by IFA. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

David Watsky
						

						

							Managing Editor / Home and Kitchen						
					

											

								

											David lives in Brooklyn where he's spent more than a decade covering all things edible, including meal kit services, food subscriptions, kitchen tools and cooking tips. 
David earned his BA from Northeastern and has toiled in nearly every aspect of the food business, including as a line cook in Rhode Island where he once made a steak sandwich for Lamar Odom. 
Right now he's likely somewhere stress-testing a blender or tinkering with a toaster. Anything with sesame is his all-time favorite food this week.

title: Fender MIX headphones now have an iPhone app for tuning your sound
snippet: In August, Fender released the $299 MIX wireless headphones. The over-ear headphones come with a replaceable battery and the FWD Tx USB-C wireless transmitter for low-latency, lossless connectivity. Fender MIX headphones also now include an iPhone app for tuning the experience. more…
fullText:
In August, Fender released the $299 MIX wireless headphones. The over-ear headphones come with a replaceable battery and the FWD Tx USB-C wireless transmitter for low-latency, lossless connectivity. Fender MIX headphones also now include an iPhone app for tuning the experience.

The Fender Audio app for iPhone offers EQ presets and a custom five-band equalizer. This provides separate controls for low, low-mid, mid, high-mid, and high frequencies. That gives listeners a way to adjust the sound to their preferences directly from the iPhone app.

The app also includes a battery indicator and configurable Home Screen widgets for quickly accessing device actions, including EQ settings.

As for the headphones themselves, MIX features 40mm graphene drivers, hybrid active noise cancellation, and Bluetooth 5.3. Fender rates battery life at up to 52 hours with ANC enabled or 100 hours with ANC turned off.

The included USB-C transmitter supports separate modes for lossless audio at up to 24-bit/96kHz, low-latency listening, and Auracast broadcasting to multiple compatible devices.

The headphones also support wired listening over USB-C or a 3.5mm audio cable.

In my listening so far, MIX sounds great with active noise cancellation enabled. Switching to Ambient Sound, Fender’s transparency mode, sounds like a drop in audio quality to my ears, at least over Bluetooth without the adapter.

I’m looking forward to trying the app’s EQ controls to see whether I can get the sound closer to my preferences.

The USB-C transmitter tucks neatly behind an ear cushion when you don’t need it, and Bluetooth without the adapter works when convenience is more important than sounds specs.

The Fender Audio app is available on the App Store now with Fender MIX headphones support.

title: Apple working on new surround sound, Party Mode features for HomePod
snippet: Apple has several new HomePod features in development, based on new code references discovered in audioOS 27. The code seemingly suggests work on a new surround sound system, something called Party Mode, and more. more…
fullText:
Apple has several new HomePod features in development, based on new code references discovered in audioOS 27. The code seemingly suggests work on a new surround sound system, something called Party Mode, and more.

New HomePod features in the works 

A user on the MacRumors forums discovered the code references this week in audioOS 27 beta 8.

Most notably, the code references support for arranging four full-sized HomePod (2nd generation) speakers into a surround sound system. Currently, HomePod supports a stereo pair configuration paired as a default speaker output for Apple TV.

In the quad placement, each speaker has its own role and sound treatment. The front speakers use left- and right-specific processing, and they compensate for their potential placement close to walls and corners. Rear HomePods get an omnidirectional treatment designed to fill the space behind and around the listener.

The new tuning has a processing pipeline to manage each HomePod’s woofer and tweeters, and control bass, EQ, synchronization, and calibration data.

The code also references dynamic surround sound audio tuning. This would enable the quad HomePod system to change its processing to match what’s playing, such as movies or music.

A new “Forklift” system is also referenced in this code. Forklift appears to combine two full-sized second-generation HomePod speakers with two other speakers with an identifier that does not match any of Apple’s existing HomePod products.

Most recently, Bloomberg reported that Apple could release a new HomePod mini within the next several months. The company is also “testing a new full-sized HomePod,” but that product is not imminent. Apple released its current full-sized HomePod in February 2023.

Another new feature referenced is something called “Party Mode.” According to the code, enabling Party Mode will spread the HomePod’s sound “into a wider, more ambient mix” in order to “fill a room more evenly instead of creating a perfect listening spot in front of the speakers.”

Whether Apple actually ships these features remains to be seen. Still, it’s encouraging to see evidence that Apple is continuing to upgrade the home theater features of its HomePod product family.

snippet: There’s a new original movie streaming today on Apple TV: a new action-comedy called Mayday, starring Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh. Streaming for free with an Apple TV subscription, Mayday sees Troy (Reynolds) infiltrate Russian territory amidst the Cold War. fullText:
There’s a new original movie streaming today on Apple TV: a new action-comedy called Mayday, starring Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh. 

Streaming for free with an Apple TV subscription, Mayday sees Troy (Reynolds) infiltrate Russian territory amidst the Cold War. Ex-KGB agent Nikolai (Branagh) becomes an unlikely ally in this caper.

Troy thinks he is going to be captured and killed, but Nikolai is sympathetic to American culture and he helps get Troy out of the country. Mayday is a twist on all the usual tropes of Cold War thrillers, with a lot of references to the cliches found in 1980s flicks like Top Gun.

If you’re looking for a Fun Friday night action comedy, Mayday just might be it, especially if you like the Ryan Reynolds shtick. The movie is getting good critical reviews too, with 84% on Rotten Tomatoes right now.

Mayday is streaming now on Apple TV. You can watch using the Apple TV app available on iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, Mac, Android, Windows, Roku, Amazon Fire Stick, Xbox, PlayStation and more. You can also watch in a web browser at tv.apple.com. 

Mayday is the latest Apple original film, joining a catalog of over 330 original TV show and movie titles on the service. 

Also coming this month is new drama Last Seen, Slow Horses season 6, and new comedy series Brothers. Other notable upcoming film releases include Matchbox and Tenzing, debuting in October.

title: MapQuest is back, at the top of the charts, and rushing to add Android Auto support
snippet: In a “that’s a name I’ve not heard in a long time” move, MapQuest is back to being a household name, as the original mapping app has found itself as the top of app store charts – it’s also rushing to add support for Android Auto. more…
fullText:
In a “that’s a name I’ve not heard in a long time” move, MapQuest is back to being a household name, as the original mapping app has found itself as the top of app store charts – it’s also rushing to add support for Android Auto.

MapQuest has been around for 30 years, but it only entered the modern era back in 2024 when it relaunched with a private mobile mapping app with a pitch around being “anti-Big Tech.” That app has since shut down, and a full MapQuest app arrived earlier this year.

Now, that app is at the top of app store charts.

On iOS, MapQuest is the #8 free app on the App Store (as of Aug 30), and #5 on Android’s Play Store (as of today) – at least in the US. In a press release, MapQuest says this is “the highest chart position in the brand’s 30-year history” and that usage is “roughly 50 times its normal rate.” 

	

Why the sudden surge? Even MapQuest acknowledges it’s mostly to do with a rejection of “Lake America,” with the brand refusing to update “Lake Ontario” on its platform in the wake of a recent executive order in the US which Google Maps and more recently Apple Maps have updated their maps to show. The viral nature of that stand reminded many that MapQuest even still exists, and brought about this wave of popularity.

In a bid to keep users on its app, MapQuest confirmed that it is rapidly building out support for Android Auto – it already supports CarPlay on iPhone. Android Auto added support for third-party navigation apps a few years ago, and there are quite a few options available.

MapQuest still lags behind Google Maps and others in terms of live transit and other features, but supports turn-by-turn navigation, live traffic data, and more. MapQuest is currently owned by System1, an advertising company.

title: Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27 has brand new design for key features
snippet: iOS 27 adds a variety of new features for popular apps like Notes, Reminders, and Calendar—and the Calendar app gets some notable design changes too. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds a variety of new features for popular apps like Notes, Reminders, and Calendar—and the Calendar app gets some notable design changes too. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27 gives Apple Calendar new design for event details view and event creation and editing screens

Apple’s Calendar app has stayed remarkably consistent over the years. The app tends to get new features less often than other popular Apple apps. And its design has changed very little over the years, even looking largely the same after last year’s Liquid Glass update.

But in iOS 27, Apple has notable design changes coming in two main areas:

Event details view

Event creation and editing

As seen in the image above, when you tap on any calendar event, the details view has gotten a revamp.

Information has been reorganized in a way that lets you view more details on-screen at a time. The addition of icons is a helpful visual cue that makes everything easier to parse. These changes, combined with smaller design updates, add up to a more modern overall feel.

iOS 27 also brings similar design updates when creating or editing events in Calendar.

As the image on the left shows, more information now fits on-screen and it’s all been reorganized and refreshed.

Icons are put to good use here, just like in the event details view. And you’ll notice headings now organize event parameters in a way that makes everything easier to navigate.

Beyond these two areas, the Calendar app also benefits from iOS 27’s systemwide enhancements to Liquid Glass. Overall, the update brings some of Calendar’s most noteworthy design changes in years.

title: Upgrade paths: Should Pixel 9 owners upgrade to Pixel 11? [Video]
snippet: We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here. Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video] more…
fullText:
We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here.

Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video]

Your 24-month cell plan might be coming to an end, so it’s timely to talk about this switch now, and we’ll do our best to help you decide which phone is right, which phone is wrong, and ultimately whether an upgrade is worthwhile.

An unchanged design

Let’s get the obvious out of the way at the start: the Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro are very, very similar. You could be forgiven for thinking they are the same. For anyone with a non-Pro phone, you’ll see more pronounced changes, but for all intents and purposes, the designs are almost identical across the entire device lineup.

Let’s get into the actual improvements. No matter what Pixel 9 phone you have, all Pixel 11 displays are better. Maybe not drastically so, but you get a jump up in maximum brightness of around 10% on the Pixel 9 to 11. The Pros get a 20% brightness jump at peak. This is something you probably would notice, but still not a major change. All the screens are well tuned, there’s no bezel reduction, just the same great experience, but brighter.

	

We know the design is the same, the core frame dimensions are identical, the same height, width, and thickness. The only visible change is in the camera bar shape and size. You can’t use your old cases on the new phone, so that is an annoyance. The Pixel 9 and 11 are within 1g, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL are almost 10 grams heavier than the 9 Pro and Pro XL. 

That could be due to the marginal battery size increases and maybe even the addition of Pixelsnap magnets, but it’s likely some internal changes that add a little extra mass, and better thermals too. Pixelsnap is great for connectivity, but a good case can mimic it pretty closely on the Pixel 9.

Similar software experience

One of the key differences between the Pixel 9 and Pixel 11 is Gemini Intelligence. It’s emblazoned all over the latest phone and adds some functionality that likely won’t come to the older devices unless Google has a change of heart.

You need to figure out if you care enough about some of the AI tools like App Automation, Rambler, the enhanced Proactive Assistant responses and replies for messaging, plus some of the other enhancements that the Pixel 10 added last year.

Some of this is merely fluff. Some are great features. Do they drastically improve your life? That remains to be seen.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 11: Where are the upgrades? [Video]

Even the move from Tensor G4 up to the G6 chip might not be a big enough leap for lots of people. Neither is an amazing performance beast, but they’re competent chips that handle most things you’ll throw at either phone.

Faster storage is arguably a bigger ingredient in the equation because apps will load faster, and you also get the benefit of a 256GB base model now. It was a long-overdue quality of life change that will make a bigger difference in the long term.

Frustratingly, getting less RAM on the Pixel 11 Pro or Pro XL versus the Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL feels like a slap in the face. It’s not necessarily noticeable right now, save that you can have more apps in memory. Some of the RAM is wired for AI task control, so you’ll lose out here unless you pay more to get 16GB RAM.

The fact is, though, that the performance gap is not exactly a chasm, and Android 17 is identical here. Unless Google specifies otherwise, you’ll get all the same updates in the future too.

Quality cameras continue to impress

If you want a telephoto lens and have the Pixel 9, then yes, you might want to upgrade. The digital zoom is not as good on the base 9. It’s capped and isn’t going to get close to the action.

The other lenses are fairly similar, but know that the main sensor is slightly larger on the Pixel 11. With the default settings, it’s a toss-up.

Camera Looks are where we get some notable improvements. These are sensor-level filters that you can customize to tune your Pixel 11 camera output. No Pixel 9 will get these tools. It’s arguably the biggest change on a Pixel camera since the addition of a triple camera setup.

If you have a Pro phone, there is a better telephoto lens that lets you zoom up to 120X. Video modes get some upgrades, AI-powered Magic Capture, plus a new Creator Mode is here too.

Like basically every other head-to-head comparison, the camera improvements are more about refinement than redefining, which makes a Pixel camera so reliable.

I don’t think someone would be disappointed at what has changed, maybe underwhelmed given the two-year leap. The reality is that a Pixel camera has mostly been about consistency, which hasn’t changed.

Is now the time to upgrade from the Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

You don’t need us to tell you that the generational “leaps” are becoming less and less pronounced, even if you skip a few new releases.

Whether brands are holding certain functions back or other factors are at play is a topic rife among practically any industry observer right now. AI is playing a big role in the physical hardware you will buy now and for years to come.

In our eyes, there is only one key reason you should consider making the switch from a Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11, and that is if your phone is on its last legs or if you have the base 9 and want a telephoto lens. Those are the only two major reasons someone should consider the jump.

The Pixel 9 Pro and Pro XL are still fine phones. There seems to be no major or widespread issues that might cause people to be desperate to upgrade or switch away. It wasn’t the best phone on the market at launch, but, like any Pixel before, these devices tend to age better than others thanks to updates and enhancements courtesy of Google’s now-extensive support window.

If you’re even considering ditching a Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL for the Pixel 11 lineup, think hard about what you’re actually getting. There isn’t anything on the software front that really warrants the substantial price increase. The new modem is good, but not a quantum leap. The camera improvements don’t provide exponential gains for photography or videography.

This is also true of most other pieces of tech right now. If your cell plan or contract is coming to an end imminently, maybe a cheap SIM plan could be a way to save cash at a time when smartphones are ballooning in price thanks to the constant march of AI development and the costs associated with the expansion.

The truth is that a two-generation upgrade cycle makes little sense today. You will simply get more bang for your buck by hanging on for another year. A battery replacement or repair would likely provide more value in most cases, given how little has truly changed over the past couple of years.

title: Here’s how much Apple is paying John Ternus as CEO, Tim Cook as executive chairman
snippet: In a new regulatory filing today, Apple revealed that new CEO John Ternus is receiving a pay package with $58 million in salary and target stock awards. The company also shared details on Tim Cook’s lucrative new deal as Apple’s executive chairman. more…
fullText:
In a new regulatory filing today, Apple revealed that new CEO John Ternus is receiving a pay package with $58 million in salary and target stock awards. The company also shared details on Tim Cook’s lucrative new deal as Apple’s executive chairman.

John Ternus’s new compensation

The numbers were disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission today. Ternus’s $58 million pay package includes two components:

Base salary: $3 million/year

Annual equity award: $55 million target value beginning fiscal 2027

75% ($41.25M) performance-based restricted stock units (RSUs)

25% ($13.75M) time-based RSUs

The performance shares depend on Apple’s total shareholder return compared with other S&P 500 companies. The time-based shares vest 12.5% every six months over four years.

For 2026, Ternus is also receiving prorated stock awards with a $2.5 million target value, covering the portion of fiscal 2026 he serves as CEO.

While Apple did not disclose Ternus’s previous salary in his role as senior vice president of hardware engineering, Bloomberg reports “that management level typically gets paid about $25 million annually when including stock, salary and bonuses.”

Tim Cook’s new compensation

Meanwhile, Tim Cook is receiving a pay package with a $47 million target value for fiscal 2027. This includes:

Base salary: $2 million/year, effective September 26

Fiscal 2027 equity award: $45 million target value

50% ($22.5M) performance-based

50% ($22.5M) time-based, vesting 12.5% every six months over four years

This is an unusually large pay package for an executive chairman role, signaling the value that Apple thinks Cook brings to the table here. Cook’s focus as executive chairman will see him managing Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government.

For fiscal 2025, Cook’s total pay package as CEO was $74,294,811. That number, however, includes things not factored into today’s SEC filing. Those include non-equity incentive plan compensation, retirement plans, vacation days, personal security expenses, and more. Cook’s salary and stock awards totaled roughly $60.5 million for 2025.

title: Syncing Hue lights to your TV now starts at $120; Nanoleaf integration too
snippet: Syncing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display used to be a rather expensive undertaking, at $385 for the company’s Sync Box 8K. A couple of new products now bring that cost down to as little as $120. Additionally, you can now integrate Nanoleaf wall panels into your Philips Hue ecosystem thanks to a new $40 Wall Light Module … more…
fullText:
Syncing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display used to be a rather expensive undertaking, at $385 for the company’s Sync Box 8K. A couple of new products now bring that cost down to as little as $120.

Additionally, you can now integrate Nanoleaf wall panels into your Philips Hue ecosystem thanks to a new $40 Wall Light Module … 

Syncing Hue lights to your TV

Synchronizing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display can create an extremely immersive experience for anything from movies to games.

The company’s Sync Box 8K uses HDMI signals to detect the colors displayed on your TV screen and then adjusts all of the Hue lighting in the same room to match in real time. At almost $400, however, it’s an expensive option, and the bundles with Gradient Light Strips can reach over $650 for the largest TVs.

The company is now offering two more affordable options:

Sync Box 4K, which also uses an HDMI signal: $150

Play Screen Sync, which uses a camera: $120

HDMI syncing is the more accurate approach, and the new 4K model reduces costs by reducing support from four HDMI feeds to just one. The maximum supported resolution is 4K at 60Hz. 

The Play Screen Sync supports whatever is being displayed, but the color matching accuracy is compromised. There are already third-party products from companies like Govee using this approach.

Nanoleaf integration

The Verge spotted that a new Wall Light Module has been jointly launched by Philips and Nanoleaf. The $40 box makes any Nanoleaf product appear to be a Philips Hue device.

While Nanoleaf products already have HomeKit support, adding Hue compatibility can be useful for third-party apps which offer more flexibility with things like animated scenes and music syncing.

title: Google’s next Pixel Fold reportedly adopting the same crease-less display as Apple
snippet: We’re still a few days out from the debut of Apple’s first iPhone foldable which, as many have expected for years, will have a crease-less display. According to a new report, Google’s Pixel 12 Pro Fold will be adopting the same technology as Apple’s foldable. more…
fullText:
We’re still a few days out from the debut of Apple’s first iPhone foldable which, as many have expected for years, will have a crease-less display. According to a new report, Google’s Pixel 12 Pro Fold will be adopting the same technology as Apple’s foldable.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is, as we’ve mentioned, a perfectly fine foldable. But as brands such as Oppo, Honor, and most recently Samsung have gone all-in on crease-less displays, Google’s foldable is noticeably behind. 

Review: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold just barely keeps up

According to a new report, Google plans a major upgrade on the Pixel 12 Pro Fold, and they’re not the only ones. The Elec reports that Google, Oppo, and Vivo are all working with Samsung Display to adopt dual-UTG (ultra-thin glass) displays for their next-gen foldables. It’s the same tech apparently set to be used on Apple’s first iPhone foldable. 

Samsung Display and partners would be building out the display and UTG assembly to the specs of each device. This sees one UTG layer above the display, with a second layer underneath and supporting the OLED panel. Samsung achieved its crease-less display using a special titanium plate under the OLED panel, while Oppo says it filled in the area of the crease using liquid 3D printing to create an even surface along with thicker glass.

	

The report mentions that Oppo and Vivo will both have releases in the first half of 2027, while Google’s next foldable will come in the second half – probably in August, as per the usual schedule.

title: Sept. 2026 Android Drop: Find Hub ‘Remembered’ list, Motion Assist, & Keep in Google Messages
snippet: Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features.

Find Hub Remembered

Find Hub and Gemini can now keep track of things that don’t have a tracker tag on them. You can now tell “Gemini to remember where you placed important items.” For example, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer,” with the ability to add a photo. 

The location will be saved to a new “Remembered” tab in the Find Hub app. You can also ask Gemini for its location with a voice command. This is rolling out on Android 16+.

Motion Assist

Motion Assist on Android 17+ will help reduce motion sickness with a subtle bubble overlay on your screen that moves with the vehicle. This is “designed to help bridge the gap between what your eyes see and the movement of your ride.”

	

You can customize the color, shape, and opacity. There’s also an option to have the color and shape change every few seconds.

Android can enable Motion Assist automatically when movement in a car, bus, or train is detected, while there’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut.

Gemini Live Guided Vision

Gemini Live is adding Guided Vision to offer verbal “descriptions of what’s in front of you.” Use cases include “reading fine print on a food label, ordering from a menu in a low-lit restaurant, or locating household objects.”

If your camera isn’t lined up, voice feedback will guide you to reframe, pan across a space, or center an object so you get the answers you need. 

Guided Vision is available as an Accessibility shortcut or via the TalkBack menu. This is “coming soon to phones running Android 9+ in countries where Gemini is available.”

Google Messages Keep integration

Following the wide rollout of Chat themes, Google Messages is adding Google Keep integration. This lets you “share and update grocery lists or vacation notes right inside your chat.”

A “Create list” suggestion and ‘plus’ menu shortcut will bring up a sheet that lets you start creating. Once done, the list will appear inline as a shared note. This integration is rolling out starting today.
